D.3
TRAIL
Data and trace representation.
We evaluate on 148 annotated traces from TRAIL
(117 from GAIA and 31 from SWE-bench Lite). TRAIL’s errors were
annotated independently of Sauron, so its real failures from other agents and task domains
complement the injected faults of
PA
Fault
\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{Fault}}
.
Evaluation uses the recorded traces, without access to the
original execution environments. The adapter converts TRAIL’s
nested spans into the event representation described in
Section
B.1
,
retaining their original identifiers and parent relationships.
Tool spans become linked call and result events, while model
spans retain their recorded inputs and outputs.
Preserving the span identifiers allows evidence references
to be mapped back to TRAIL’s annotated locations.
Category-to-criterion adaptation.
Each trace receives a rubric with one criterion for each of
TRAIL’s 21 error categories. Each criterion states that the
trace contains no error of that category and includes a brief
category description and instructions for locating supporting
evidence. Its reference label is
unmet
when the
annotations contain at least one error of that category,
and
met
otherwise. A criterion can yield multiple
error locations through its verified evidence atoms.
Baseline inputs.
Gandalf receives the same 21 criteria as Sauron, together
with the original task request and final response.
Its workspace contains both the original TRAIL trace and
a flattened event representation, preserving the original
span identifiers. It can inspect these files through its
existing tools and is instructed to cite the relevant span
identifiers when reporting errors. We retain its batch-size
target of 16. Judge
TRAIL
uses the benchmark’s
released evaluation prompt, receiving the full original
trace in one model call and returning error categories
and span locations. Both baselines use the same models
as Sauron.
Evidence-to-span mapping.
For Sauron, we map the event identifiers in the verified atoms
cited by each
unmet
verdict to the original TRAIL span
identifiers. Each resulting span is paired with the criterion’s
error category. We retain all distinct span–category pairs,
so a criterion can identify multiple locations and a span
can carry multiple categories. An
unmet
verdict without
a verified atom locating the error produces no error prediction,
either for the category or for its location.
For Gandalf, we extract all valid span identifiers cited in
its rationale or evidence and pair them with the criterion’s
category. Judge
TRAIL
provides span–category
pairs directly in its structured output.
Location normalization.
TRAIL can record one interaction across a step, a model call,
and a tool call. Before scoring, we apply the same location
mapping to all three verifiers to use a consistent span
convention. For reasoning and planning errors, step citations
map to the last model call within that step. Tool citations,
and steps without a model call, map to the nearest preceding
model call. For system-execution errors, step citations map
to the first tool call within the step. Existing model-call
citations and citations without an applicable target remain
unchanged. We remove duplicate span–category pairs after
mapping. This procedure uses no reference annotations and
leaves category-level wF1 unchanged.
Scoring.
We apply TRAIL’s official scorer to the normalized predictions,
reporting GAIA and SWE-bench Lite separately.
For each category, F1 measures its presence or absence across
traces, and wF1 weights these scores by the number of traces
annotated with that category. Location accuracy measures
recovery of distinct annotated span identifiers, while joint
accuracy requires both the span and category to match.
Both are computed per trace and averaged equally across
traces. Location and joint accuracy measure recall of annotated
errors and complement wF1, which also reflects false category
predictions. Sauron’s span predictions come only from locations
cited by verified atoms.
For all verifiers, runs producing no predictions remain in
the evaluation with empty prediction sets, and usable partial
outputs are retained.

Ablation Details
Evaluation set.
PA
Abl
\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{Abl}}
combines 506 rubric criteria from 20 episodes in
PA
100
\mathrm{PA}_{100}

Fault
\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{Fault}}
,
sampled with stratification by fault family, giving 860
verification decisions in total. The two parts
use disjoint source episodes and retain the reference labels
from their respective suites. Since process criteria account
for only about 16% of
PA
100
\mathrm{PA}_{100}
, adding fault and control variants
provides more cases that require checking the execution
process. This gives us a compact evaluation covering both
outcome and process verification.
Evidence access and navigation.
State only
(trace-blind) disables the investigator’s trace-query
tools while retaining access to the final response, state,
and artifacts.
Trace in context
places the full execution
trace, without truncation, directly in the investigator’s context and removes
trace-query tools, while retaining state and artifact queries.
No gist
removes gist generation and its advisory
context from investigation sessions.
Evidence verification.
No faithfulness checker
retains mechanical checks but
accepts other claims once their cited sources are retrieved,
without assessing whether those sources support the claims.
No mechanical checks
routes all claims to the
faithfulness checker.
No claim verification
disables both kinds of checks, accepting claims once their
cited sources are retrieved. All three variants retain
source-locator validation, the evidence store, and verdict
finalization.
Joint investigation.
Unclustered
runs a separate investigation session for
each criterion. Each session maintains its own context and
evidence store, so retrieved content and verified atoms
cannot be reused across criteria. All other settings,
including the gist and budget-setting rule, remain unchanged.

article.headline: 证据先行的智能体验证器在多项基准领先
article.lede: Scale AI 的 Sauron 先独立核验状态与轨迹中的证据再下判定，在八个骨干模型上 F1 均最高、成本更低。
article.problem: 长程、半可验证的智能体任务常用评分准则（rubric）来评判，但判断所需的证据分散在最终环境状态和执行轨迹里，常规模板式 LLM 评审只能看到被放进输入的那部分证据。评审可能找错地方漏掉证据，或接受没有来源支撑的说法，其中就包括智能体自己声称的成功。当准则判定被当作强化学习奖励时，这类错误会直接强化不良行为，形成奖励攻击。
article.method: Sauron 把「调查」与「核验」拆成两步：轻量规划模型按可能共享的证据把准则聚类并生成任务提要，每个簇由一名调查员通过有界查询按需读取状态、轨迹和产物，提出待验证的 claim。独立的证据核验器用定位符取回原始来源，精确声明做机械比对，解释性声明交给只能看到该声明与引用片段的隔离忠实性检查器，被拒的 claim 会带原因退回。最终只有已验证 claim 支持的判定才被终结器接受，每条准则都附带列明证据的收据。
article.results: 在含 2,586 条人工标注准则的 100 个个人助理 episode（PA100）上，Sauron 在全部八个骨干模型上取得五个验证器中最高的 F1，且成本低于最强基线 Gandalf；以 GPT-5.6 Sol 为例，F1 为 0.96 对 0.92、MCC 0.94 对 0.89，成本低 23%，过程类准则上为 0.97 对 0.90。在 13 个故障族、637 对故障-对照的 PAFault 上，它检出 97% 的注入故障、只误报 2% 的干净对照（Δfault=0.95），而拿到完整轨迹的 Gandalf 与 Autorubric 分别只有 0.67 和 0.71。TRAIL 上以 GPT-5.6 Sol 跑 GAIA 子集，wF1、定位准确率、联合准确率分别为 0.53、0.73、0.44，高于两个基线的 0.46、0.55、0.25。
article.why_it_matters: 如果准则判定要当 RL 奖励用，验证器就必须把判定钉在可核查的证据上，而不是相信智能体的自述，否则策略会学会只把报告写得漂亮。Sauron 的 claim 级核验加证据收据给出了一条可审计、成本可控的路径。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖英文任务，PA100 与 PAFault 均来自单一智能体（Opus 4.8）的个人助理场景；故障注入是人工构造的，并不能证明它对专门针对 Sauron 优化的策略依然稳健。在 TRAIL 上 Sauron 成本是基线的两到三倍，作者也承认有界查询在需要覆盖整条轨迹的错误检测任务上省不了多少；65 例与人工判定不一致的案例中有 48 例源于判读比标注者更严格。
article.figure_caption_zh: Sauron 架构：两步轻量规划按可能共享的证据对准则聚类并生成提示性任务提要，每个簇并行开展一次调查会话，调查员经有界查询访问轨迹与状态并提出 claim，证据核验器逐条对照来源校验后写入证据库，判定终结器只在已验证 claim 支持时接受判定，每条准则都附证据收据。

figure.caption: {Sauron architecture.} Two lightweight planning steps cluster the rubric criteria $C$ by likely shared evidence and produce an advisory task gist $g$. Each cluster runs as a parallel investigation session. The investigator reaches the trace $ $ and state $S$ through bounded queries and proposes claims. The evidence verifier checks each claim against its source, records the result in the session's evidence store, and returns rejected claims with a reason. The investigator separately proposes verdicts, and the verdict finalizer accepts one only when verified claims support it. Each criterion receives its own verdict and a receipt of the evidence it cites.

page_papers.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
page_papers.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.

Abstract
Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters.
To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone’s causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost.
This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge.

Introduction
Human brain encoding models predict neural responses to stimuli, providing computational insights into how the brain processes information.
State-of-the-art (SoTA) encoding models mostly follow a goal-driven paradigm
(
Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016
)
: a large model pretrained on behavioral tasks is used as a
frozen
feature extractor, and only a readout is learned from neural data
(
Adeli et al., 2025
;
Hwang et al., 2025
;
Gokce et al., 2026a
;
d’Ascoli et al., 2026
)
. This approach leverages strong pretrained priors, but misses the opportunity to exploit the backbone’s expressiveness to specialize for brain encoding.
Adapting large pretrained backbones with neural data promises to scale models to the complexity required to capture human brain computation, and to best combine neural information and behavioral task training. In practice, however, such adaptation is difficult, because neural data are costly and scarce relative to the size of contemporary models. Methods that do let neural data shape the representation have had mixed success. Training smaller models from scratch
(
St-Yves et al., 2023
;
Khosla and Wehbe, 2026

Low-rank adaptation won Algonauts 2023

Moreover, we show the adapted multimodal model remains interpretable. Prior work often identifies a region’s preferred modality by determining which unimodal encoder its readout relies on. With multimodal backbones, we instead use feature attribution to identify modality contribution, which recovers the canonical topography: early visual cortex is driven by video, and auditory and lateral temporal cortex by audio. Comparison with the frozen backbone shows that adaptation reweights the contributions of the three modalities, particularly increasing the contribution of the audio inputs, and increases cross-modal mixing within the backbone (§

Finally, to scale the number of adapted models, we develop a batched multi-LoRA kernel that trains many LoRAs jointly on one shared backbone, significantly reducing training time. This enables 200+ independently adapted models, whose ensemble ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard, surpassing unpublished entries as well. We additionally show that the ensemble performance is jointly governed by ensemble size, individual model quality, and model diversity (§

Discussion
Three axes for scaling PEFT for brain encoding.
Together, our results suggest three complementary scaling directions for future brain encoding models:
1) Scale up
the pretrained prior by leveraging increasingly capable backbones;
2) Scale down
the adaptation by updating only a small number of parameters; and
3) Scale out
by training a large number of lightweight adapters to shared backbones with various inductive biases
(
Mind Lab et al., 2026
)
. Together, PEFT turns a single powerful pretrained model into a family of specialized encoding models without training each backbone from scratch.
Toward a brain foundation model.
Our experiments do not constitute a brain foundation model, but scaling along the three directions discussed above could lead to one. A large pretrained backbone could use a single shared adapter trained on neural data spanning tasks, datasets, subjects, and even species. In this work, we only scale out the number of adapters for ensemble. However, future work could train a separate adapter for each task, dataset, subject, or even ROI with a hierarchical structure or with meta-learning.
Together, this hierarchical approach and the three scaling directions we discuss above can create a brain foundation model with efficient specializations for different downstream tasks.
Limitations.
Our models are trained on one benchmark with four subjects, all watching audiovisual narrative. The adapters transfer to a held-out subject (App.
19
) and to a second dataset (App.
20
), but neither test leaves the domain of narrative film. We leave the joint training on multiple datasets and modalities to future work.

article.headline: 用LoRA微调104B主干做大脑编码
article.lede: 冻结主干加读出渐遇瓶颈；作者用LoRA适配104B多模态主干，九个主干均提升，集成模型登顶Algonauts赛后榜。
article.problem: 当前最强的脑编码模型大多采用「目标驱动」范式：把在行为任务上预训练的大模型冻结，只从神经数据学习一个读出层。这样虽能利用强大的预训练先验，却无法让主干针对脑编码做特化；而神经数据昂贵稀缺，从头训练小模型尚未在全脑人类基准上达到SoTA，已有工作报告全量微调反而不如冻结主干。
article.method: 作者改用参数高效微调（PEFT）：在Qwen3-Omni的注意力模块中插入rank-16的LoRA，并只保留到第32层解码器，搭配线性或交叉注意力读出，训练后再对线性读出做闭式岭回归重拟合。为降低计算开销，他们利用主干的因果结构，一次前向预测多个时间点，取代滑动窗口，从而大幅减少特征提取成本；此外还实现了批量多LoRA内核，可在同一共享主干上联合训练大量适配器。
article.results: 方法在九种多模态主干上一致提升脑编码性能，最大适配到104B参数，为目前已报道适配脑编码的最大模型。主配置在Qwen3-Omni上仅引入8.91M个LoRA可训练参数，读出为52.3M参数；交叉注意力读出把约19.3k个token池化为894个向量，交叉注意力版本改用约3.2k个token、只增加0.2M参数。在与先前SoTA相同的Qwen3-Omni主干上，BrainLoRA成为已发表方法中的新SoTA，但摘要与引言未给出具体提升数值，论文未给出具体数字（种子间波动阈值为0.00077）。用批量多LoRA训练出200多个独立适配模型，其集成在Algonauts赛后公开榜单排名第一，超过未发表条目；在1,000个脑区、四名被试的CNeuroMod/Algonauts 2025数据上评测。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「一个强预训练主干」变成「一族专用脑编码模型」：不改动主干权重就能特化，还能廉价地批量复制出集成所需的大量模型；特征归因显示适配后仍保留视觉—听觉的经典地形，只是音频贡献与跨模态混合增强，说明性能提升并非以可解释性为代价。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖一个基准、四名被试，且全部是观看视听叙事影片（《老友记》）；适配器虽能迁移到留出被试和第二个数据集，但都未离开叙事影片这一域。另外，摘要未报告相对先前SoTA的具体提升幅度，部分读出消融（如门控MLP读出+0.0007、池化特征上的交叉注意力+0.00030）落在0.00077的种子波动内，无法可靠区分。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从冻结主干到PEFT：作者提出放大、缩小、扩展三条规模化路径，分别对应更强的主干先验、更小的适配器和更多不同专长的适配器。

The backbone prior is strong, but it is not specialized for brain encoding. {(b)}~We advocate using PEFT to adapt strong pretrained backbones, retaining the powerful prior while allowing flexible neural adaptation. This suggests three complementary scaling directions: {Scale up} to stronger priors leveraging more capable backbones; {Scale down} the size of trainable adapters for brain encoding with limited data; and {Scale out} the number of adapters with different specializations.

page_papers.title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
page_papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects.
Interlock
compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00–4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20–6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89–4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.
1
Introduction
Long-horizon agents increasingly work with records, rules, resources, and partially completed artifacts. A short request can require reconciling conflicting evidence, determining which objects need attention, selecting a feasible plan, and updating several related results. The environment supplies the facts and constraints that determine this work. A decision can also activate further obligations: deferring an action may require an explanation and a handoff, while changing an allocation may require corresponding revisions to schedules and budgets. These obligations can outlive the interaction in which they are discovered: after many intervening reads, computations, and edits, the agent must still apply the earlier evidence and decisions to every affected result.
Local progress can coexist with an incomplete outcome (Figure
1
). A correct decision can leave necessary consequences unfulfilled, and mutually consistent outputs can share an unsupported assumption. These failures concern the relationships that connect evidence, decisions, and the requested outcome. They motivate our central question:
how can task synthesis preserve conditional obligations and turn their fulfillment into transferable training experience?

We characterize this structure as a typed completion graph.
Grounding
connects environmental evidence and rules to the decisions they support.
Coupling
links components that must share a feasible choice or satisfy a joint constraint.
Realization
connects a decision to every downstream record, artifact, or state that must reflect it. Their interaction is especially demanding over long executions: an early finding can constrain work completed many interactions later, and a revised decision can require coordinated changes to several existing artifacts.
Task synthesis and environment generation provide a scalable basis for agent training. Prior work constructs verified tool-use data
(
Qin et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2024
)
, generates environments and task scenarios
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Song et al., 2026
)
, and composes extended tasks through tool dependencies and reusable workflows
(
Tu et al., 2026
;
Shi et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Common specifications can also align instructions, environments, and verifiers
(
Ivanov and Rana, 2026
)
. Our organizing unit is the complete set of conditional obligations for an outcome. It determines both the unresolved work placed in an environment and the evidence needed to accept the result.
We propose
Interlock
to make this graph an explicit synthesis constraint. Reusable domain descriptions and archetype contracts define evidence roles, task-specific decisions and shared states, joint conditions, and downstream consumers. Three generation roles compile the same graph into a workspace, task/contract, and rubric while leaving concrete associations and decisions to the agent. A source-coverage review traces every typed relation from the original graph through these artifacts; a public-input critic independently checks whether the resulting criteria are supported by solver-visible materials and assessable from execution artifacts. Completion-filtered training then selects executions that realize every applicable effect.
Our evaluation connects task structure, execution behavior, and training utility. Statistical analyses and case studies examine dependencies and completion failures. The training protocol uses Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B separately, retaining each model’s own accepted rollouts for SFT of that same model. Both backbones improve on AutomationBench, JobBench Main and Easy, and Harvey LAB. Gains over the original checkpoints reach 4.00–4.50 percentage points in AutomationBench task pass rate, 3.20–6.64 points in JobBench weighted score, and 3.89–4.16 percentage points in Harvey LAB criterion pass rate. These results show that experience from complete synthetic executions transfers to independently authored tasks across different environments. Our contributions are threefold:
•
A typed representation of task completion.
We model long-horizon tasks as completion graphs whose grounding, coupling, and realization relations connect public evidence, consequential decisions, joint constraints, and required effects.
•
Graph-grounded synthesis and review.
We compile the same graph into the environment, task specification, deliverable contract, and outcome criteria, with complementary reviews for source coverage and public support.
•
Empirical validation of training utility.
We evaluate the generated experience through completion-filtered fine-tuning of two backbones and measure transfer across three external benchmarks.

Main Results
Interlock-RFT achieves the highest score in every evaluation column for both backbones (Table
1
), outperforming the original checkpoints and ClawGym-SFT. Each backbone is trained on its own accepted trajectories, and the gains extend across coordinated API execution, professional deliverables, and legal work.
For Qwen3.6-27B,
Interlock
improves AutomationBench task pass rate by 4.00 percentage points, JobBench Main and Easy weighted scores by 4.35 and 6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rate by 3.89 percentage points over the original checkpoint. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the gains are 4.50 percentage points on AutomationBench, 3.20 and 4.31 score points on JobBench Main and Easy, and 4.16 percentage points on Harvey LAB. Operating recovery.
A four-week recovery plan must reconcile supply, order commitments,
and financial effects. In attempt 1, Qwen3.6-27B allocates 970 HX units against
770 available; advancing an inbound shipment changes its arrival time,
not the total supply. Its 3,920-kit plan also exceeds 3,250 shared trays,
partially serves an unsplittable 230-unit order, and omits a selected
$6,800 expedite cost from contribution margin despite recording the
cash outflow. In attempt 2, the same model uses 760 HX units, caps kits at
3,250, excludes the whole unsplittable order, and deducts its own
selected action costs.
Training schedules.
The February 2026 training cycle links due employees, shift availability,
instructor credentials, and publication records. Attempt 1 of Qwen3.6-27B produces
matching schedule and publication rows but omits two of six due
trainees, schedules a 12:00–14:00 class outside an 08:00–11:30 release
window, and assigns an instructor on February 16 whose credential
expires on February 12. Attempt 2 of the same model retains all six
trainees, uses a shared 09:30–11:30 window, and schedules that
instructor on February 11. Appendix

5
Conclusion
Interlock
organizes long-horizon task synthesis around typed completion graphs. Grounding, coupling, and realization relations constrain how public evidence, consequential decisions, joint conditions, and required effects are compiled into task environments and outcome criteria. Dual-view review checks both graph preservation and public support, while completion-filtered RFT selects executions that realize every applicable graph effect. Training improves both Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B across AutomationBench, JobBench Main and Easy, and Harvey LAB, supporting the value of complete synthetic execution experience for transfer across task environments.
AI use statement
We used generative AI tools to assist with prompt design and manuscript
preparation, including language polishing, bilingual editing, and the
preparation of figures and captions. As described in
Section
3
, AI agents are integral to the task synthesis and
training-data collection procedure: they generate initial workspaces,
task instructions, and outcome rubrics; review task requirements and
quality; execute tasks; and assess the resulting artifacts. The roles
and verification procedures for these agents are documented in the
methodology and experimental setup. We have manually reviewed all
AI-assisted work, including manuscript revisions, prompts, generated
task materials, and execution and evaluation records. We take

analyses, claims, and artifacts produced with AI assistance.

Appendix I
Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Agents
Long-horizon benchmarks provide concrete settings in which successful interaction must produce the requested outcome.
WebArena
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
and OSWorld
(
Xie et al., 2024
)
evaluate realistic web and desktop tasks with execution-based outcome checks.
AppWorld
(
Trivedi et al., 2024
)
tests stateful multi-application coding and unintended changes, and ToolSandbox
(
Lu et al., 2025
)
emphasizes implicit state dependencies and intermediate milestones.

WorkArena++
(
Boisvert et al., 2024
)
targets compositional planning and reasoning in knowledge work, while TheAgentCompany
(
Xu et al., 2026a
)
combines websites, code execution, and workplace communication.

(
Merrill et al., 2026
)
couples challenging command-line tasks with dedicated environments and tests, and Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench
(
Li et al., 2026c
)
evaluates extended workflows with graded subtasks and partial credit.
Their emphasis on coordinated work and outcome evaluation complements
Interlock
’s focus on preserving completion requirements during task synthesis.
Our external evaluations span three forms of consequential work.
AutomationBench
(
Shepard and Salimans, 2026
)
brings together cross-application orchestration, autonomous API discovery, and layered policy compliance.
JobBench
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
evaluates expert-prioritized delegations in heterogeneous reference workspaces using fact-anchored chains of binary rubric criteria.
Harvey LAB
(
Harvey AI, 2026
)
evaluates legal work in document-rich matter workspaces through deliverable-specific binary criteria covering factual support, analysis, and required content.
Using each benchmark’s own evaluation protocol, these independently authored tasks assess the downstream value of the synthesized environments and data for agents facing new evidence, constraints, and required effects.

article.headline: Interlock：用完成图约束长程任务合成
article.lede: Interlock 把长程任务表示为带类型的完成图，再编译成工作区、请求与评分标准，只保留全部要求达成的执行轨迹用于微调
article.problem: 长程智能体常在碎片化证据和半完成状态中工作，可能满足了单条要求，却漏掉这些要求之间的关系：决策是否真有证据支撑、多个决策能否同时成立、决策是否落实到所有下游产物。这类「局部正确、整体未完成」的失败，根源是任务完成取决于证据、决策与所需效果之间的条件性义务，而现有任务合成多围绕工具依赖或技能关系组织生成。
article.method: Interlock 把每个任务写成带类型的完成图：grounding 边把公开证据和规则连到决策，coupling 超边给出跨组件的联合约束，realization 边列出决策必须产生的下游效果；三个生成角色再把同一张图编译成初始工作区 W0、公开请求 q 和私有评分标准 V。随后做两类互补复核（成果保留性检查与公开输入支持性检查），并用有终端权限的 agent-as-judge 实际执行、按需写并运行验证脚本，只把全部必需 criteria 通过的轨迹留作 rejection-sampling 微调。
article.results: 语料保留 3,278 个任务（覆盖 128 个 domain、484 个 task family），两个 backbone 各 5 次尝试共 32,780 次执行，其中 32,370 次正常终止，每个 backbone 各取 8,957 条自己接受的轨迹、约 154M 监督 token。相对原 checkpoint，Qwen3.6-27B 的 AutomationBench 任务通过率由 14.33% 升至 18.33%（+4.00 个百分点），JobBench Main/Easy 加权分分别 +4.35、+6.64，Harvey LAB criterion 通过率 73.96%→77.85%（+3.89）；Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 分别为 9.00→13.50（+4.50）、+3.20 与 +4.31、54.18→58.34（+4.16）。合成轨迹平均 84,293 token、27.63 个 assistant turn、42.10 次工具调用，约为 ClawGym 轨迹（14,940 / 11.92 / 14.76）的 5.64×、2.32×、2.85×；把文本 judge 换成 agent-as-judge，判官平均输出从 11.03k token 升到 12.28k token（+11.3%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「任务完成」建模成证据、决策与下游效果之间的条件性义务，而不是一组互相独立的 criterion，并初步证明这种从完整合成执行中学到的经验能迁移到三个独立编写的外部基准。若成立，就为长程智能体提供了一条不依赖人工标注、可规模化的训练数据路径。
article.limitations: 增益都是个位数百分点，AutomationBench 上两个 backbone 的绝对通过率仍只有 18.33% 和 13.50%，JobBench 两个子集各仅 65 个任务，且 JobBench 与 Harvey LAB 均由 GPT-5.5 担任 judge；论文未给出主结果在多次运行下的方差或显著性检验。此外，任务由 LLM agent 合成和审核，作者没有报告评审漏放的比率，评测本身也部分依赖模型判分。

page_papers.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose RSIFlow, a Recursive Self-Improvement framework that integrates adaptive workflow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose
RSIFlow
, a
R
ecursive
S
elf-
I
mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work
flow
orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.
Figure 1:
Motivation of RSIFlow.
(A) Two coupled challenges in RSI.
(B) The execution loop of RSIFlow.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answering
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Schick et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2023
)
. To continuously enhance the development of agents’ capabilities in task domains, existing methods have adopted complementary approaches, including evolving execution harnesses
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, optimizing model parameters
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
, and refining executable artifacts
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
. These routes can be organized into self-improvement workflows that propose and evaluate changes using task feedback. Beyond executing such workflows, recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Duan et al., 2026
)
.
Research on agent self-improvement spans three increasingly broad scopes of optimization. Component-level approaches optimize a predefined part of the system, such as the model or the harness (execution workflows)
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. System-level approaches coordinate updates across components, including joint model–harness optimization and feedback-driven selection of update targets
(
Chen et al., 2026d
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
. Meta-level approaches make improvement procedures editable through operator scheduling, program modification, and recursive skill evolution
(
Tan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. These developments expand both what can be modified and how modifications are organized. However, broader editability alone does not establish how effectively a workflow addresses the agent’s current bottlenecks, or whether the ability to organize that workflow improves with experience. This motivates a central question:
how can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize these workflows more effectively?
We formulate this challenge as
dynamic workflow adaptation
in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks and evolving workflow orchestration must be considered together. As illustrated in Fig.
1
, self-improvement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks that vary with task requirements and the agent’s capability state. Even within a fixed domain, successful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestration. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself a capability that can improve through experience. Feedback from workflow execution supports the accumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution. These processes form a feedback loop: task-level updates reshape improvement requirements, while workflow experience refines the orchestration capability that guides subsequent updates.
To address this challenge, we propose
RSIFlow
, a framework that couples
adaptive workflow orchestration
with
meta-agent capability evolution
. We instantiate three self-improvement workflows targeting the
Harness
,
Model
, and
Artifacts
. A meta-agent uses execution trajectories and environmental feedback to diagnose the task agent’s bottlenecks, select a workflow, and orchestrate candidate generation and validation. It then distills orchestration outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles to revise its own harness, including execution procedures and skill invocation. This experience-driven self-revision closes a recursive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that guides subsequent improvements.
Our main contributions are:
•
We formulate
dynamic workflow adaptation
as a key challenge in RSI, highlighting the coupling between evolving performance bottlenecks and continual refinement of workflow orchestration.
•
We propose
RSIFlow
, which adaptively organizes self-improvement workflows and uses their observed outcomes to evolve the meta-agent’s own harness, including its execution procedures and reusable skills.
•
We evaluate
RSIFlow
across six benchmarks and two backbones, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of the 12 benchmark–backbone settings. Ablations support the benefits of both adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution.
2
Related Work
Component-Specific Self-Improvement.
Many approaches to agent self-improvement optimize a single predefined component. STaR
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
)
improves model parameters by repeatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers. AFlow
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories. Related approaches include DSPy
(
Khattab et al., 2024
)
for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
for meta-agent-guided search over agent programs. In contrast, AlphaEvolve
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s improvement procedure. Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
iteratively revises outputs using self-feedback, while Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
accumulates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
and HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization. Their coupled updates address model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks.
Figure 2:
Overview of RSIFlow.
(A)
Definition of task domains and agent workflows.
(B)
The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback.
(C)
The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows.
(D)
Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness.
The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.
Adaptive and Recursive Self-Improvement.
Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
uses trajectory and performance feedback to choose between harness and weight updates, while its selection policy relies on a frozen language-model prior. HASE
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
integrates task solving and harness editing into one action space and trains the policy with GRPO. A complementary direction makes the improver itself editable: Hyperagents
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
co-evolves task-agent and meta-agent programs and demonstrates transferable improvement strategies, whereas MetaSkill-Evolve
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
recursively updates task skills and their improvement procedures on different timescales. Building on these complementary directions, RSIFlow couples bottleneck-aware workflow orchestration with feedback-driven Meta-Harness evolution.

Ablation Study
Table

evaluates adaptive workflow orchestration and Meta-Agent evolution over five rounds. Compared with Vanilla, RSIFlow improves Code, Tool Use, and SearchQA by 19.04%, 3.92%, and 18.20% , respectively, increasing the three-domain average by 13.72 %. While fixed-component workflows exhibit domain-specific strengths, adaptive orchestration achieves the highest scores across all three domains, outperforming the fixed workflow by 4.13% - 8.81% on average. Overall, RSIFlow exceeds the average of all four ablated variants by 6.17 %. Disabling Meta-Agent evolution reduces average performance by 5.74 % , highlighting the importance of distilling historical feedback into reusable skills and principles. These results demonstrate that adaptive component orchestration enables balanced cross-domain improvements, while experience-driven Meta-Harness evolution further strengthens workflow effectiveness.

Rollout-budget and performance efficiency.
Fig.
3
compares performance under varying rollout budgets on all six benchmarks. RSIFlow generally lies on or near the empirical
Pareto frontier and achieves the highest observed score on each
benchmark. This advantage is consistent with its adaptive component
selection and Task–Meta co-evolution: RSIFlow reuses rollout
evidence to guide targeted updates to the Task-Agent’s Model,
Harness, or Artifacts, rather than relying solely on additional
exploration under a fixed harness. The co-evolving Meta-Agent
further distills workflow outcomes into reusable skills and
refines its improvement procedure, allowing accumulated experience
to guide subsequent updates. Together, these mechanisms help
concentrate the rollout budget on informed workflow orchestration. Overall, RSIFlow offers a stronger performance–budget trade-off than the evaluated baselines.
Meta-agent backbone sensitivity.
We evaluate RSIFlow with three Meta-Agent backbones over five evolution rounds on HumanEval+. As shown in Fig.
4
, all three models achieve overall performance improvements, with gains of 11.48%, 5.09%, and 24.41% for Claude-Sonnet-5, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and GPT-5.6-Sol, respectively. GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest final performance of 68.29%, albeit with greater API token consumption. From Round 3 to Round 5, it improves by 13.08%, compared with 6.15% and 4.17% for the other two backbones, suggesting that stronger Meta-Agents may better leverage accumulated intervention feedback. These results demonstrate that RSIFlow supports different Meta-Agent backbones, while the Meta-Agent’s underlying capabilities influence the cumulative effectiveness of recursive self-improvement.
Meta-evolution necessity analysis.
Table 3 compares different Meta versions improving the same initial Task-Agent, with scores averaged over two benchmarks per domain. Meta0 improves SearchQA by 10.10%, reaching 44.62% through harness updates. Although Meta4 also selects the harness, it further outperforms Meta0 by 20.56% and 9.51% on Code and SearchQA, respectively. Meta3 achieves the highest Tool Use score of 31.83% through artifact updates. These results indicate that the evolution of meta-agent capabilities not only enables better adaptive workflow orchestration but also enhances the performance of workflow orchestration across different task domains. 5
Conclusion
We presented
RSIFlow
, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling adaptive workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show a favorable performance–budget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual Meta-Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.
Limitations
RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This setting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained agent deployments, where adaptive workflow orchestration enables targeted modifications to identified bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evolution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and orchestration capabilities. However, whether these benefits remain significant with larger backbone models and at cluster scale remains unexplored. Future work will extend the evaluation to larger-scale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow.
RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable skills and general principles to improve workflow orchestration without updating the Meta-Agent’s model parameters. However, this process introduces additional computational overhead, while adopting a lower-cost Meta-Agent may compromise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains to be fully investigated. Future work will explore counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent deficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to improve evolution efficiency and stability.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup
We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix
B
gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes.
A.1
Training and Reporting Data
Our evolution pool contains 3,000 distinct training tasks,
partitioned into five task-disjoint batches of 600 tasks each.
Each round uses 200 code-generation tasks, 200 tool-use tasks,
and 200 multi-hop questions. The fixed reporting set contains
744 tasks. Table
4
gives the
dataset-level allocation.
Code generation.
TACO
Li et al. (2023)
contains algorithmic programming problems that
require implementing a program from a natural-language
specification and satisfying its input/output contract.
We use 1,000 training problems from the TACO portion of the
DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset
.
The selected tasks include standard-input/output and
function-based interfaces, with correctness assessed by
executing the submitted program against task-specific tests.
They provide execution trajectories and feedback for
improving program construction, interface handling, and
algorithmic reasoning. The allocation contributes 200 tasks
per evolution round; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are reserved for
reporting evaluation.
Tool use.
EnvScaler
Song et al. (2026)
provides executable, stateful environments
in which agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls.
Each task specifies a user goal and an initial environment
state; the agent must choose tools, construct arguments, and
adapt its actions to returned observations. Task-specific
validation checks assess whether the resulting state satisfies
the goal.
We allocate 1,000 scenarios to training, comprising 824 from
the source dataset’s
train
split and 176 from its
heldout
split. Both source partitions are assigned to
the training role in our study; tool-use reporting uses
BFCL-v3 and ACEBench. Each evolution round contains 200
EnvScaler scenarios. Different training tasks may share an
environment, so the round-disjoint allocation refers to task
instances rather than environment families.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
contains
questions that require combining evidence across Wikipedia
passages, including bridge and comparison questions.
2WikiMultiHopQA
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
requires following multi-hop relations across entities and
combining the retrieved facts into an answer. We select 500
questions from the official training split of each dataset.
The Task-Agent retrieves evidence through the search interface
and produces an answer, providing trajectories for improving
evidence retrieval and multi-step reasoning. Each round uses
100 HotpotQA and 100 2WikiMultiHopQA training questions.
Reporting uses a separate fixed set of 100 questions from
each dataset’s official development split.

A.2
Benchmark Descriptions
The reporting set contains 744 tasks: 342 code-generation tasks, 202 tool-use tasks, and 200 multi-hop questions. Each method is evaluated on the same task IDs with the same benchmark-specific scorer. Table
5
summarizes the task counts and reported metrics.
Code generation.
HumanEval+
asks the agent to implement a Python function from its signature and natural-language specification. Its 164 tasks test functional correctness, including edge cases exposed by the augmented EvalPlus tests
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
MBPP+
asks for short Python programs from natural-language descriptions and illustrative tests, covering basic algorithms, data structures, and program construction. We use a frozen 178-task subset of MBPP+ v0.2.0.
For both benchmarks, a task succeeds when the final submitted program passes the base and augmented test suites. We report system pass@1: one final submission per task after the allowed agent execution. HumanEval+ uses v0.1.10, and both benchmarks use EvalPlus revision
26d6d00
with the recorded parser and process-isolation adapters.
Tool use.
BFCL-v3
evaluates function selection and argument construction in single-call, multiple-call, parallel-call, relevance, and multi-turn settings
(
Patil et al., 2025
)
. These settings cover complementary aspects of tool use: selecting an appropriate function, supplying the required arguments, coordinating multiple calls, and determining whether an available tool is relevant to the request. The multi-turn tasks also test whether the agent maintains context across stateful tool interactions, connecting individual call decisions to the evolving interaction history. Our subset contains 152 tasks across 17 categories; native category-specific checks determine correctness, and the aggregate is weighted by the number of tasks. This weighting reflects the composition of the evaluated subset, with categories containing more tasks contributing proportionally more to the reported aggregate.
ACEBench
evaluates API use under Normal, Special, and Agent settings, including ordinary function calls, incomplete or ambiguous instructions, and multi-step interactions
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
. Together, these settings examine how agents translate user requests into API actions under different instruction and interaction conditions. We use 50 English tasks, which produce 57 native scoring records. We report the native weighted score and separately retain complete-task success; these quantities use different denominators. The distinction matters because one task can contribute more than one native scoring record. Record-level scoring describes the evaluator’s individual scoring units, whereas complete-task success summarizes outcomes at the original task level. We therefore specify both task and scoring-record counts when describing this evaluation.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
requires combining evidence from multiple Wikipedia passages to answer bridge or comparison questions
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
. We use 100 development questions with the v1 fullwiki protocol.
2WikiMultiHopQA
requires composing facts about multiple entities along multi-hop reasoning chains
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
; we use 100 development questions and the original v1 evaluator.
These tasks test whether agents can connect dispersed evidence and resolve questions requiring relational reasoning.
For both benchmarks, the agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and submits an answer. The main metric is normalized answer-token F1, with exact match (EM) retained separately. The evaluator revisions are
3635853
for HotpotQA and
13800e5
for 2WikiMultiHopQA.

A.3
Training–Evaluation Separation
We separate training-time evolution from evaluation on the
744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon
n
n
, we first complete
n
n
rounds on training tasks and then
evaluate the resulting system on the reporting set. Reporting
tasks are excluded from Task-model fine-tuning. Reporting-set
scores and item-level evaluation feedback are never used for
workflow selection, candidate acceptance, skill maintenance,
Meta-Harness revision, or manual selection of system versions.
Evaluations at different horizons measure the corresponding
training-derived states; their results are not fed back into
subsequent evolution.
The gain-based acceptance
rule in the evolution algorithm applies only to training-time
batches. The batch-level Artifacts procedure, including its
two-attempt allowance and fallback to the parent, is not run on
the reporting set. During reporting, the skill library and
Meta-Harness remain fixed across tasks. Permitted environment
feedback includes execution-interface signals such as
context-length limit errors and output-length or format
violations; it does not provide access to the reporting
evaluator for optimization or output selection. Reference
answers and hidden-test correctness signals are likewise
excluded from generation and output selection. All compared
methods receive the same environment feedback, tool permissions,
and per-task execution budgets.
We additionally checked the frozen training and reporting
manifests for overlap in task identifiers, recorded normalized
prompt hashes, and recorded task-group identifiers, finding no
matches between the two sets. This check establishes separation
under these matching criteria; it does not assess semantic
paraphrases or contamination in the backbone models’
pretraining data. Equal per-task execution budgets likewise do
not imply equal total evolution cost.

A.4
Baseline Configurations
We compare seven baselines using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
. Within each backbone scale, the comparison protocol uses a common initial checkpoint and Task-Harness, task IDs, and evaluators. Table
6
summarizes editable Task components, weight training, Harness updates, adaptive component selection, and Meta-Agent evolution. These dimensions distinguish how each baseline allocates adaptation across model parameters, task components, and orchestration.
Model updates.
SFT
trains on successful Task-Agent trajectories while keeping the Harness fixed.
GRPO
samples groups of trajectories, scores their task outcomes, and updates the model using group-relative rewards
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
. Both methods improve the Task model without a component-selection mechanism.
Harness and joint updates.
AFlow
searches executable agent workflows through iterative proposal and evaluation
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
MermaidFlow
represents workflows as graphs and searches their structure
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
. These are the Harness-only configurations used in the main comparison.
HarnessForge
combines feedback-guided Harness modification with model training in a prescribed co-adaptation procedure
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
.
SIA
uses execution feedback to choose between Harness and model updates
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
.
Meta-Agent evolution.
HyperAgents
makes both the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent programs editable, allowing the improvement procedure itself to evolve
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
. Its code-editing mechanism differs from parameter training.
RSIFlow
selects among Model, Harness, and Artifacts interventions and updates its Meta-Harness through accumulated intervention skills. The comparison therefore separates access to multiple Task-update routes from the ability to revise the Meta-Agent that chooses and implements them.
A.5
Hyperparameter Settings
The main configuration uses Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-8B as the Task model and GPT-5.6 Sol as the Meta model. Each of the five evolution rounds permits at most two candidate attempts. Candidates share the same parent, training batch, and evaluator; the first valid candidate with positive paired gain is accepted. Meta model parameters remain fixed throughout evolution.

B.1

Algorithm
A.5

The loop has two coupled outputs: an accepted Task state and an updated improvement mechanism. Every candidate starts from the same round parent, so rejected edits do not accumulate. Failed implementation attempts and non-improving evaluations still enter the experience record. On a new task batch, task-bound outputs are generated anew; reusable knowledge is carried by the Meta-Harness and accepted changes to the Task model or Harness.
B.2
Workflow Orchestration
The Meta workflow connects six operations: evidence collection, diagnosis, skill retrieval, component intervention, paired evaluation, and skill integration. Diagnosis returns a bottleneck hypothesis with trajectory references; retrieval returns applicable procedures and counterexamples; intervention returns a candidate and its change record; evaluation returns paired outcomes; integration returns the next active skill set and the Action changes needed to use it.
A decision record binds the selected component to its expected behavioral effect and preservation constraints before construction. The Model branch receives eligible trajectories and a training configuration; the Harness branch receives a localized modification brief and interface contract; the Artifacts branch receives the Task’s own output and permitted feedback. Evaluation determines Task acceptance, while the entire record informs Meta evolution. An accepted Task change and a revised Meta procedure are thus separate decisions within the same loop.

Preserving Artifacts in this branch refers to the intervention scope; the candidate model generates its own outputs during evaluation. B.4
Harness Updates
Harness intervention changes how the agent executes tasks. Meta localizes a recurring execution defect, refines a modification brief, generates a complete implementation, and validates it. The functional components are Action, Skill, and Planning; concrete modules may implement context organization, action handling, memory retrieval, or verification. Localization identifies the mechanism to change, rather than merely listing files. Executable checks establish that a candidate can run. Acceptance additionally requires a positive paired task gain. An output-contract check can ensure that a coding task receives source code, whereas a receipt-grounded completion check can ensure that a tool operation has actually succeeded. These are changes to reusable execution behavior.

D.3
Component-Specific Skills and a General Principle
The cards in Appendix
F.3
present three component-specific procedures
and one general selection principle. The Harness and Model cards
summarize stored procedures and their observed feedback.
The Artifacts card formulates feedback-guided revision of the
Task-Agent’s own output under a limited budget. The final card
synthesizes how failure scope and intervention cost guide
component selection.
Applicability conditions determine when a procedure can be reused.
On a new task, Meta retrieves relevant revision guidance and
uses it to guide the Task-Agent in revising that task’s own output from its feedback.
The Artifacts procedure and general principle express
methodological guidance rather than additional measured
intervention outcomes.
Harness skills: repair a reusable execution rule.
The submission-contract skill applies when the required deliverable is source code but the agent returns prose or execution output. Its reusable content is the condition under which a complete-source check should be invoked and the execution behavior that enforces it. Reuse therefore changes how subsequent tasks are handled by the Harness. A valid submission can still contain an algorithmic error, so satisfying the output contract resolves an interface failure without establishing semantic correctness. This distinction explains why later feedback can motivate a different intervention route.
Model skills: construct an eligible learning signal.
The replay skill describes how verified successful Task-Agent calls become training examples. Checkpoint provenance, task identity, native success, and target validity determine whether a call provides suitable evidence for the update. Reusing this skill means applying the same data-selection and training procedure to the current parent and available trajectories. R4 supplements M1 because it provides another observed response to that procedure. The added evidence informs when replay is useful; it does not imply that increasing replay volume always improves every task domain.
Artifacts skills: revise the current deliverable.
The output-revision skill targets a defect that permitted feedback localizes within the Task-Agent’s current submission. Its steps operate through the existing interface: inspect the feedback, edit the relevant output, test the revision, and resubmit within budget. The reusable element is this conditional repair procedure, including the circumstances in which further retries are unlikely to help. A later task supplies its own program or answer and its own feedback. Thus, the skill can guide a new revision without transferring the earlier answer or changing the Task-Harness.
General principles: connect diagnosis to intervention scope.
A general principle connects these procedures through a shared decision criterion. The same failed coding task may require a submission check, learning from successful trajectories, or a local program edit. The relevant distinction is where the failure occurs and which available intervention can address it under the remaining budget. A bounded output repair is appropriate when the feedback identifies an actionable defect; a recurring execution problem motivates a Harness change, while a persistent capability gap with eligible training data motivates a Model update. The principle guides this comparison while component-specific skills supply the concrete procedure.

Updating a record and updating its invocation flow are recorded separately. The result is a changed Meta-Harness, not just a larger collection of text.
Reuse and generalization.
HHMMA illustrates knowledge development: H1 supplies a contract-checking criterion for H2 at R2; M1 accumulates training response evidence at R4; and R5 formulates a bounded output-repair procedure for local code defects. R2-to-R3 shifts from execution checks to Model updates when semantic errors persist. The case illustrates reuse within an evolving system; it does not isolate the causal contribution of an individual skill.
From a retrieved record to an executable intervention.
Retrieval provides Meta with a procedure; integration guides its use in the next attempt. Applicability informs diagnosis, procedures inform modification briefs, and preservation requirements constrain construction and validation. For example, a receipt-grounded skill links an unsupported completion claim to the evidence needed for assessment. The Harness change implements this check; paired evaluation determines whether it improves task outcomes. This chain connects the stored lesson to an intervention whose effects can be examined.
Using feedback to refine subsequent decisions.
Intervention responses inform library maintenance.
Improvements support procedures under observed conditions;
regressions reveal preservation failures.
Failed candidates can inform diagnosis even when the parent
Task state is retained. Supplementation adds evidence;
revision updates inappropriate guidance.
Task acceptance and Meta learning thus respond differently,
while lessons remain linked to their source cases.
Appendix E
Extended Related Work
Agent System Design and Adaptation.
Recent work on LLM agents explores approaches to adapting execution structures, maintaining persistent memory, and coordinating information acquisition. HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
jointly evolves execution harnesses and reasoning policies through failure-guided harness modification and harness-conditioned policy alignment. For persistent memory, All-Mem
(
Lv et al., 2026a
)
separates online retrieval from offline topology consolidation, preserving evidence while supporting retrieval under bounded computational budgets. Typed links enable budgeted expansion from anchors to archived evidence. For breadth-oriented information gathering, moreover, A-MapReduce
(
Chen et al., 2026c
)
decomposes wide-search objectives into parallel retrieval tasks and aggregates results, using experiential memory to refine task allocation and recomposition. These approaches improve how agents organize execution and retain or acquire information, with emphases on system compatibility, memory maintenance, and scalability.
Structured Supervision and Credit Assignment.
A complementary line of research studies the structure and granularity of supervision for agent learning and language model post-training. GEAR
(
Lv et al., 2026b
)
models prerequisite and activation dependencies among rubric criteria with a probabilistic graphical framework, suppressing unsupported criterion contributions when constructing scalar rewards. The resulting reward captures criterion dependencies at the response level. For long-horizon agent distillation, AlignOPSD
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
aligns privileged supervision with functionally corresponding decisions and distributes outcome-based credit across variable-duration decision spans and their constituent turns. TRCA
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
derives step-level supervision from action-induced state transitions using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics. Its foundational reward evaluates local transition quality, while its breakthrough reward recognizes newly satisfied task conditions, providing fine-grained learning signals without requiring successful reference trajectories or learned process evaluators, even when terminal success feedback is sparse.

article.headline: RSIFlow：元智能体自进化编排改进工作流
article.lede: 六个基准、两个骨干上 11/12 设置领先，总体 51.21% 与 59.86%，比最强基线高 6.06 与 3.86
article.problem: 递归自我改进（RSI）把优化对象从任务能力扩展到改进机制本身，但现有方法多在预设组件或固定的模型—harness 交替顺序上做更新。性能瓶颈会随任务要求和智能体当前能力状态漂移，而「如何组织改进流程」本身也是一种可随经验提升的能力，二者如何耦合仍是开放问题。
article.method: RSIFlow 让任务智能体执行任务、收集轨迹与环境反馈，元智能体据此诊断瓶颈，在 Model、Harness、Artifacts 三种组件特定改进工作流中选择其一，并编排候选的生成与验证；每轮最多两次尝试，首个有效且配对增益为正的候选被接受，否则沿用父代。随后系统把编排结果蒸馏为组件特定技能与跨组件原则，用来改写元智能体自身的 Meta-Harness（执行接口、技能检索与调用），而元智能体的模型参数始终固定。
article.results: 在 HumanEval+、MBPP+、BFCL-v3、ACEBench、HotpotQA、2Wiki 六个基准和 Qwen3-4B、Qwen3-8B 两个骨干上，RSIFlow 在 12 个基准—骨干设置中 11 个领先，总体得分 51.21%（4B）与 59.86%（8B），分别超过最强基线 6.06 和 3.86 个百分点，平均每指标高 3.11%。HumanEval+ 上 4B 的 pass@1 提升 14.02%，MBPP+ 两骨干平均提升 3.91%，2Wiki 的 F1 两骨干平均提升 5.20%，8B 在 HotpotQA 上提升 6.38%。消融中，自适应编排比固定组件工作流平均高 4.13%–8.81%，禁用元智能体进化使平均性能下降 5.74%；五轮案例沿 Harness–Harness–Model–Model–Artifacts 序列从 32.23% 升到 51.21%（+18.98%），其中第三、四轮分别用 3,798 和 5,397 次 replay 调用做 LoRA 微调。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「改进流程本身」当作可学习对象：不再预设该改模型还是改 harness，而是让元智能体依据执行反馈选择干预范围，并把成功与失败经验沉淀为可复用技能。这为 RSI 提供了一条不更新元模型参数、只演化 harness 的实现路径。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 Qwen3-4B/8B 两个较小骨干，更大模型与集群规模下收益是否保持尚未验证；元智能体参数固定、靠改写 harness 进化会带来额外算力开销，论文也承认经验驱动的 Meta-Harness 更新稳定性有待研究，且案例研究未隔离单个技能的因果贡献。
article.figure_caption_zh: RSIFlow 总览：任务智能体执行任务并采集轨迹与反馈，元智能体检索技能自适应编排工作流，工作流结果被蒸馏为技能、原则与 Meta-Harness，更新后的 Meta-Harness 指导后续编排，闭合递归自我改进回路。

figure.caption: {Overview of RSIFlow.} {(A)} Definition of task domains and agent workflows. {(B)} The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback. {(C)} The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows. {(D)} Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness. The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.

page_papers.title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents
page_papers.abstract: Recursive language-model agents decompose tasks and delegate subtasks to child instances of the same policy, forming a tree of work. Training them, however, is hard: the final outcome is verifiable, but the self-invented intermediate subtasks are numerous and carry no ground truth. Existing methods score each node with a verifier or judge, which is costly at scale and blind to decomposition quality. We argue that a recursive agent must learn three coupled capabilities within one set of weights: decomposing problems into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating the outcomes, each requiring its own training signal. SERA (Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents) turns evaluation into a learned capability of the policy itself. Before delegating, the parent writes a rubric of weighted success criteria for each child subtask; a ranking objective against verified outcomes then trains rubric generation so that the criteria track genuine subtask success. In addition, a complementary leaf-coverage signal provides direct credit for task decomposition. Our central finding is that training the policy to generate aligned rubrics is what drives the gains: because the same weights both evaluate and execute, learning to judge subtasks sharpens the agent's ability to solve them. Notably, external supervision is also reduced: the judge is consulted only to train the rubric generator, while solving is trained against the agent's own rubric scores, which outperform direct use of the judge. Beyond training, the learned rubric doubles as an inference-time selector for tree search. On TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync, SERA improves over strong recursive-agent baselines by 5.38 and 13.14 points on average, and rubric-guided tree search at inference adds a further 2.43 points on TextWorld-Sync.

represents equal contribution
