†
represents Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Language-model agents are deployed on tasks that cannot be solved in a pass: multi-hop research questions require coordinating evidence across retrieval steps; repository-scale code changes involve interdependent edits. A natural response is to decompose the problem and delegate each piece to a child agent
(
Prasad et al., 2024
;
Schroeder et al., 2025
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
, turning one query into a tree of work where each child handles a focused subproblem in a fresh context. When the children are instances of the
same
policy, the system is
recursive
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
: a single set of weights drives every node. This is the design behind frontier coding and research agents
(
Anthropic, 2025
;
OpenAI, 2025
;
Tie et al., 2026
)
, and it composes across depth: a policy trained at shallow recursion generalises to deeper trees at inference
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
, making recursion a distinct axis of test-time scaling alongside longer chains of thought and wider sampling.
Training recursive agents is hard because supervision is scarce and unevenly distributed across the tree. The final outcome is typically verifiable (a research answer can be checked, code can be tested), but the intermediate subtasks the agent invents rarely admit a ground-truth check. The natural remedy is to score each node by its own success instead of broadcasting the root reward, using a verifier or an LLM judge (e.g.,
Gandhi et al., 2026
). This localises credit, but the resulting signal has three limitations. It is
coarse
: a binary per-node signal cannot separate a clean solution from a barely adequate one, or flag weak work inside a tree that still succeeds. It is
expensive
: a reliable signal at every node needs a verifier or judge call throughout the tree, which scales poorly. And it is
silent about decomposition
: rewarding whether subtasks were solved says nothing about whether they were the
right
subtasks to create, though that choice often decides whether the tree succeeds.
The root issue is structural: a recursive agent is not doing one thing but three. The same shared weights must
decompose
hard problems into tractable pieces,
solve
the subtasks that result, and
evaluate
whether delegated work was actually accomplished. Every child is a fresh instance of the parent, so all three functions live in a single policy. Training the agent well means giving each capability its own signal without the three interfering on shared parameters.
A self-invented subtask has no ground-truth check, so the agent must judge for itself whether it succeeded. We make this self-evaluation concrete with a
rubric
: when the parent delegates a subtask, it commits a short set of weighted natural-language success criteria for the child before the child runs, so they cannot be fitted to the trajectory they will later score. Applying the rubric to the child’s output yields a continuous, subtask-specific score in place of the coarse per-node signal.
However, a rubric helps only when its criteria align with subtask success. An untrained policy writes misaligned criteria, and using its scores as rewards helps little, inconsistently across tasks (§
4
). We therefore train rubric generation, but the signal for that training cannot be the task reward itself: since rubric generation and solving share weights, rewarding the rubric through task reward would let the two co-adapt, inflating rubric scores together without improvement. Instead, the signal comes from an external check: we score subtask rollouts with a verifier or judge and train the rubric to rank verified successes above failures. Importantly, the judge is used only here, never to reward nodes directly as common approaches do; the rubric provides the dense per-node signal itself, so external supervision is lighter overall. Grounded this way, shared weights become an asset: learning to judge subtasks reshapes how the policy solves them, which is our central empirical finding (§
4
).
A capability,
subtask decomposition
, is the choice of how to split a task into subproblems to delegate. We assign it a reward. In a solved tree, a delegation is credited by the fraction of the task’s leaf-level work its subtree covers, so a delegation that shoulders a large, well-scoped share of the solution scores high, while trivial hand-offs score near zero and delegations in failed trees score zero. This rewards the agent for using delegation to carry structural load, something no execution signal captures. The reward adds little on shallow, near-independent subtasks but helps when subtasks are interdependent, as in tasks with dependency chains, shared state, or coordination (§
4
).
Finally, since the learned rubric captures genuine subtask quality, it is useful beyond training. At inference we search the tree depth-first and select among candidate resolutions by rubric score, propagating the best upward. This further improves final task success without additional training (§
4.3
). The evaluation capability thus pays off as a reusable inference-time selector, a further scaling axis for recursive agents. We call the method
SERA
(Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents). Our contributions are as follows:
1.
A framing of recursive-agent training as learning three coupled capabilities (decomposing, solving, and evaluating subtasks) in a single shared policy, with evidence that each requires its own training signal (§
3
).
2.
A learned self-evaluation mechanism: policy-generated rubrics trained by a ranking objective against verified outcomes. We show that training rubric generation is what improves execution, that it reduces external supervision while outperforming direct use of the judge (§
3
).
3.
A leaf-coverage decomposition reward that credits a delegation by how much of the verified task it covers, with gains concentrated when subtasks are interdependent (§
3
).
4.
State-of-the-art results on TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync (§
4
), and the learned rubric as an inference-time selector for tree search, with further gains (§
4.3
).
2
Related Work
Recursive and multi-agent training.
Recursive and multi-agent scaffolds decompose tasks and route subproblems to child agents, scaling language-model agents at inference time
(
Prasad et al., 2024
;
Schroeder et al., 2025
)
, but most treat recursion as a fixed scaffold around a frozen model. Recent work instead trains agents to delegate, though largely at depth 1 with fixed or restricted workers: parallel delegation with reinforcement learning
(
Team et al., 2026b
)
and jointly trained organizer–worker systems
(
Sun et al., 2025
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
. Recursive Agent Optimization (RAO) is the closest prior work, combining recursion beyond depth 1, asynchronous subagent execution, and end-to-end RL training of both root agents and subagents
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
. We adopt this setting and use RAO as our primary baseline, but depart from it in the signal each node receives: RAO scores nodes with a binary success label from a verifier or judge and says nothing about decomposition quality, whereas SERA gives each node a trained continuous rubric and credits decomposition directly.
Dense rewards and process supervision for agents.
A large body of work densifies sparse outcome rewards with step- or process-level supervision, from process reward models
(
Lightman et al., 2024
)
to agentic variants that assign credit to intermediate actions
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
; these operate on flat, linear trajectories with the intermediate signal supplied by a separate critic or an additive decomposition of the return. Classical hierarchical RL such as options
(
Dietterich, 2000
)
and goal-conditioned hierarchies
(
Nachum et al., 2018
)
assigns credit across levels but assumes a fixed set of subtask types or hierarchy depth. In contrast, SERA operates on a dynamically generated tree where the hierarchy, the subtasks, and the evaluator are all produced by a single policy and vary from rollout to rollout.
Rubric-based reinforcement learning.
A separate question from where credit is assigned is what form the per-node signal takes. Rubrics extend RL beyond exactly verifiable domains by scoring outputs against generated criteria
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
. Because static rubrics saturate as the policy improves, recent work co-trains the rubric generator with the policy through per-step return decomposition
(
Tian et al., 2026
)
, alternating generator–judge optimization
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, or adversarial co-evolution
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
, with RubricEM the closest in domain family
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
. All assume flat or fixed-stage computation with a rubric model separate from the policy. SERA instead applies learned rubric generation to recursive, policy-invented subtasks whose topology varies across rollouts, uses the policy itself as the evaluator, and trains rubrics with a ranking objective anchored to verified outcomes. We find that the label-free discriminativeness signal favored in prior rubric learning degrades performance in a tree, where score spread reflects subtask-difficulty variation more than rubric quality (§
4.2
); relatedly, work documenting reward hacking under learned reward signals
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
motivates our verified-outcome anchoring.
Figure 1:
Recursive Agent Optimization with rubric-based trajectory

3.3
Leaf-coverage reward for decomposition
Execution credit evaluates what an agent does after a decision, but it does not directly evaluate whether the decision to delegate was structurally useful. We therefore assign a separate reward to each delegation event. We measure coverage by leaf nodes (nodes with no children), since leaves are the nodes that solve atomic subproblems and contribute directly to the final answer, while internal nodes serve as orchestrators. Leaf coverage thus captures how much of the final solution is produced through a given delegation, independent of tree depth. 3.6
Alternating optimization schedule
SERA jointly optimizes three objectives on shared parameters. Combining all three gradients in a single update risks instability, since the objectives can interfere and their scales differ. We instead alternate: each optimizer step activates exactly one objective, and the updates cycle in the fixed ratio
n
exec
:
n
leaf
:
n
rub
n_{\mathrm{exec}}:n_{\mathrm{leaf}}:n_{\mathrm{rub}}
. Execution updates receive the largest share because, in preliminary experiments, execution training is the primary driver of performance and covers the majority of tokens in a typical tree. The leaf-coverage and rubric-generation stages are lighter, each requiring only a small number of periodic updates to improve decomposition and refine the rubric that supplies the dense execution signal. Alternation keeps the credit sources well separated, and the ratio can be adjusted per domain without changing the method. The same learned rubric is then reused at inference time to rank candidate node resolutions during the bottom-up tree-search procedure described in Section
4.3
.
4
Experiments
Benchmarks.
We evaluate on two benchmarks that differ in a property central to our method: whether intermediate subtasks can be verified independently.
TextCraft-Synth
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
is a procedural crafting environment requiring hierarchical planning, tool use, and recursive delegation, in which the agent crafts a target item by looking up recipes and delegating sub-crafts to child agents. Crucially, each subtask has a deterministic program verifier returning a binary pass/fail outcome, so SERA’s rubric training requires no external judge here. Tasks span four difficulty levels defined by recipe depth; we train on Medium and evaluate across all levels to test generalization.
TextWorld-Sync
is our multi-agent extension of TextWorldExpress
(
Jansen and Côté, 2023
)
, a shared-state text environment for evaluating coordination under constraints, with seven task families spanning dependency chains, resource conflicts, load balancing, and hierarchical decomposition. Unlike TextCraft, subtask outcomes are not independently verifiable; rubric training instead uses an LLM judge that provides binary success/failure labels for counterfactual rollouts, making this the benchmark that tests SERA’s ability to amortize a sparse external signal. On both benchmarks the verified outcome

b

3

Conclusion
We presented SERA, a method for training recursive language-model agents that casts training as three coupled capabilities: decomposing tasks into subtasks, solving them, and evaluating their outcomes. Each capability receives its own training signal, and the three are optimized by alternating updates on a single shared policy.
The central finding is that training the policy to generate its own evaluation rubrics, through a ranking objective anchored to verified outcomes, is what drives the largest performance gains. Since evaluation and execution share weights, learning to judge subtask quality directly improves how the agent solves them. This trained rubric also reduces reliance on external supervision: the judge is needed only to train the rubric generator, and the resulting self-generated signal outperforms using the judge directly. Additionally, a leaf-coverage reward provides a direct signal for decomposition quality, with the largest gains on tasks requiring coordination among interdependent subtasks. Beyond training, the learned rubric serves as an inference-time selector for tree search, further improving task success without additional training.
Several limitations remain. We evaluate only Qwen3-4B on two synthetic benchmarks, so generalization to larger models and real-world agent tasks remains untested. Because the policy both writes and applies its own rubrics, self-evaluation could be gamed by scores that drift from genuine task success; we mitigate this by training rubric generation only against verified outcomes—a label-free dispersion reward instead degrades performance (Section
4.2
)—but robustness under sparser or noisier verification, and the residual dependence on verified outcomes to anchor rubric training (Table
2
), remain open. Finally, the leaf-coverage reward treats all leaf nodes equally, and subtask-level importance weights may improve decomposition training.
Looking ahead, the rubric mechanism suggests learning rubrics that generalize across tasks, using the rubric to guide exploration during training, and extending self-evaluation to settings where even the root outcome is not exactly verifiable. Framing recursive-agent training as three coupled capabilities offers a useful foundation for this work.
AI use statement
In this work, we used generative AI tools in a limited capacity for grammar correction and polishing of author-written text, and for coding assistance and debugging. All research ideas, method design, experimental design, result analysis, figures, and tables were produced entirely by the authors. Every AI-suggested text edit was reviewed and accepted or rejected by the authors, and all AI-assisted code was reviewed and tested by the authors before use. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, code, and artifacts.
Ethics statement
This work trains language-model agents to decompose and solve tasks in simulated text environments. The benchmarks (TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync) are procedurally generated and do not involve human subjects, personal data, or real-world deployment. The self-evaluation mechanism enables agents to generate and score their own rubrics, which could in principle be misused to produce misleading self-assessments; we mitigate this by anchoring rubric training to externally verified outcomes and reporting all results against deterministic environment verification. We do not foresee significant negative societal impacts from this research.
Reproducibility statement
All hyperparameters, training schedules, and evaluation protocols are reported in Section
4
and Appendix
B
, including the alternating-update ratios, rollout group sizes, context lengths, and checkpoint steps for each method variant. The base model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507) is publicly available. Both benchmarks use deterministic environment verification for all reported success rates. We plan to release the training code and the TextWorld-Sync benchmark upon publication.

The root agent delegates subtasks to child instances of the same policy, which can delegate further or solve their assigned tasks directly.
Independent branches can run in parallel, while parents incorporate returned results into their own execution.
In SERA, each parent generates a subtask-specific rubric before the child runs and freezes it throughout that child’s execution.
After completion, the policy applies this rubric to the child’s trajectory and final environment state, producing its execution reward.
The rubric scorer and external verifier serve different purposes in this framework.
RAO uses externally supplied subtask outcomes directly as execution rewards; SERA uses them to train rubric generation on counterfactual rollouts.
These outcomes come from a program verifier on TextCraft-Synth and an external LLM judge on TextWorld-Sync.
SERA’s ordinary subtask execution instead receives the policy’s own rubric scores, while the root retains its environment-verified outcome.
The leaf-coverage reward separately credits delegation using the completed tree and root outcome, without additional subtask labels.
Thus, the three signals train execution, decomposition, and evaluation through distinct updates, as specified in Section
3
.

Appendix C
TextWorld-Sync Dataset Construction
TextWorld-Sync extends the CookingWorld environment in TextWorldExpress
(
Jansen and Côté, 2023
)
to test recursive delegation under shared-state constraints.
Its design separates local subtask completion from joint task success, complementing the independently verifiable crafting subtasks in TextCraft-Synth.
C.1
Shared World and Agent-Local Contexts
The standard TextWorldExpress interface exposes one mutable game through a single avatar.
We retain the CookingWorld dynamics and introduce a coordinator that lets recursive agents interact with one shared world.
Objects, containers, inventory, tools, doors, recipe progress, and task score are shared across agents.
Each agent maintains its own logical location, dialogue history, observation stream, and step budget.
Model calls may run concurrently, but environment reads and state transitions are serialized under a lock and committed atomically.
Consequently, an item acquired by one agent becomes unavailable to others, while their locations and histories remain separate.
This distinction permits concurrent planning while preserving consistent state updates and exposing dependencies between agents’ actions.
C.2
Procedural Tasks and Coordination Structures
An original CookingWorld instance specifies one recipe, its required ingredients, and a target meal.
TextWorldExpress procedurally samples recipes, layouts, object placements, and difficulty parameters.
We extend this generator to sample multiple disjoint recipes per seed, assign ingredients to dishes, and introduce one of seven coordination structures.
The complete instance is recorded in a fixed manifest and reconstructed at runtime by a multi-dish adapter.
Independent dish branches can be delegated in parallel, subject to the instance’s resource and dependency constraints.
Table
8
summarizes the seven task families and the coordination decisions they require.
They range from independent branches to shared-resource conflicts and nested dependencies, providing different conditions for evaluating decomposition quality.
The deterministic root evaluator reads structured environment state and requires every ingredient to be collected and correctly processed, and every dish prepared and consumed.
Completing an individual dish yields partial progress but does not terminate the root task.
This root-level check does not provide labels for arbitrary policy-generated subtasks; SERA therefore uses an external judge for rubric-training labels on this benchmark.
Table 8:
Coordination structures in TextWorld-Sync. The seven task families vary branch dependencies, workload allocation, resource constraints, and recursion. Every family uses a shared world and requires completion of all dishes for root-task success.
Task family
Structure and coordination requirement
Fork–join
Independent dish branches converge on shared preparation and consumption, requiring their results to be coordinated.
Critical path
One branch has a longer workload; launching it early reduces delays before the branches can join.
Load balanced
Branch workloads differ, requiring work to be distributed across agents.
Resource constrained
Inventory capacity, available tools, or a shared step budget limit concurrent work.
Dependency gate
A branch can proceed only after a prerequisite, such as opening a door, has been satisfied.
Conflict
Branches compete for a unique shared tool, such as a knife or stove, requiring coordinated access.
Hierarchical
Dish-level tasks contain ingredient-level subtasks, supporting delegation across multiple recursion depths.
C.3
Dataset Splits and Difficulty Levels
Tasks are assigned to Easy, Medium, Hard, or Extreme according to the number and scale of their constraints.
The fixed TextWorld-Sync split contains 1,500 training tasks, 200 validation tasks, and 1,400 test tasks.
Training comprises 900 Medium, 150 Hard, and 450 Extreme tasks; validation and test contain 50 and 350 tasks per difficulty, respectively.
For comparison, TextCraft-Synth training uses the fixed subset of 852 Medium tasks, with evaluation on 632 tasks spanning all four levels.
Thus, TextCraft-Synth tests transfer from Medium training tasks across recipe depths, whereas TextWorld-Sync training covers several levels of coordination difficulty.

article.headline: 递归智能体学会给自己写评分标准
article.lede: SERA 让递归智能体在委派子任务前写出加权评分标准，用验证结果训练它，再把自评分当作密集执行奖励。
article.problem: 递归智能体把任务拆开、交给同一策略的子实例执行，最终结果可以验证，但中间那些自己发明的子任务没有标准答案。现有做法用验证器或 LLM 裁判给每个节点打二值分：信号粗糙、全树调用代价高，而且完全没有评价「拆得对不对」。
article.method: SERA 把评估变成策略自身的一项能力：父节点在子任务执行前生成一份冻结的加权评分标准（rubric），子任务结束后由同一策略按标准打出连续分数，作为该节点的执行奖励；外部验证器或裁判只用来训练 rubric 生成器，方法是要求它对同一子任务的多次反事实 rollout 按验证结果正确排序。另设 leaf-coverage 奖励，按一次委派所组织的叶子节点占整棵树的比例给分解决策记功。三路信号以 16:2:2 的更新比例交替优化共享权重。
article.results: 在 TextCraft-Synth 上平均成功率 74.31%（列第二），在 TextWorld-Sync 上 65.07%（列第一），分别比递归智能体基线 RAO 高 5.38 和 13.14 个百分点。去掉 rubric 训练的版本只有 72.26% 和 51.10%，说明增益主要来自 rubric 训练本身；分解奖励在 TextWorld-Sync 上再加 4.81 点，其中 Hard +8.58、Extreme +17.43，但在 TextCraft-Synth 上反而低 0.53 点。外部监督方面，TextCraft 的程序验证器调用从 550.94K 降到 257.96K（约 2.1 倍），TextWorld 的裁判调用从 147.80K 降到 35.79K（4.1 倍），输入 token 从 633.80M 降到 125.32M（5.1 倍）。推理时用学到的 rubric 做自底向上树搜索选择，TextWorld-Sync 上再从 65.07% 提升 2.43 点至 67.50%，与外部 Kimi-K3 裁判的 67.29% 基本持平。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「评价子任务」当成和「拆解」「求解」并列的第三种可训练能力，而不是外挂一个裁判，从而在减少外部监督调用的同时提高了执行质量；学到的 rubric 还能在推理阶段复用为树搜索的选择器。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 Qwen3-4B 和两个合成文本基准，更大模型与真实任务尚未验证；评估与执行共享权重，自评分存在偏离真实成功的风险，目前靠验证结果锚定 rubric 训练来缓解，但验证更稀疏或更嘈杂时的稳健性仍未解决。此外 leaf-coverage 对所有叶子等权，且 TextWorld-Sync 上训练耗时 24 小时 14 分，长于 RAO 的 13 小时 08 分。
article.figure_caption_zh: 基于 rubric 轨迹打分的递归智能体优化：共享策略的根智能体递归委派子任务，每条完成的子智能体轨迹可同时获得 rubric 奖励与程序或 LLM 裁判奖励。

page_papers.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
page_papers.abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

Introduction
An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages interactions between a large language model (LLM) and its environment
(
Grace et al., 2026
)
.
Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI)
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
uses past execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates that improve performance on future tasks
(
Suzgun et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026a
)
.
However, these methods often pursue performance gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification
(
Lin et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026a
)
.
These efforts improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption and increased latency.
This trade-off is less appealing in practical deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter.
We therefore ask:
Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better performance at lower execution cost?
Toward this goal, we introduce

HarnessPro
, a label-free method for recursive harness self-improvement that uses both performance and cost metrics to guide harness updates and candidate selection.
It orchestrates several specialized agents to turn execution feedback into successive harness updates.
A trajectory analyzer examines repeated rollouts to identify failures and avoidable overhead.

differs from prior work.

article.headline: HarnessPro：以帕累托优化兼顾性能与成本
article.lede: 无需真值标签的智能体框架自改进方法：多智能体诊断轨迹，按性能-成本前沿挑选候选，提升通过率同时降低单任务成本。
article.problem: 智能体框架（harness）决定了大模型与环境如何交互，近期用递归自改进（RSI）来优化框架的工作往往靠更长的探索和更强的验证换取性能，代价是 token 消耗与延迟上升。在实际部署中执行成本和延迟同样是硬约束，因此作者提出的问题是：递归式框架自改进能否在更低成本下取得更好性能。
article.method: HarnessPro 是一个无需标签的框架自进化流程：专用智能体分析多次 rollout 的执行轨迹，定位失败模式与可避免的开销，再由规划器按不同的性能-成本优先级生成更新方案，并实现为候选框架。候选框架用 LLM 生成的测试来评估，不接触标准答案或官方测试。方法不返回单一框架，而是保留一组位于性能-成本前沿的代表性候选（Pareto 选择），并提供 Lite、Medium、Heavy 等不同取舍的档位。
article.results: 作者以 RHO 为主要对照：在 SWE-Bench Pro 上 RHO 虽然提升通过率，但单任务平均成本从 1.88 美元升至 2.68 美元，上涨 42.6%。结果表中，HarnessPro-Heavy 在第一组基准上达到 80.8% 通过率、平均成本 0.72 美元、单次通过成本 0.89 美元，而 RHO 为 76.3%、1.09 美元、1.43 美元；在第二组基准上 Heavy 为 80.7%、1.97 美元、2.44 美元，RHO 为 80.0%、2.68 美元、3.35 美元。较轻的 Lite 档在这两组基准上分别为 72.9%/0.43 美元与 72.3%/0.80 美元。消融显示规划器与测试合成器都不可缺少：去掉规划器后 Heavy 从 80.8% 降至 79.7%，去掉测试合成器后降至 74.6%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「自改进」的评价标准从只看通过率改成同时看性能与执行成本，并用帕累托前沿给出多档可选方案，这更贴近智能体真正上线时的工程约束。
article.limitations: 成本数字依赖具体模型版本与 API 定价，换环境后未必可迁移；候选评估完全依赖 LLM 生成的测试，这些测试与官方测试的一致性论文未给出具体数字，因此「无标签评估」的可信度仍待验证。此外，去掉规划器或测试合成器都会明显掉点，说明收益高度依赖这套多智能体流水线自身的复杂度与开销。
article.figure_caption_zh: HarnessPro 的整体流程：每个 epoch 分析 rollout 轨迹、生成候选框架，并依据性能与成本挑选代表性候选。

figure.caption: Overview of {}. In each epoch, it analyzes rollout trajectories, generates candidate harnesses, and selects representatives based on performance and cost.

page_papers.title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
page_papers.abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation?
Existing OR benchmarks commonly begin with self-contained problem descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, leaving the work of translating original business materials into professionally validated solutions underrepresented.
We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios drawn from paid OR engagements totaling $3.68 million in project value.
It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification.
To evaluate information acquisition throughout optimization, we further introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise.
Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction.
Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero credit to infeasible deliveries.
Across 11 frontier LLMs evaluated with coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1.
Client information acquisition extends beyond initial clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages exhibiting higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions.
Trajectory analysis identifies failures spanning formulation and implementation, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks.
These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

Introduction
Operations research (OR) supports high-value decisions across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and many other domains. Deploying an OR system, however, requires experts to transform incomplete business materials into an executable decision process through requirement elicitation, problem formulation, solution strategy selection, and solver implementation. Gurobi’s
State of Mathematical Optimization Report 2024
reports that 82% of survey respondents hold a master’s or doctoral degree
(
Gurobi Optimization, 2024
)
. We ask whether large language model (LLM) agents can carry out this work.

Trajectory Analysis Methodology

feedback (S2), before the first candidate (S3), before a complete candidate
(S4), before the self-check passes (S5), and before final submission
(S6). We also record whether the agent asks again after solving feedback when
another decision opportunity remains.
For scientific inquiry, we annotate research opportunities: consequential
uncertainties visible to the agent and potentially reducible through
investigation. For each opportunity, we identify a testable hypothesis
(H), a mechanistic explanation (C), an executed diagnostic experiment
(A), evidence interpretation (E), and an evidence-grounded update (U).
A complete HCAEU chain links these behaviors within the same issue and
branch: H and C precede A, the experimental result informs E, and E
leads to U. We report chain completion and, among opportunities with
a complete chain, stage quality based on a three-level rubric.

Settings
We use Harbor 0.18.0 as the execution framework. The harness versions used in our experiments are Claude Code 2.1.278 and Codex 0.155.1. The interaction policy imposes a hard maximum of 500 rounds. Harbor-native tasks are allocated a 12-hour (43,200-s) wall-clock budget, and each solver invocation is limited to 3,600 s, including the solver subprocess and feedback paths. These values are upper bounds; an episode may terminate earlier after successful completion or verification.

3. Boundaries for interpreting rules and deriving conclusions
A definitive judgment about a rule, calculation convention, or feasibility must be explicitly supported by the available evidence or follow directly from rules explicitly stated in it. You may derive conclusions, but you may not guess the business rules, field meanings, parameter mappings, or other premises required for the derivation.
When explaining or summarizing a rule, retain the objects, stages, conditions, scope, and quantifiers that affect the conclusion, such as “only,” “the last time,” and “within the same stage.” If shortening a statement would broaden what is allowed or prohibited, retain the full wording.
Distinguish business meaning from execution mechanisms. You may explain the business consequences of an explicit rule, but you may not infer that the system uses a particular calculation, comparison, validation, or execution method. Do not turn “this condition already guarantees the result” into “the system additionally performs the corresponding check.” A specific mechanism requires explicit evidence.
Distinguish the scope of an individual rule from overall feasibility. “This rule does not restrict a situation” does not mean “this arrangement is feasible overall.” If overall feasibility also depends on unknown rules or conditions, state only what the current rule establishes. Do not present a specific arrangement as definitively feasible.
When identically named fields, similar concepts, or similar processes occur for different objects, stages, or calculation conventions, do not assume they follow the same rules. Do not transfer clipping, updating, filtering, restrictions, or other processing from one context to another without evidence, in either direction.
For events that cross time boundaries, answer using the explicitly stated timestamps, boundaries, and attribution rules. State conditional conclusions that can be established directly; do not avoid answering merely because an event crosses a boundary.

article.headline: 真实运筹项目上LLM智能体综合质量不及专家
article.lede: 31个真实付费运筹项目、11个前沿LLM智能体：最强配置严格可行率88.39%，但综合质量仍低于专家。
article.problem: 现有运筹（OR）基准大多从自包含的问题描述或预先定义好的优化任务出发，因此没有覆盖「把原始商业材料翻译成经专业验证的可执行方案」这一环节。而真实部署中，专家必须先做需求获取、问题形式化、求解策略选择与求解器实现，才能交付系统。论文要问的是：LLM智能体能否直接从原始客户材料出发，做到专家级交付。
article.method: 作者构建了 OR-License 端到端基准，涵盖10个工业场景的31个实例；脱敏后保留原始需求、输入数据、交付格式与信息边界；参考解由专家筛选，并且是客户在基准构建前已接受的方案。为评估求解过程中的信息获取，论文还提出 ORSim 受控客户模拟器，它只披露业务事实，不提供运筹专业知识。评测采用隐藏方式，检验交付可行性，并比较目标质量与专家解；部署调整质量（DAQ）按实例对专家相对质量取平均，不可行交付记零分。11个前沿 LLM 在编码智能体框架中运行（Harbor 0.18.0，Claude Code 2.1.278 / Codex 0.155.1），最多500轮交互，墙钟上限12小时，单次求解调用限3600秒。
article.results: 基准覆盖10个工业场景的31个实例，来自付费运筹项目，项目总值368万美元。11个前沿 LLM 在编码智能体框架下评测：若干模型在「条件目标质量」上超过专家参考解，但没有一个在 DAQ 上追平专家。最强的主 Claude Code 配置达到88.39%严格可行率，DAQ 为0.87，专家参考为1。轨迹分析显示失败同时出现在问题形式化与实现环节，按任务对齐统计的研究链完成率在可评测任务上为24%至45%。客户信息获取并不止于初始澄清，还延伸到方案开发与验证阶段，部分较晚阶段的已确认问题解决比例更高。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评测锚定在真实付费项目与客户已接受的解上，说明高价值运筹落地的瓶颈不只在建模与求解，还在于持续消除与客户之间的信息差、忠实形式化问题。这为长程智能体提供了一个更贴近部署的考核方式，而不只是做数学建模题。
article.limitations: 样本仅31个实例、10个场景，且全部来自可脱敏、可交付评测的付费咨询项目，泛化性有限。隐藏评测只检查可行性与相对专家解的目标质量，而专家解是被客户接受的单一方案、并非最优解；评测也绑定特定编码智能体框架与 harness 版本，换配置后结论可能变化。
article.figure_caption_zh: 评测框架：专家从真实运筹项目中整理任务与参考解，智能体在求解全过程中可向客户提问，最终提交由隐藏评测检验可行性与相对专家的方案质量。

page_papers.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
page_papers.abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.

\galbotdata

Where is Physical RSI capability from?
An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
Zekai Li
Jiayi Yu
Jinlu Zhang
Luyang Niu
Zekun Qi
Jun Zheng
Xuchuan Chen
Dairu Liu
Yintianrun Zhang
He Wang
Li Yi

Galbot Team

Abstract
In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement.
We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric:
First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget
and
Improvement
from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget.
The analysis of experimental results motivates the
Physical Barrel Hypothesis
: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. Systems with similar public benchmark averages can still differ widely on the five axes, and a system that reaches a high final score may improve late or consume more of its budget. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve.
Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.
Figure 1
:
PhysRSI-eval at a glance.
(Q1) Capability sources and the Physical Barrel Hypothesis. (Q2) Five-axis quantification and observational scaling of performance, gain timing and model rankings.
T
50
T_{50}
is the half-gain round, the first round at which the best mean score reaches half of its K1–K17 gain. (Q3) Overfitting and generalization across tasks and scenes.
1
Introduction
Frontier LLM agents demonstrate remarkable capabilities in directly generating actions for robotic manipulation.
Through iterative trial and error, they continually improve manipulation ability by updating skills, generating code, and using tools.
[
22
,
9
]
We call this process physical recursive self-improvement, or physical RSI.
In this work, rather than further demonstrating the impressive capabilities of frontier LLM agents, we pose three more fundamental questions:
What is the origin of physical RSI capabilities? What scaling laws govern this process? Do the resulting improvements reflect overfitting or generalization?
Q1: Where is Physical RSI capability from?
What allows an agent to turn physical feedback into a better policy? Perception helps it interpret outcomes, spatial reasoning relates observations to actions
[
31
]
, and coding and harness use allow it to implement and test revisions. These capabilities may play different roles. We ask whether strengths behind a good first attempt also explain improvement after feedback.
We introduce PhysRSI-eval to study these questions under a common protocol (
Figure
2
). Six systems revise persistent code, tools and notes across 18 manipulation tasks, with frozen model weights and a fixed physical interaction budget. Gemini 4 is reported separately on ten tasks.
An exploratory comparison of four public capability profiles on the 18 tasks associates spatial reasoning most strongly with initial performance, and perception with attained performance and recovery (
Figure
4
). This pattern motivates the
Physical Barrel Hypothesis
: the capability that limits an agent may depend on which aspect of improvement we measure. Starting well and learning from failure may require different strengths. These associations suggest candidate bottlenecks, not causal requirements.
Q2: How can we quantify Physical RSI and its scaling law?
An endpoint score alone cannot quantify physical RSI. It says little about when gains occur or what they cost. Repeated attempts can also increase the chance of success without useful revision. Our
five-axis metric
separates initial performance, gain timing, attained score, physical budget savings and recovery from failure (
Section
3.4
). These axes reveal different strengths. Opus 5.5 attains a higher score than GPT-6.1 Sol, but has lower gain-timing and budget-savings scores. Higher scores need not mean improving earlier or using fewer physical interactions.
With these outcomes defined, we study
observational scaling
across model capabilities and physical interaction budgets. Following
Ruan et al. [34]
, we first ask whether public capability scores can predict the relative order of held-out systems, in attained performance and gain timing (
Section
5.2
).
We then ask whether early physical progress predicts the gains from a larger interaction budget. This connects physical RSI to the study of learning curves
[
19
,
12
]
, with the interaction round as our budget variable. Calibrating the improvement shape of a reference model to a few early rounds forecasts the rest of a related model’s trajectory (
Figure
8
). The two analyses address complementary questions: what improvement to expect from a model’s capabilities, and how much further it may progress after its first attempts. Both remain exploratory.
Q3: Does Physical RSI reflect overfitting or generalization?
Does the agent acquire a reusable procedure, or adapt to its practice scene? A rising score alone cannot answer this question. We first remove history to test whether retained experience helps beyond repeated attempts. We then freeze workspaces on unseen layouts and transfer them across tasks.
In a six-task Astra ablation, removing history lowers late-round success from 41.7% to 8.3% (
Table
8
). With further revision disabled, frozen workspace files support success in 25 of 60 trials on unseen layouts (
Table
9
). Three cross-task cases also reach first success earlier when initialized from other tasks’ workspaces (
Figure
9
). These results support a role for retained experience and show that some artifacts remain useful beyond the scenes where they were refined. Scene-specific gains and useful transfer can coexist. Explaining which retained skills or memories enable transfer connects this question back to the origins of physical RSI.
Our contributions follow this progression:
•
Five-axis evaluation and capability diagnosis.
A fixed-budget protocol separates five physical RSI outcomes and relates them to four capability profiles, motivating the Physical Barrel Hypothesis.
•
Observational scaling and prediction.
Cross-model rank prediction and early-round forecasting probe how model capabilities and interaction budget relate to physical improvement.
•
Specialization and generalization.
Ablations, frozen-workspace tests and cross-task adaptation examine whether gains depend on retained experience and whether that experience remains useful elsewhere.

3
PhysRSI-eval: Benchmark Design
PhysRSI-eval makes the three questions measurable by recording both physical attempts and the workspace carried between them. The attempt sequence reveals where an agent starts and how it progresses under a fixed budget. Workspace interventions test what agents retain and whether it transfers.
3.1
What Must the Benchmark Distinguish?
A strong first attempt and useful revision are different abilities. We therefore score a first-attempt baseline separately and follow subsequent attempts under a fixed budget. Per-round scores show when gains occur; charged physical steps show what they cost. Reaching a high score, reaching it early and using fewer interactions are separate outcomes.
Success alone does not show whether the agent has accumulated useful experience. Code, tools and notes must remain accessible for intervention. Clearing the workspace tests whether retained experience helps; freezing it on unseen layouts tests whether it remains useful; transferring it to new tasks tests whether it can support a different goal. We report these tests separately from the main profiles in
Section
6
.

The pattern motivates the

Does Physical RSI reflect overfitting or generalization?
With fixed model weights, generalization concerns the code, tools and notes the agent retains. Do they encode reusable procedures, or do they become specialized to the refinement setting? We first test whether retained experience helps beyond repeated attempts. We then evaluate frozen workspaces on unseen layouts and transfer them to new tasks.

6.1
Does Retained Experience Help Beyond Repeated Attempts?
The Astra ablation varies which information from earlier rounds reaches the agent: the workspace, grader feedback, images and action records (
Table
7
). It covers six tasks with two chains each; layouts change every round over K1–K6, and execution continues after success. The full loop keeps all four channels, whereas the no-history condition keeps none, so its six rounds are independent attempts. Late-round success over K4–K6 is 15/36 (41.7%) for the full loop and 3/36 (8.3%) without history (
Table
8
). This supports a role for accumulated information under this protocol.
The remaining conditions withhold individual channels. Withholding grader feedback causes the largest drop, to 5/36 (13.9%), and withholding earlier-round images yields 12/36 (33.3%). Keeping only the workspace and grader feedback yields 17/36 (47.2%), so past images and action records add little once these two channels are kept. The no-history control supports a role for retained experience, but leaves open whether that experience is specific to the refinement setting.
6.2
What Survives When Revision Stops?
To test whether the stored artifacts work beyond practice, we freeze Astra workspaces after K6 and test each on five unseen layouts, with no further revision or outcome feedback (
Table
9
). Across 12 sources, workspace files alone succeed in 25/60 tests (41.7%). Adding prior raw records gives 23/60 (38.3%). The stored artifacts remain useful under layout changes, while these point estimates show no benefit from exposing the raw history at test time.
Fixed-layout source workspaces reach 27/60 (45.0%) on held-out layouts, compared with the reported 14/16 (88%) on their own layout. The different denominators prevent a matched paired interpretation. Still, the comparison suggests that scene-specific gains and transferable experience can coexist. These tests establish some cross-scene usefulness for Astra on this task subset; they do not establish generalization across all systems.
6.3
Can Experience Help on a Different Task?
Traces from five models suggest two forms of reusable experience: executable routines and textual operating knowledge. Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 increasingly encode control in self-written tools, which generate over 96% of their actions in later rounds. GPT-6 Sol also builds a substantial tool library, but tools generate 67% of actions while the model generates 33% directly. These shares measure tool reliance.
These tool libraries grow across rounds, combining tools created from scratch with those derived from earlier implementations. We use tool lineage to identify reuse across rounds. Direct use, modification and derivation of an existing tool all count as reuse. A directed relation A → B indicates that tool B is derived from tool A. Tracing these relations across rounds reveals how later tools build on earlier implementations. Among the three models with substantial tool libraries, Opus exhibits broader reuse and lower concentration. Its lineage reuse rate is 0.347, compared with 0.167 for Sonnet and 0.086 for GPT-6 Sol. The top 10% of reused lineages account for 48% of subsequent calls in Opus, compared with 76% in Sonnet and 83% in GPT-6 Sol. Together, these patterns suggest that Opus accumulates a broader reusable toolbox, while reuse in Sonnet and GPT-6 Sol remains concentrated in a smaller subset of tools (
Figure
10
).

Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol follow a different pattern. Approximately 99% of their actions remain directly generated by the model. They use only a very small number of tools for verification, but their reasoning time decreases across rounds. File-access traces show repeated use of memory, skills and policy notes to recover successful actions and subtask solutions, diagnose failures and guide revisions. These observations suggest that both executable routines and retained operating knowledge can reduce repeated reasoning.
We further find that the workspace and generalization analyses align with the Physical RSI Barrel Hypothesis across its four capability factors: spatial reasoning, perception, coding and harness operation. Spatial tools account for 14.5% of Sonnet’s tool calls and 13.7% of Opus’s, with 408 of 2,819 calls and 183 of 1,332 calls, respectively. Astra makes only seven tool calls, including one to such a tool, or 14%. Astra’s minimal reliance on these modules suggests stronger intrinsic perceptual and spatial capabilities. Sonnet and Opus repeatedly reuse these modules across tasks, suggesting that they rely more on tools to compensate for limitations in these capabilities.
During cross-task transfer, agents also consult memory and skills from semantically similar tasks. In Organize Table, Opus combines a parameterized move tool from Pack Objects Into Box with a memory from Store Tools In Toolbox: “the PITCHED 30 deg grasp… reaches the +y half…” The tool supplies an operation, while the memory identifies a grasp orientation that extends its reach. This shows how a reusable procedure and knowledge of when it works can jointly support transfer (
Figure
9
).
The transfer traces suggest that performance gains depend on experience relevant to the target task’s bottleneck and the agent’s ability to assess its applicability from failure evidence. Semantic similarity helps identify candidate experience; failure evidence guides whether to reuse, adapt or discard it. The teaser illustrates this mechanism through the reuse of a closed-loop grasp-and-transfer routine from stacking blocks to covering blocks with a cup, and an insertion routine from key insertion to charger plugging.
7
Limitations
The main comparison covers six model-plus-configuration systems, with one improvement chain per task. K0 repeats do not estimate variability across complete chains. First-success stopping records one success; reliable repeated execution needs a separate test. Budget and Improvement use conditional task sets that differ across systems. Astra’s outcomes differ between the main evaluation and the experiment without supplementary hints.
The capability analysis relies on public benchmark scores whose evaluation settings differ from our runs, and it covers six systems without independent validation. Capability bottlenecks and gain-timing predictions therefore remain hypotheses to test. The ablation and frozen tests cover Astra and six tasks, while cross-task results are three first-run cases. These limits constrain the scope of the observed transfer and the mechanisms that can be inferred from it.
8
Conclusion
PhysRSI-eval studies the origins, measurement, scaling and generalization of physical RSI under a fixed interaction budget. Capability associations motivate the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: the strengths needed to start well may differ from those needed to improve. The five-axis metric makes these outcomes explicit and shows that high scores, early gains and efficient interaction need not coincide. Cross-model prediction and early-round forecasting probe how these outcomes vary with capabilities and interaction budget. Workspace interventions support a role for retained experience and show that it can remain useful on new layouts and tasks. Physical RSI can thus involve both scene-specific adaptation and reusable improvement. Understanding it requires measuring how agents improve and examining what they retain.

Metric Definitions and Computation
Metrics are computed after averaging the task curves; in particular, Efficiency is a ratio of aggregate gains, not an average of task-wise ratios. The A3 threshold is the first integer Harness round reaching 90% of the observed peak gain, without interpolation. Budget charges each extra attempt once, supplements only failed reasoning-timeout rounds to their full step quota, and clips task savings at zero. Undefined denominators stay undefined. The summary in
Figure
6
is the equally weighted arithmetic mean of A1–A5, multiplied by 100. It is neither radar polygon area nor a success probability.

article.headline: 物理RSI能力从哪来：五轴评测与观测缩放
article.lede: Galbot团队提出PhysRSI-eval，用固定交互预算在18个双臂操作任务上拆解LLM智能体的物理自我改进能力。
article.problem: 前沿LLM智能体已能通过试错改写代码、工具与记忆来提升操作能力，但单看最终分数看不出这种「物理递归自我改进」从何而来，也分不清它是早早到手还是靠更多物理尝试堆出来的。论文追问三件事：能力来源是什么、改进如何随模型能力和交互预算缩放、提升究竟是过拟合练习场景还是可迁移。
article.method: PhysRSI-eval在RoboDojo的18个双臂任务上跑两阶段循环：先做无工作区的K0首试，再进入最多H=17轮的自改进，每轮一次带原生评分的物理尝试，随后在机器人动作关闭的状态下修改持久工作区。评测用五轴指标分开度量首试表现、增益出现早晚、最终得分、物理预算节省和从失败中恢复的比例。作者再用17项公开基准分数做跨模型的等级预测与早期轮次曲线外推，并通过清空历史、冻结工作区、跨任务迁移三类干预计检验保留经验的作用。
article.results: 六个系统在18个任务上的首试均分从0.012到0.368不等，到评测结束时升到0.104至0.842，分别解出15、12、7、1、13和11个任务。Opus 5.5的Success（0.744）高于GPT-6.1 Sol（0.703），但Efficiency更低（0.609对0.822），在其已解任务上省下的预算也更少（0.579对0.808）；Astra在五个轴上均居首。探索性秩相关显示空间推理与首试表现关联最强（ρ=0.94），感知与最终得分和恢复关联最强（ρ=0.94），编码最弱（ρ≤0.37）。六任务Astra消融中，去掉历史使K4–K6后期成功率从41.7%降到8.3%；冻结工作区在未见布局上取得25/60（41.7%）成功；三个跨任务案例把首次成功分别从K9提前到K1、K14到K7、K15到K8。用Astra的改进曲线外推GPT-6.1 Sol的后半程，MAE为0.019，而直接保持最后观测值为0.112。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「智能体会自我改进」这一笼统说法拆成可分别测量的五个量，并首次给出物理场景下从公开能力分数预测改进幅度与增益时机的初步证据，为评测具身智能体的持续学习提供了可复用的协议。
article.limitations: 能力关联与增益时机预测都只是观测性的：只有六个系统，未做独立验证，能力分数来自评测设置不同的公开基准，最小校正q值为0.11，因此「物理木桶假说」仍是待检验的假设。消融与冻结测试只覆盖Astra和六个任务，跨任务迁移仅三个首跑案例，且每任务只有一条改进链、成功即停，无法估计完整链条间的波动。
article.figure_caption_zh: 两阶段共用一套机器人接口：左侧K0为无工作区的单次首试，右侧K1–K17每轮从持久工作区出发，经原生评分后在动作关闭状态下修改并提交，直到首次成功或轮次用尽。

figure.caption: {Two stages, one interface.} Top: the task input and robot interface shared by both stages (observations, physical actions, memory and files, history). Left, {Evaluate} (first-attempt round K0): one in-context episode of observe--reason--act through the shared tools, with no workspace; history and notes stay inside the episode. Right, {Optimize} (self-improvement rounds K1--K$H$): each round runs from a persistent workspace of skills, tools, policy and memory, is graded natively, revised with robot actions closed, and committed as the start of the next round, until the first native success or the round limit.

page_papers.title: Manga2Animate: An Agentic Framework for Faithful Manga Animation with Script and Storyboard Planning
page_papers.abstract: Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga's structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. Extensive experiments and a user study demonstrate that Manga2Animate produces animations more faithful to the source manga and more consistent across shots than state-of-the-art approaches. Project page: https://annchenn.github.io/Manga2Animate/
page_papers.content:
Manga2Animate: An Agentic Framework for Faithful Manga Animation with Script and Storyboard Planning
Sheng-Wei Zhang
†

Abstract
Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga’s structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose
Manga2Animate
, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. Extensive experiments and a user study demonstrate that Manga2Animate produces animations more faithful to the source manga and more consistent across shots than state-of-the-art approaches.
Project page:
https://annchenn.github.io/Manga2Animate/
Figure 1:
Manga2Animate turns existing manga pages into coherent animation that stays faithful to the original manga.
Given a few manga pages
(left)
, our multi-agent framework first builds an animation script and a visual storyboard as intermediate representations, iteratively refining both through creator-reviewer collaboration, and then generates the final animation from them
(right)
. The resulting animation preserves the manga’s plot, character identity, and art style, while flowing coherently from clip to clip.
1
Introduction
Figure 2:
Limitations of existing methods to manga-to-animation generation.
(a) Text-based storytelling methods (AniMaker, ViMax, StoryMem) access the manga mainly through text, losing its art style (
1
) or distorting characters (
2
). (b) Feeding manga pages into a video model (e.g., Seedance 2.0) tells the wrong story (
3
) and shows manga panels as video frames (
4
).
Manga is one of the richest sources of stories for animation. Popular titles are routinely adapted into anime, and fans expect these adaptations to move smoothly and tell the story coherently while remaining faithful to the characters and art style they love. Yet producing such an adaptation remains slow and costly, often taking large teams of artists months of storyboarding, key animation, in-betweening, and coloring.
At the same time, a manga already specifies much of what an animation needs, including who the characters are and what they look like, how each shot is framed, and how the plot unfolds. With recent advances in video generation, it is natural to ask whether a manga can be brought to life automatically. However, as Fig.
2
shows, storytelling systems that first describe the manga in words discard its visual appearance, so the original art style is lost (
1
) and characters change appearance or drift between anime and photorealistic styles (
2
). Feeding manga pages directly into a video model fails for a different reason. The model knows neither the order in which the panels should be read nor what speech balloons mean, so it tells the wrong story (
3
) or even places manga panels, or entire pages, directly into the video as frames (
4
).
Our key observation is that today’s video generation models already know how to animate. What they cannot do is understand a manga. Given a manga page, they produce smooth and appealing motion, yet they follow the panels in the wrong order and misread the speech balloons, so the result looks convincing but tells a completely wrong story (Fig.
2
b). We therefore do not replace these models. Instead, we keep their rich visual knowledge and give them what they are missing, a clear understanding of the manga. Much like an animation studio, Manga2Animate (Fig.
1
) first turns the manga into an animation script, which describes what happens in each panel, and a storyboard, which shows how each shot should look. Both are built by AI agents and checked against the original panels, so the video model receives a faithful plan instead of raw manga pages. We find that this plan effectively constrains generation. With the script fixing the plot and the storyboard fixing the characters, composition, and art style, the video model no longer has to interpret the manga on its own and can focus on what it does best, bringing the story to life.
Experiments show that Manga2Animate produces animations that are more faithful to the original characters, art style, and plot than existing storytelling and video generation methods, even when these methods are given the same script as ours. Because our framework guides existing models rather than replacing them, it works with both open-source and commercial image and video generators, and outperforms prior methods with either. In a user study, participants selected our results as the best overall in over 90% of responses, for both storyboards and videos.
In summary, our contributions are threefold:
•
We present Manga2Animate, to the best of our knowledge the first automated framework that turns existing manga into animation that is faithful to source manga.
•
We show that planning through a script and a storyboard, iteratively refined with dual-level feedback from both and verified against the original manga, is key to preserving the characters, art style, and plot.
•
We establish an evaluation protocol for manga-to-animation generation, under which Manga2Animate outperforms existing methods, and we further validate these results with a user study.
2
Related Work
Manga understanding.
Built on annotated corpora
(
Matsui et al., 2017
;
Aizawa et al., 2020
;
Vivoli et al., 2024a
;
Li et al., 2024a
)
, manga understanding has progressed from detecting panels, characters, and text
(
Shen et al., 2023
)
to ordering panels and attributing dialogue
(
Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2024
)
, naming characters across chapters
(
Sachdeva et al., 2024
)
, and narrating chapters as prose
(
Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2025
)
. Vision-language models are now benchmarked on manga
(
Baek et al., 2026
;
Ikuta et al., 2025
;
Vivoli et al., 2025
)
, yet still misread cross-panel narrative
(
Baranwal et al., 2025
)
and can rely on memorized popular content rather than visual evidence
(
Szu-Tu et al., 2025
)
; generation from comics remains largely unexplored
(
Vivoli et al., 2024b
)
. We use
Sachdeva & Zisserman (2024)
for pre-processing and, given this fragility, review every intermediate output against the source panels.
Story visualization.
Story visualization renders a narrative as a consistent image sequence, evolving from GANs
(
Li et al., 2019
)
to diffusion models with visual memory
(
Rahman et al., 2023
)
, identity conditioning
(
Ye et al., 2023
)
, shared attention
(
Tewel et al., 2024
;
Zhou et al., 2024
)
, frame context
(
Liu et al., 2024a
)
, multi-subject personalization
(
He et al., 2025b
;
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Wu et al., 2025b
)
, iterative refinement
(
Mao et al., 2026
)
, and language-model layout planning
(
He et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Cheng et al., 2024
)
, with dedicated benchmarks
(
Zhuang et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2025
)
and extensions to manga generation
(
Wu et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
. These methods generate from text, whereas our storyboard is conditioned on and selected against the manga panels.
Multi-shot video generation.
Video diffusion has advanced from short clips
(
Ho et al., 2022
)
to foundation models
(
Kong et al., 2024
;
Wan et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Polyak et al., 2024
;
Seedance et al., 2026
)
, whose adherence to explicit specifications is now benchmarked
(
Huang et al., 2026d
)
. Cross-shot consistency is pursued through long-context tuning
(
Guo et al., 2025
;
Xiao et al., 2026
;
Meng et al., 2026
)
, keyframe memory
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
;
Zhou et al., 2026
)
, storyboard anchoring
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
, and reference-based identity injection
(
Jiang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025a
;
Hu et al., 2025
)
. For animation, anime-oriented models and datasets
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Qiu et al., 2025
)
and in-betweening and colorization methods
(
Xing et al., 2024
;
Meng et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025b
;
Tang et al., 2025
)
create motion and color from sparse inputs. We use such models as interchangeable backends and, in the spirit of decoupling explicit state from generative rendering
(
Huang et al., 2026c
)
, obtain consistency from the reviewed script and storyboard rather than from architecture (Sec.
4.4
).
Agentic storytelling video generation.
Language and vision-language agents increasingly orchestrate video production from script to storyboard, clips, and assembly
(
Lin et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2024b
;
Xu et al., 2025a
;
Wu et al., 2025c
;
Hu et al., 2024
;
Xu et al., 2025b
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Huang et al., 2026b
)
, some with critics that select clips by tree search
(
Shi et al., 2025
)
, gate anime production stages
(
Zhang et al., 2025b
;
Yan et al., 2026
)
, or self-improve at test time
(
Long et al., 2026
)
, following self-feedback in language agents
(
Madaan et al., 2023
;
Shinn et al., 2023
)
, a pattern also adopted to verify generated images and figures
(
Huang et al., 2026a
;
Tseng et al., 2026
)
. Our creator–reviewer design is closest to these systems, but they invent characters, shots, and plot from a prompt and can only check outputs against their own script, whereas our reviewers check against the manga panels. Earlier manga-to-animation systems only moved a virtual camera over panels or added synthesized speech
(
Cao et al., 2016
;
Gupta et al., 2021
)
; to our knowledge, ours is the first to generate faithful multi-shot animation from manga pages.
3
Methodology

3.3
Pre-processing
Manga pages often exhibit non-trivial panel layouts, making reading order an important prerequisite for preserving the narrative flow. We therefore detect the panels on each page and determine their reading order using a manga-specific detection model and its associated ordering algorithm
(
Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2024

. The resulting ordered panel sequence is then passed to the subsequent stages of the pipeline. In parallel, the same model also detects and transcribes the text on these pages, which we merge into a single transcript spanning all pages to help the Script Creator write each panel’s dialogue and plot (Sec.
3.4
). Also, we use a Character Description Creator to establish a consistent representation of each character from the reference image
R
R
. It extracts relatively stable, identity-defining traits, such as facial features and body build, while excluding variable attributes such as clothing and accessories. These character descriptions are then provided to the downstream Script and Storyboard Creators to help maintain character consistency throughout the generation process.

Script and Storyboard Refinement
To improve generation reliability while controlling API costs, we combine a small number of candidates per stage with iterative refinement, in which reviewer feedback guides the next round of generation. We run

In each refinement round, the Script Creator generates

Errors in scripts are largely local, a candidate may describe one panel precisely yet misread another, and different candidates tend to make different mistakes. Selecting a single script as a whole would discard the correct descriptions contained in the other candidates. The Script Reviewer therefore performs compositional selection at the clip level (Fig.

), preserving complementary strengths across candidates, and records the remaining weaknesses of each selected component as feedback for the next round.
The Storyboard Creator then generates

Unlike scripts, closed-source storyboards are selected as a complete image because their panels are generated jointly and share style, color, and lighting; recombining panels across candidates could introduce visual inconsistencies. The Storyboard Reviewer compares candidates pairwise in the first round and, in later rounds, compares each new candidate with the previous best, judging each storyboard against the script that produced it. If no new candidate wins, the previous best storyboard is retained with its script and feedback, keeping the final pair consistent. The open-source backend instead generates and selects panels individually before compositing them due to its constraints (more details in Appendix
B

Script-level and storyboard-level feedback are jointly provided to the next-round Script Creator, together with the best script from the previous round and the source manga panels. This dual-level feedback allows the pipeline to refine the textual specification using evidence from its visual realization. Issues flagged by the Storyboard Reviewer are treated as symptoms of ambiguous or inaccurate script descriptions: the Script Creator is instructed to identify the responsible part of the script, such as an ambiguous spatial description or a missing detail. To prevent unnecessary changes to already correct content, the Script Creator revises only the script clips or character descriptions explicitly identified as problematic by the reviewers, while leaving all other entries unchanged. When feedback from different reviewers conflicts, the corresponding source manga panel is used as the primary reference for deciding the revision. The script and storyboard selected in the final round are then passed to the video-generation stage.
3.5
Video Generation Pipeline
To accommodate different input formats of video generation models, our video generation pipeline supports two modes: a first-frame mode and a reference-conditioned mode. The former is used for models that take a single image as the first frame, while the latter is used for models that can take the complete storyboard as a reference and generate a multi-shot video at once. Our main experimental results use the reference-conditioned mode.
In first-frame mode, each storyboard panel serves as the first frame of its corresponding clip. For each clip, the Video Creator generates

This greedy and clip-by-clip process enforces cross-clip continuity at selection time, after which the selected clips are concatenated in story order. In reference-conditioned mode, the Video Creator instead uses the complete best script and full storyboard to generate

5
Conclusion
We present Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework for faithfully adapting existing manga into coherent multi-shot animation. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations grounded in the source manga, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Creator and reviewer agents iteratively generate, review, and refine both. Since the two representations fail in different ways, we compose scripts clip by clip, select storyboards as a whole, and feed storyboard-level issues back to the script. Under MangaEval, an evaluation protocol adapted from ViStoryBench and VBench++, Manga2Animate outperforms state-of-the-art storyboard and video generation methods on manga-fidelity and consistency metrics, even when baselines receive the same refined script and character references, and is strongly preferred in a user study. Promising future directions include improving robustness to complex or roughly sketched art styles, developing source-grounded evaluation of story events, and extending narrative understanding across pages and chapters.
Limitations.
Our method has several limitations. First, as an agentic pipeline built on stochastic generative models, its outputs may vary across runs. Second, API-based models may restrict generation of copyrighted or policy-sensitive content. Finally, when the source manga is highly sketchy, cluttered, or compositionally complex, or a scene requires context from elsewhere in the story, the pipeline may misinterpret panel content.

Hardware and cost.
Gemini and Seedance calls go through hosted APIs. MAGI runs locally on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB). FLUX.2-dev runs on an NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe, MiniMax-H3 on two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96 GB) GPUs, and Index-AniSora V3.2 on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96 GB). For each story, the closed-source pipeline makes 34.5 calls on average in the script and storyboard stages (28.5 Gemini text calls and 6 image-generation calls) and 3 in the video stage (2 Seedance generations and 1 Gemini review), costing about US$5.65 per story in total, of which US$4.55 is Seedance. Appendix B
Open-Source Storyboard Backend
In our experiments, the open-source image model we tested (FLUX.2-dev) did not reliably generate a complete, high-quality multi-panel storyboard in a single pass. We therefore adopt a panel-wise generation strategy, producing multiple candidates for each panel and selecting the best one before composing the final storyboard. For each panel in the selected script, we construct a prompt that incorporates the character descriptions, the corresponding script content, and constraints derived from the original manga panel to preserve its composition, camera viewpoint, and character pose. When character reference crops are available, they are explicitly associated with the corresponding characters during generation.
FLUX.2-dev is conditioned on the source manga panel and the available character references to generate multiple candidates for each panel. A Gemini-based reviewer then scores each candidate independently on manga/script follow (the primary criterion), character identity consistency, art style and colorization quality, and background fidelity, each on a 0–4 scale, and the highest-scoring candidate is retained. The selected panels are then assembled into a
3
×
2
3\times 2
storyboard grid, following the same output format as the closed-source backend to enable evaluation under a unified protocol. Since every panel is conditioned on its source manga panel and the shared character references, these common conditions help maintain cross-panel consistency.

Results.
Table

compares storyboard generation across methods. The two Manga2Animate configurations jointly achieve the best results on all four manga-fidelity metrics: the open-source FLUX.2 backend reaches the highest CSD and OCCM, while the closed-source Gemini backend achieves the highest CIDS and PA, each improving over the best baseline. Since all baselines use the same refined script as our method, the PA gap reflects content adherence under an identical specification, and this advantage holds for both an open and a closed image backend rather than relying on a specific image model.
In contrast, StoryDiffusion and Story-Iter score higher on the anime-specific aesthetic metrics but considerably lower on manga fidelity (CIDS, PA, OCCM), since both freely generate imagery from text without being constrained by the original characters and composition. This indicates that single-image aesthetics and adaptation fidelity are distinct aspects: an aesthetic predictor assesses the appeal of an individual illustration without considering whether it is consistent with the source. The strengths of Manga2Animate lie in character preservation, content alignment, and cross-panel consistency, which matter most for this task, and participants in our user study also clearly preferred our results overall (Sec.
4.6
).
The two backends offer different cost trade-offs: FLUX.2 avoids external image-generation APIs but takes 1 h 59 min on local GPUs, while Gemini takes 20 min 2 s with 6 image-generation calls. Both are slower than StoryDiffusion and AnyStory but considerably cheaper than AniMaker, another multi-agent pipeline (8 h 9 min); users can choose a backend according to their compute resources and API budget.

StoryDiffusion’s official multi-character mechanism takes only plain-text, per-shot prompts that tag which characters appear, with no interface for image-conditioned identity. ViMax supports a screenplay as input and automatically performs storyboarding, shot planning, character image generation, and video clip generation. article.headline: 多智能体框架把漫画改成忠实动画
article.lede: 先由创作者与审稿智能体反复打磨动画脚本和视觉分镜，再交给视频模型生成；角色、画风与剧情更贴近原作。
article.problem: 现有做法要么先把漫画转成文字再讲故事，原作的角色外观与画风在转述中丢失，人物还会在动漫与写实风格之间漂移；要么把漫画页直接喂给视频生成模型，而模型既不知道分镜格的阅读顺序，也不懂对话框的含义，于是讲错剧情，甚至把整页漫画当成视频帧。作者的关键观察是：视频模型已经会做动画，缺的是「读懂漫画」。
article.method: Manga2Animate 把任务拆成动画脚本与视觉分镜两个中间表示，每个表示都由创作者智能体生成，再由配对的审稿智能体逐项对照原漫画分镜格审查，共进行 2 轮迭代精修。脚本层按分镜格做组合式挑选（每轮 3 个候选，逐格选优再拼装），分镜层则整体挑选（每轮 3 个候选），并把分镜层发现的问题回传给脚本层，形成双层反馈。最终由视频模型以「整张分镜作为参考」或「分镜格作首帧」两种模式各生成 2 个候选，再由视频审稿智能体择优。
article.results: 在 8 个故事、每个 6 个分镜格的评测集上，主设置（Gemini + Seedance 2.0）的 I2VS 为 0.791，高于 AniMaker 的 0.775、ViMax 的 0.774/0.753/0.771 和 StoryMem 的 0.728，背景一致性 BC 达 0.958，动漫美学分 Waifu-v3 为 5.090、Shadow-v2 为 0.518。37 名参与者的用户研究中，分镜与视频两项均有超过 90% 的投票把「整体最佳」投给该方法。闭源流水线每个故事在脚本与分镜阶段平均调用 34.5 次 API、总成本约 5.65 美元，端到端耗时 24 分 49 秒。值得注意的是，直接把漫画页送进视频模型的方法 DD 高达 13.941（本方法 9.457），但作者强调 DD 只衡量运动幅度，不代表动作正确。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明不必替换视频生成模型，只要补上「读懂漫画」这一环并让每一步都可回溯到原分镜格，就能明显提升改编的忠实度。框架与具体图像、视频后端解耦，开源与商用模型都能接入，脚本和分镜也可以单独复用。
article.limitations: 评测集只有 8 个故事、每个 6 个分镜格，规模偏小，且自动指标与人眼判断并非一一对应（如 CSD、CIDS 等与原作风格和角色一致性相关的指标，仍依赖替代骨干网络）。作者也承认：基于随机生成模型的智能体流水线输出会逐次波动，API 可能限制版权或敏感内容，遇到草稿感强、画面杂乱或需要跨页上下文的分镜时仍会误读。
