page_papers.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
page_papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately 1.86times end-to-end inference speedup and a 66times reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information.
To this end, we introduce
MemT-1.0

Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn.
We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity.

To improve memory capabilities, we introduce

4.3

Scaling Protocol
We conduct all scaling experiments based on MemT-1.0-Nano under a controlled experimental protocol.
We explore two scaling aspects, including data and training scaling and memory capacity scaling.
The backbone architecture, training objectives, and evaluation protocol are kept consistent across different configurations unless otherwise specified.
We evaluate memory capability using the same memory benchmarks to characterize performance changes across different scales.
Specifically, for data and training scaling, we evaluate checkpoints along a continuous post-training trajectory spanning two consecutive epochs over the same corpus.
The model architecture and training corpus remain fixed, while cumulative training exposure and optimization steps increase throughout training.
For memory capacity scaling, we vary the number of memory experts in MoS to expand native memory capacity, while keeping the remaining architectural components and training configurations consistent.
By examining the resulting performance curves, we investigate how native memory capability evolves with additional post-training and increased memory capacity.
5.3

The results are presented in Figure
7
.
The 4-expert configuration consistently outperforms the 2-expert configuration across all three checkpoints, with relatively modest gains of 0.41 points in the average score and 1.42 points on LoCoMo at 200 post-training steps.
At 3,400 and 5,500 steps, increasing the number of experts improves the average score by 2.01 and 2.69 points, respectively, and LoCoMo by 3.25 and 2.20 points.
The 4-expert configuration continues to improve between these later checkpoints, with its average score increasing from 44.29 to 44.68 and its LoCoMo score rising from 53.51 to 55.58.
These results suggest that expanding memory capacity through additional experts benefits downstream performance, with larger gains at the later post-training checkpoints than at 200 steps.

Memory Capabilities
The results for memory capabilities are presented in Table
2
.
MemT-1.0-Flash and MemT-1.0-Nano achieve average scores of 50.6 and 47.0, respectively, ranking first and second among the parametric memory methods, ahead of the strongest parametric baseline by 12.5 and 8.9 points.
The results support native memory as a shared representation for diverse memory tasks without providing historical text in the query context.
The comparison between MemT-1.0-Flash and MemT-1.0-Nano reveals distinct strengths across tasks, though the aggregate gap between them remains modest and is driven mainly by memory operations.
MemT-1.0-Flash improves most clearly on memory operations, personalized understanding, conversational recall, and implicit learning.
MemT-1.0-Nano remains stronger on PerMemSafe and Memora, whereas MemT-1.0-Flash scores higher on Persona-grounded PS-Bench.
The advantage over parametric memory baselines also extends to long histories, where MemT-1.0 leads this group on LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench, and BEAM-1M.
However, the remaining errors on these benchmarks show that processing an extended trajectory does not by itself ensure reliable access to its contents.
Answering later queries requires earlier information to survive successive updates and remain distinguishable from other stored associations.
The results motivate further improvements in selective retention and query-dependent readout.
The strongest textual memory systems still achieve substantially higher performance, particularly on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-1M.
These systems provide explicit historical evidence at query time, whereas MemT-1.0 must recover the required information from its evolving states.
This gap is consistent with the difficulty of preserving detailed evidence through recurrent memory updates and highlights memory fidelity as an important target for further development.
6.3

The results are presented in Table

MemT-1.0-Flash performs comparably to its DeepSeek-V4-Flash backbone on average under the same noise setting.
The largest gain occurs on BigCodeBench-Hard, with smaller improvements on IFEval and LongBench v2.
Performance decreases modestly on MMLU-Pro, GPQA Diamond, and LiveCodeBench v6.
These results suggest that MemT-1.0-Flash broadly preserves general capabilities under distracting memories.
We next examine MemT-1.0-Nano, whose average decrease is around one point.
Under the noise setting, most benchmarks remain close to the backbone, with gains on IFEval and BigCodeBench-Hard.
The degradation is concentrated rather than uniform.
The largest decrease occurs on LiveCodeBench v6, followed by smaller decreases on LongBench v2, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA Diamond.
The contrasting changes on BigCodeBench-Hard and LiveCodeBench v6 further suggest that the impact varies even across benchmarks within the same capability domain.
Overall, the results support broad capability preservation alongside native memory, while highlighting that resistance to distracting memories should be evaluated at the task level.

PersonaMem follows the same shape but saturates much earlier.
Its accuracy rises quickly and then flattens out before reaching full rank, with the highest observed accuracy at an intermediate rank and no further improvement once additional components are retained.
Overall, memory performance improves as the retained rank increases, but the returns diminish quickly, and on PersonaMem they eventually vanish.
Because theoretical factor storage grows roughly linearly with the retained rank, increasing the rank yields diminishing returns in downstream accuracy.

Case Study and Discussion
To better understand how native memory affects agent behavior, we illustrate a representative task from SWE-bench Verified involving the two-digit year parsing logic in Django’s
parse_http_date
function.
We compare execution trajectories under the No Experience, Textual Experience, and Native Memory settings. Without experience, the agent modifies the relevant parsing logic shortly after locating the implementation, introducing targeted reproduction and verification steps later in the execution. In contrast, agents in both the Textual Experience and Native Memory settings construct reproduction tests before applying modifications. In the MemT-1.0-Nano trajectory, the agent further revisits a boundary condition after its initial modification, corrects the implementation, and performs additional verification.
These observations show how stored procedural experience can guide task execution without appearing in textual context. Together with the benchmark improvements, they demonstrate that MemT-1.0 can reuse procedural experience to improve agentic task performance. This supports its potential for developing self-evolving agents:
experience from past interactions can be stored in native memory and applied to new tasks.
Several challenges remain. The current framework relies on externally constructed experience, making its effectiveness dependent on experience quality and retrieval. Storing experience also introduces computation, so reduced textual context does not necessarily imply lower overall execution costs. Extending experience reuse into an autonomous continual learning process remains an open direction.
Future work will explore the co-evolution of the harness and MemT-1.0 through continued interaction with the environment. The harness can improve experience acquisition and selection, while MemT-1.0 learns to reuse that experience more effectively. Together, these advances could support continual learning in self-evolving agents for long-horizon tasks.
8

Limitations and Discussion
Despite the progress of MemT-1.0 in native memory, it still has several limitations.
The fixed-size memory state imposes a capacity constraint.
For the fixed memory, MemT-1.0 maintains an
O
⁡
(
1

state with respect to the interaction history length
N
N
.
Compared with methods whose stored representations grow as
O
⁡
(
N

O(N)
, this bounded state has limited capacity to preserve detailed historical information.
As interactions accumulate, new information must be incorporated into an existing representation, creating trade-offs between retaining earlier details and adding recent information.
The resulting loss of memory fidelity remains a challenge for tasks requiring precise recall.
At the same time, a fixed-size state offers opportunities beyond reducing storage.
Each update incorporates new information into a representation, which has already been shaped by earlier interactions.
This enables successive compression of accumulated history.
Compared with maintaining a growing collection of historical records, this recurrent organization may provide a basis for latent reflection.
It potentially allows iterative consolidation of experience within the memory state.
Such a mechanism could support online self-evolution by allowing accumulated experience to influence subsequent behavior.
Finally, the relationship between local memory and hyper memory also deserves further study.
Local memory represents information accumulated during interaction, while hyper memory encodes learned capabilities for storing and utilizing that information.
An important question is whether experience accumulated in local memory can be consolidated into hyper-memory parameters through further training, and how knowledge encoded in hyper memory can be instantiated and adapted through local memory.
Therefore, memory capability itself can be viewed as a higher-order form of learned information.
Exploring this relationship may help connect adaptation within individual interactions with improvements in memory capability across tasks.
9

Conclusion
In this report, we presented MemT-1.0, a family of memory foundation models that integrates persistent memory into model computation.
Through the token-level stable memory updates, Mixture-of-Storage, a deliberate backbone preparation, and a two-stage training pipeline, MemT-1.0 supports efficient storage and utilization of historical information.
Both models outperform the evaluated parametric memory baselines on average, while largely preserving the general capabilities of their respective backbones under the noise setting.
Applications to coding agents further demonstrate that native memory can internalize procedural experience to improve task success and execution consistency.
Future work will focus on improving long-term memory, scaling memory capacity, and reducing the cost of memory updates.
We will explore autonomous experience acquisition and continual memory consolidation across tasks, moving toward agents learning through memory-native evolution.

article.headline: MemT-1.0：让记忆成为模型原生能力
article.lede: 记忆基础模型MemT-1.0用门控DeltaNet-2做token级稳定记忆更新，并用Mixture-of-Storag
article.problem: 当前大模型的记忆大多依赖外部上下文或外挂检索系统，模型本身无法在长期交互中持续累积并复用信息。作者此前提出的Metis首次把记忆作为基础模型的原生能力，但用token选择方式实现记忆更新，在稳定性和容量扩展上受限。MemT-1.0要解决的就是如何在模型计算内部稳定地写入记忆，并把原生记忆容量做得更大。
article.method: MemT-1.0在Metis的动态局部记忆与可训练超记忆结构上做升级，用基于Gated DeltaNet-2的token级稳定更新机制替换原有的token选择。为扩展容量，作者引入Mixture-of-Storage（MoS），通过增加记忆专家数量放大原生记忆。训练上采用继续预训练加后训练的两阶段流水线，配合34B tokens训练数据和自研的高效训练、推理基础设施。
article.results: 在记忆能力评测中，MemT-1.0-Flash与MemT-1.0-Nano平均分分别为50.6和47.0，在参数化记忆方法中排第一、第二，比最强参数化基线高12.5和8.9分。消融显示后训练相对CPT检查点在记忆任务上平均提升约10.69分；MoS从2个专家增至4个专家，在200步时平均分与LoCoMo分别提升0.41和1.42分，到3400步和5500步时平均分提升2.01和2.69分，LoCoMo提升3.25和2.20分。效率方面，Nano相对全上下文推理在64K、128K、256K长度上端到端加速约1.20×、1.86×和3.99×；查询TTFT稳定在约104–112ms，而全上下文在128K和256K时升至约257ms和445ms，对应约2.44×和4.19×的查询首字延迟加速。
article.why_it_matters: 把记忆放进模型计算而非上下文窗口，意味着历史交互可以直接改变模型状态，为在长程任务中积累并复用经验的自我演化智能体提供了可训练的基础形态。
article.limitations: 固定大小记忆状态相对交互历史长度为O(1)，细节保真度受限，文本记忆系统在LongMemEval-S和BEAM-1M等基准上仍明显更高。此外经验仍需外部构造，效果依赖经验质量与检索，减少文本上下文也不必然降低整体执行成本。

page_papers.title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
page_papers.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

]

Since each edit builds on the results of prior turns, multi-turn image editing is inherently causal

in UMMs.
Such a design enables later edits to draw on the accumulated interaction history while responding to new user instructions.
However, existing methods often exhibit drift after only a few editing turns (see Fig.

for examples), manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable

inconsistent

During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories.
To overcome these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a training paradigm for UMMs based on AR diffusion that enables stable and consistent multi-turn image editing. First, we introduce Single-Turn

istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
) to counteract visual-quality drift across editing turns.
Our design follows two observations: 1) a single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation
[
72
]
; and 2) editing models can execute multiple actions in one turn
[
73
]
(see Fig.
4
).
These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of a multi-turn student.
Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into a
bundled prompt
that expresses their cumulative editing intent as a single edit to the source image.
Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing a quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation.
The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training
[
29
,
1
]
, conditioning each edit on its own imperfect outputs.
At each turn, a DMD loss
[

,
94
,
16
,
44
]
aligns the student’s rollout output distribution with the teacher’s single-turn output distribution for the same cumulative editing intent.
This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation.
However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig.
4
), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency.
To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories

,
31
,
99
]
.
We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages.
1)
Teacher-Forcing Warmup
: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories.
2)
Teacher-Forcing Regularization
: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with a lower weight as a regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation
[
97
,
78
,
8
]
.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns.
To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Bench’s
[
6
]
assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality.
We additionally introduce
Pixel
\mathrm{Pixel}
, a metric based on image matching
[
24
]
that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs.
MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns.
In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with a single-turn teacher;
2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.

5  Conclusion
We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs.
Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using a teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision.
Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the history–output dependencies needed for content preservation.
Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.

article.headline: 单轮蒸馏加教师强制，稳定多轮图像编辑
article.lede: 提出 MT Forcing，用单轮蒸馏与教师强制指导，缓解自回归多模态模型多轮图像编辑的漂移。
article.problem: 多轮图像编辑要求模型按一串指令逐步修改同一张图，但现有方法往往几轮后就出现漂移：视觉质量不稳定，伪影累积、细节退化；内容不一致，未请求区域被改动，先前编辑也保不住。作者将原因归结为训练与推理条件不匹配造成的暴露偏差——训练时条件于参考历史，推理时却递归条件于模型自己生成的历史。
article.method: MT Forcing 包含两个互补目标。Single-Turn DMD 把截至当前轮的全部指令重组为一个 bundled prompt，让冻结的单轮教师在源图上一次性完成累计编辑，并用 DMD 损失把学生自 rollout 的每轮输出分布对齐到该教师分布，从而避免递归误差进入监督信号。Teacher-Forcing Guidance 则在参考轨迹上用 flow matching 监督历史相关转移，先做 warmup，蒸馏时再以较低权重作为正则，补足单纯逐轮分布匹配无法保证的跨轮一致性。
article.results: 在 MTEdit-Bench 的 step-wise 子基准（100 个会话、每会话 8 轮）上，Turn 8 时 SenseNova-U1 的 IF 和 CC 分别提升 7.45 和 6.82，SenseNova-U1.5 分别提升 4.65 和 4.46；SenseNova-U1.5 的 DRS 在全程维持 4.20–4.35，基线从 4.09 降至 3.03。其八轮平均 Pixel 从 6.34 降至 0.74，降低 88.4%。消融中完整方法八轮平均为 IF 9.66、CC 8.40、DRS 4.30、Pixel 0.74，优于仅 Single-Turn DMD 的 9.02/7.64/4.12/2.51 和仅 Teacher-Forcing Guidance 的 9.10/7.83/3.92/2.74。
article.why_it_matters: 多轮编辑是交互式视觉创作的核心交互形式，漂移问题直接决定模型能否被连续使用。MT Forcing 把自 rollout 分布匹配与参考轨迹监督结合，为自回归扩散 UMM 的多轮训练提供了一个可复用的训练范式。
article.limitations: 单轮教师只约束每轮输出的边际分布，无法唯一确定学生对历史的自回归依赖；λ_TF 较大时输出会变模糊，质量与一致性需要权衡。实验仅覆盖两个 SenseNova 模型和 MTEdit-Bench 的 8 轮、100 会话子基准，论文也未给出训练与推理开销的具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: MT Forcing 总览：单轮 DMD 将学生自 rollout 的边际分布对齐单轮教师分布，教师强制指导在参考轨迹上监督历史相关转移，整体训练先 warmup 后联合 DMD 与教师强制正则。

figure.caption: {Overview of MT Forcing.} (a)~Single-Turn DMD matches student rollout marginals to single-turn teacher distributions. (b)~Teacher-Forcing Guidance supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories via flow matching to encourage cross-turn consistency. (c)~Overall training: teacher-forcing warmup followed by DMD with teacher-forcing regularization.

page_papers.title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References
page_papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.

Abstract
Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce
BlenderWorld
, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks.
BlenderWorld
comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.
1
Introduction
Visual agents built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret visual references, operate design tools, and refine their outputs through visual inspection
(
Qwen Team, 2026
;
OpenAI, 2026
)
. These agents have gained traction in two-dimensional (2D) design tasks, including webpage, poster, layout, and presentation creation
(
Si et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026a
)
, and are increasingly being extended to three-dimensional (3D) modeling and scene creation.
3D modeling is a crucial task and provides a practically valuable testbed for visual agents. First, it involves complex, long-horizon workflows in which agents must coordinate extensive tool use across dozens of interaction turns. Second, it supports applications ranging from everyday personal projects to professional scientific visualization, while spanning scales from individual household objects to entire city blocks. Third, mastering this domain requires spatial reasoning, active visual verification, and sustained tool manipulation within open-ended digital environments, all of which are essential for extending the productivity frontier of AI agents.
However, evaluating agents on practical 3D modeling tasks presents three major challenges: environment selection, task coverage, and output assessment. First, evaluation requires an accessible environment that supports 3D creation, editing, and inspection, yet few available environments provide all three capabilities. We therefore turn to Blender, an open-source platform that supports these capabilities through Python scripting and Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces and has been used for agent-driven creation and editing
(
Hu et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2024
;
Noor et al., 2026
)
. Second, practical requests vary widely in their reference sources and design goals, ranging from reconstruction based on photographs or illustrations to open-ended design briefs. A realistic benchmark must therefore cover diverse application contexts and user requirements. Existing Blender-based benchmarks typically focus on narrower task classes: 3DCodeBench and 3DHarnessBench emphasize individual objects
(
Gao et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026b
)
, BlenderBench contains a small set of camera and scene-editing tasks
(
Yin et al., 2026
)
, and SceneActBench covers broader scenes but focuses on predefined geometric objectives
(
Zhao et al., 2026b
)
. Finally, realistic requests often lack ground-truth 3D assets, while open-ended briefs may admit multiple valid solutions. Reliable evaluation must therefore assess both visual properties and underlying structures, requiring evidence beyond what a single rendered view can reveal.
Figure 1:
BlenderWorld
taxonomy and examples. References are shown left/top and GPT-6-Astra results right/bottom.
To address these challenges, we introduce
BlenderWorld
, a benchmark for evaluating visual agents on realistic 3D reconstruction, modification, and design tasks in Blender.
BlenderWorld
contains 223 tasks spanning 16 practical application scenarios, organized into 9 main categories and 22 subcategories (Fig.
1
). The tasks represent diverse user needs, driven by text, image, and video references, with 59 tasks additionally including structured specification files. Agents must synthesize these inputs to produce fully editable Blender projects. To rigorously evaluate these diverse deliverables without a single canonical asset, we design an evidence-routed evaluation protocol. An automatic agent selects and renders multiple task-conditioned views, which are then assessed via 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics and continuous visual-quality dimensions. Crucially, we employ a dual-judge system: a VLM-as-Judge for visual and spatial properties, and an Agent-as-Judge for direct programmatic inspection of scene structures that bypass visual shortcuts. Benchmarking 13 frontier models reveals a stark reality: while models can generate visually plausible outputs and plan extensive tool invocations, they profoundly struggle to translate passive visual feedback into structurally sound 3D corrections.
Contributions.
We summarize our main contributions as follows:
(1)
We introduce
BlenderWorld
, a comprehensive benchmark of 223 realistic Blender tasks spanning 22 subcategories, covering diverse text, image, and video reference sources alongside specifications for practical 3D reconstruction, modification, and design requests.
(2)
We provide a unified evaluation protocol that combines task-conditioned multi-view rendering, task-specific binary rubrics (verified via both visual judges and programmatic scene-state inspection), and a holistic visual quality assessment.
(3)
We evaluate agents built on thirteen frontier models under a shared task and protocol, establishing strong baselines. Our results reveal that while top-performing models like GPT-6-Astra achieve high overall fused scores (79.9), they still fail to fully satisfy all task requirements, reaching a perfect pass rate on only 42.2% of tasks.
(4)
Through in-depth trajectory and failure analysis, we expose fundamental bottlenecks in current 3D agents: they frequently rely on 2D visual shortcuts (e.g., view-dependent geometry) and profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence, physical contact constraints, and translating passive visual inspection into effective structural refinements.

Illustrating the end-to-end workflow from diversified task and reference curation, application-grounded brief specification with dual-track validation, to multi-model verified and frozen binary rubrics.
3.2
Benchmark Construction
Inspired by practical uses of 3D content in social media, we organize task coverage along two dimensions: category taxonomy and application scenarios. These dimensions guide
task specification and MLLM-assisted brief generation. We then check
the resulting briefs for structural and semantic consistency before
deriving task-specific rubrics (Figure
2
).
Task and reference diversity.
Task design varies both the production requirements and how references guide the output.
(1) Production requirements.
We vary the target domain, scene complexity, user expertise, and request length. For example, a teaching task may briefly describe a biological cell with multiple internal structures.
(2) Reference use.
We curate diverse reference images spanning interiors, architecture, products, mechanical structures, and natural environments. An MLLM then assesses image quality and structural complexity and we favor images with clearly identifiable structures and detailed information about shape, layout, or materials.
We assign each visual reference one of three roles:
recreation
preserves the main shapes and spatial relationships,
modification
makes requested changes while retaining specified structures, and
reference-based design
draws on the depicted form, style, or layout to develop a new design. The reference image and its assigned role guide both initial task generation and request rewriting.
Application-grounded specification.
Given the production target and reference role, we situate each specification in a realistic application scenario. For example, construction reports emphasize structural relationships, whereas product presentations emphasize visibility and appearance. We express each specification as a natural-language request that states the production goal and key requirements. Tasks with detailed specifications may also include
Markdown
,
YAML
, or
JSON
attachments containing dimensions, material lists, camera settings, or asset budgets. The request explicitly references these files, which retain the details required to complete the task.
Dual-track validation.
We validate each brief for structural and semantic consistency.
Structural checks
ensure that the metadata are compatible, images and attachments are accessible, structured files can be parsed, and the brief explicitly requests both rendered outputs and an editable project. For
semantic review
, a model distinct from the task generator independently examines the initial specification, rewritten request, reference image, and attachments together. It checks image–text alignment, constraint consistency, preservation of key requirements, and task feasibility. Tasks that fail validation are fed back into the generation process for revision.
Rubric generation.
A generator extracts requirements from validated briefs, converting them into binary criteria with source links. Each criterion is assigned to one of 13 categories, weighted (3/2/1 for major/secondary/detail), and designated an evidence type:
render
(for visual properties) or
scene_summary
(for project/file inspection). We iteratively refine drafts via pilot evaluations (using GPT-5.6-Sol) to flag ambiguities. Next, at least two independent reviewer models cross-check coverage, source support, and evaluability using concrete counterexamples. An editor resolves flagged issues, with any semantic changes triggering re-review, before freezing the final schema (details in Appendix
B
).

BlenderWorld
contains 223 production briefs across 9 main task
categories and 22 subcategories (Figure

architecture and interiors, products and manufacturing, vehicles and machinery,

The tasks serve 16 application scenarios, with the largest shown in

Specification files in Markdown, YAML, or JSON accompany 59 tasks (26.5%),
adding requirements on dimensions, materials, and camera settings
(Figure

co-occur, combining visual guidance with explicit production constraints.
Evaluation uses 2,651 binary criteria across 13 rubric categories, with 6–22
criteria per task (mean 11.9).
Function and geometry together account for 41.7% of criteria. Of all
criteria, 83.3% have major importance (weight 3). For judging, 41.8% of
criteria are assigned to rendered views and 58.2% to scene inspection. Explicit requirements from

4
Evaluation and Metrics
4.1
Evaluation Protocol
For each task, an agent uses a harness equipped with Blender MCP to review the task brief and any provided references or attachments,
construct the scene, and save the requested deliverables. We archive the
agent’s final workspace, including the editable
.blend
project,
exported media, and auxiliary files. This artifact package is then processed
through automatic agent rendering to produce more visual evidence, and finally to get rubric and dimension scores with model judgment.
Automatic Agent Render (AaR).
Given the task query, rubrics, reference files, and submitted deliverables,
AaR selects eight complementary views to reveal task-relevant details.
This adaptive view selection aims to make the required properties observable
while maintaining a common rendering budget across submissions.
The rendering agent opens the submitted Blender projects and renders each
view at
1024
×
1024
1024\times 1024
resolution with 64 samples using Cycles.
It may adjust cameras, framing, and rendering settings, but must preserve
the submitted geometry, materials, lighting, animation, and color management.
Invalid views can be re-rendered within two attempts, but defects in the submitted work must
not be repaired. Visual judging proceeds only when newly rendered views are
available; otherwise, the evaluation is marked as failed.
The original exported media remain available as additional evidence
alongside the evaluator-generated views.
Evidence-routed rubric judging.
Each rubric specifies a binary criterion, an evidence type, and an importance
weight. We route criteria to two complementary judges according to the
evidence needed to verify them.
Agent-as-Judge
handles
scene_summary
criteria, which cover
requirements on internal scene structure and native-file properties that
cannot be reliably verified from rendered views alone. The agent Judger
inspects the deliverables through multiple tools provided by Blender and records
evidence about internal states. Judger also consults visual evidence when necessary and emits a binary decision with
supporting evidence for each assigned criterion.
VLM-as-Judge
handles
render
criteria,
which cover requirements on visual appearance, spatial layout, and motion
that can be verified from rendered views and exported media.
It receives the task context together with three evidence groups: AaR views, original exported media,
and additional ordered frames sampled from exported videos.
When visual evidence conflicts, original exported media take precedence
over other views to keep scoring faithful to the
agent’s final deliverables. Moreover, a separate blind pass produces
prompt-free descriptions of submission and reference images as auxiliary
grounding evidence. These descriptions supplement the images and are used
only by the visual judge. Unsupported rubric claims receive zero.
Dimension Judging.
To address the limitations of binary rubrics in quantifying continuous perceptual attributes, the VLM additionally evaluates artifact quality along eight dimensions: scene fidelity, physical plausibility, style and color, realism, spatial layout, proportion and scale, lighting and materials, and completeness. Each dimension receives an integer score from 1 to 10 based on the task requirements and available references, with a justification grounded in the visual evidence. Detailed scoring guidelines are provided in Appendix
C
.

5
Experiments
5.1
Evaluation Setup
Models and environment.
We compare thirteen agents on the same 223 tasks: 78 Text and 145 multimodal tasks with image or video references. GPT-6-Astra and GPT-5.6-Sol use Codex, while all other agents use Claude Code. Each agent is tested once per task, operating at its highest available reasoning intensity. Agents work in isolated Linux containers, each equipped with one NVIDIA GPU and a pre-installed Linux version of Blender LTS. Crucially, artifact generation and evaluation are executed in strictly separated containers; the evaluation rubrics remain completely invisible to the agents during the generation phase to prevent rubric hacking. Shell, file, image-viewing, and Blender MCP tools support scene creation, rendering, inspection, and revision. Appendix
D
details the tools and runtime settings.
Evaluation metrics.
Following the scoring protocol in Section
4
, we report
mean scores on text-only tasks (Text), multimodal tasks (MM), and all
223 tasks (Score). Rubric / Dimension reports the two component means
on a 0–100 scale, measuring weighted requirement satisfaction and overall
visual quality. Perfect is the percentage of tasks passing every
rubric criterion. Submissions without a
.blend
file automatically
receive a score of zero because they cannot be rendered for evaluation
and do not meet the task’s delivery requirements. For generation
trajectories, we report mean turns, mean output tokens, and the
mean number of tool calls per task. To balance computational cost and evaluation accuracy, we employ
GPT-5.6-terra
for automatic agent rendering, rubric judging, and dimension judging. A detailed analysis of the judge model is provided in Appendix
E.1
.
5.2
Main Results
GPT-6-Astra leads across all completion metrics.
It achieves an overall Score of 79.9, ahead of Opus-5 at 73.0
(Table
2
).
Its lead over Opus-5 is larger on multimodal tasks
(80.7 vs. 72.1) than on text-only tasks (78.6 vs. 74.8).
GPT-6-Astra also ranks first in both Rubric and Dimension, indicating
advantages in both requirement satisfaction and overall visual quality.
However, satisfying every rubric criterion remains challenging.
GPT-6-Astra achieves a Perfect rate of 42.2%, compared with 25.6% for
Opus-5 and at most 15.7% for the remaining agents.
Thus, even the highest-scoring agents fully satisfy the rubric
on fewer than half of the benchmark tasks.
GPT-5.6-Sol matches DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on multimodal tasks and achieves a slightly
higher overall Score, yet their rollout statistics differ substantially.
GPT-5.6-Sol averages 39.9K output tokens and 44.0 tool calls per task,
compared with 209K tokens and 168 calls for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
The difference in tool use includes GPT-5.6-Sol’s fewer Blender executions and
image view tool calls (Figure
6
).
GPT-6-Astra reinforces this pattern: it achieves the highest overall Score
while using fewer output tokens and tool calls than both Opus-5 and
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
These patterns suggest different balances between planning
and iterative tool use.
The GPT Series Models may favor more extensive planning before acting, whereas DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash relies more on repeated execution and inspection to refine its scenes. Further trajectory analysis could further clarify how planning and iterative refinement contribute to scene quality and interaction efficiency.

5.3.2
Tool Use
Tool Allocation Discrepancy vs. Interaction Volume.
As decoupled in Figure
6
, examining proportional tool allocation alongside absolute volume reveals fundamentally different agent strategies. While top performers like
GPT-6-Astra
and
Opus-5
allocate similar budget fractions to
Blender execution
and
Image viewing
, their absolute workloads diverge substantially:
Opus-5
requires roughly twice as many executions (45.5 vs. 23.3) and views (27.1 vs. 15.0) per task, alongside an inflated volume of auxiliary operations. In contrast,
Grok-4.6
uniquely leads in
Asset operations
(13%), demonstrating a new paradigm by prioritizing asset manipulation.
Passive Inspection vs. Effective Corrective Feedback.
Conversely, higher visual call volume does not inherently guarantee effective artifact refinement. Models such as
Seed2.1pro-0915
and
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
make the most frequent visual queries across all agents (33.9 and 31.3 calls per task), yet their multimodal scores remain moderate or poor. In stark contrast,
GPT-6-Astra
achieves the top multimodal score (80.7) and rubric completion (87.3) with merely 15.0 image inspections.
Viewing volume captures the opportunity for feedback without ensuring that the agent can diagnose defects or enact valid corrections.
These aggregate statistics show that more visual inspections do not necessarily coincide with higher scores. They do not establish how effectively each agent uses visual feedback.

Failure Analysis

Failure Analysis and Bottlenecks.
A qualitative audit of failure modes (Figure
7
) reveals four recurring failure mechanisms across agents.
(1)
Missing Dynamic Interactions
: In Figure
7
a, GPT-6-Astra satisfies object presence but fails to generate physical interactions, leaving the canvas blank without converging trails.
(2)
Viewpoint Inconsistency
: Figure
7
b demonstrates a lack of true 3D spatial coherence, where people visible in the submitted camera vanish entirely under alternate viewing angles, revealing brittle, view-dependent shortcuts.
(3)
Fine-grained Geometric Distortions
: The generated lion cub exhibits unnatural, finger-like paws and distorted eyes, reflecting the model’s inability to inspect and refine high-frequency anatomical details.
(4)
Contact Constraint Violations
: The character visibly floats above the lawn, underscoring weak spatial construction and physical simulation ability.
Together, these patterns show that current agents tend to rely on 2D visual shortcuts to make things look right at a glance, but they still struggle to build genuinely solid and physically sound 3D scenes. More thorough failure analysis is provided in Appendix
E.8
.
6
Conclusion
We introduced
BlenderWorld
, a benchmark for evaluating visual agents on practical 3D reconstruction, modification, and design in Blender. Its 223 tasks span text-only, image-conditioned, and video-conditioned requests across 9 categories and 16 application scenarios, requiring editable projects and task-specific deliverables. Our evaluation combines task-conditioned multi-view rendering, scene inspection, 2,651 binary criteria, and visual quality assessment to measure both requirement satisfaction and artifact quality. Across 13 agents, GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall score of 79.9, yet passes every rubric criterion on only 42.2% of tasks. Qualitative analyses expose incomplete interactions, inconsistencies across views, geometric distortions, and contact violations, highlighting the challenge of translating task requirements and visual references into coherent 3D structure and behavior.
BlenderWorld
provides a basis for comparing complete agents and diagnosing these gaps, supporting future work on agents that verify and refine their artifacts against both visual evidence and explicit constraints.
7
Future Work
We plan to extend BlenderWorld in five directions, covering evaluation,
task design, and experimental scope.
Interactive and Parametric Evaluation.
We plan to give the agent judge Computer-Use Agent (CUA) tools to interact
with
.blend
projects and check rigs, animations, and simulations.
By manipulating specified controls and inspecting the resulting states,
the judge could test whether mechanisms behave as intended. We will pair
structured parameter extraction with deterministic scripts for reproducible
checks of dimensions, tolerances, and geometric constraints. For
precision-critical tasks, reference solutions and geometric metrics could
supplement rubric-based judgments. For example, voxel
intersection-over-union would be computed using consistent alignment and
scale conventions.
Higher Complexity and Task Diversification.
We will expand the benchmark to cover more categories and application
scenarios, with an emphasis on demanding professional workflows. Planned
tasks include localized editing, mesh fault diagnosis and repair, topology
optimization, and retopology, alongside scene creation from scratch. We
also plan to introduce engineering drawings and dimensional tolerances as
richer specifications, and tasks that require revisions to previously
delivered projects. These tasks will assess whether agents preserve
existing content, satisfy interacting constraints, and keep projects
editable as they revise them.
Expert-Aligned and Fine-Grained Rubrics.
We will work with professional 3D artists to iteratively refine the rubrics
to reflect practical acceptance standards, with particular attention to
modeling reliability, geometric stability, structural consistency, and
production readiness. For organic subjects and other cases in which binary
checks offer limited discrimination, we will explore graded assessments
of individual parts against reference materials. Expert review and
agreement studies will guide rubric calibration and assess consistency
across viewpoints, animation frames, and application domains.
Multi-DCC Ecosystem and Asset Integration.
We aim to support other mainstream digital content creation (DCC)
applications, including Maya and 3ds Max, as well as additional Blender
versions and MCP tools. Shared task specifications and comparable checks
of submitted artifacts will support evaluation across applications. We
also plan to integrate external asset repositories, such as the Mixamo
motion library, to study workflows that retrieve, adapt, and compose
existing assets. Evaluating settings with and without access to these
repositories will help assess how external assets affect performance.
Broader Model, Reasoning, Harness, and Platform Coverage.
We plan to evaluate more models across supported thinking-effort settings
and agent harnesses. Within-model studies will vary reasoning effort under
a fixed harness, or compare harnesses with reasoning settings and tool
access kept comparable where supported. Experiments will run under
documented resource budgets and report task quality together with token
usage, latency, tool calls, and cost. Repeated runs on representative
configurations will estimate variability and assess the stability of
rankings. We will also extend the current Linux-based evaluation to Windows
and macOS, and explore providing models with CUA tools for operating
Blender through its graphical interface. This would let us observe how
models navigate the viewport, manipulate objects, and use visual feedback
to inspect and revise their work. Comparisons with API/MCP-based workflows
will examine how task performance, interaction efficiency, and failure
modes differ across interfaces and operating systems.

Appendix B
Rubric Construction
From sources to acceptance conditions.
The generator reads the query, actual references, and full attachments,
then records binding requirements with source locations and verification
methods. This ledger covers structure, space, appearance, function,
presentation, and delivery as applicable. Requirements are extracted before
compression, preserving both explicit constraints and allowed design freedom.
Related requirements form a coherent acceptance unit, such as a component,
interface, functional outcome, or deliverable. Each criterion records its
identifier, subject, source, category, importance, evidence type, and
self-contained pass/fail conditions. A merged criterion passes only when
all
constituent conditions hold; its fail condition is the logical
complement. Major, secondary, and detail criteria receive weights 3, 2,
and 1.
Category vocabulary.
Each criterion receives one of the 13 categories in
Table
4
, according to its principal focus.
Its full acceptance conditions retain any requirements spanning several
aspects. The six ledger dimensions guide source coverage; these categories
describe the resulting criteria. The
holistic
category is a

Findings cite sources and a counterexample: a valid output that would

Appendix D
Runtime and Resource Accounting
D.1
Runtime Configuration
The reference runtime uses Blender 4.2.10 LTS, Codex CLI 0.147.0,
Claude Code 2.1.220, and Node.js 22.17.0. GPT-6-Astra and GPT-5.6-Sol use
Codex; the other eleven systems use Claude Code. MiniMax-M3’s 48-task
batch uses Claude Code 2.1.241. Isolated Linux workspaces provide one
NVIDIA GPU per task, a virtual display, and Cycles rendering through
OptiX or CUDA. The final workspace is archived for evaluation.
D.2
Available Tools
The harness provides shell execution, file operations, and local image
viewing. Agents can write scripts, launch Blender in background mode,
inspect renders, and revise their projects. FFmpeg and ImageMagick support
media processing, alongside NumPy, Pillow, SciPy, and ImageIO.

D.3
Resource Accounting
We record resource counters (including output tokens, interaction turns, and tool calls) across the full suite of 223 tasks for all evaluated agents. These counters incorporate unsuccessful calls. Output tokens reflect provider-reported completion counts. A turn is uniformly defined as a single model-response round within the agent runtime.
As shown in Figure
6

Blender execution
(direct Blender/Python and MCP code calls);

(reference images, renders, and viewport screenshots);

(discovery, status, retrieval, generation, import, and texture assignment); and

These metrics strictly describe requested operations, rather than guaranteed successful executions or matched compute costs.

article.headline: 3D建模智能体基准：最高79.9分
article.lede: 223个3D任务、2,651条二元评分项，13款模型；GPT-6-Astra 79.9分，但全项通过率仅42.2%。
article.problem: 多模态大模型已能通过代码或软件操作创建3D内容，但真实工作流要求从文本、图像、视频和规格文件中推断形状、材质、布局与光照，并交付可编辑工程。现有Blender基准多聚焦单个物体、固定视角或预设几何目标，缺少对开放式真实3D创作请求的覆盖。
article.method: 作者构建BlenderWorld，含223个任务，覆盖9大类、22子类、16个应用场景，145个任务带图像或视频参考，59个附带Markdown、YAML或JSON规格文件。评测采用证据路由：自动渲染代理选择8个任务相关视角，以1024×1024、64采样Cycles渲染；2,651条任务特定二元评分项分别交给VLM裁判和Agent裁判，后者直接检查.blend工程结构，再融合8维视觉质量分。
article.results: 13款模型中，GPT-6-Astra总分79.9（Rubric 87.3、Dimension 72.6），Opus-5为73.0，GPT-5.6-Sol为67.7；多模态任务上GPT-6-Astra为80.7，高于Opus-5的72.1。全项通过率仅42.2%，Opus-5为25.6%，其余模型最高15.7%。评分项中41.8%依赖渲染证据、58.2%依赖场景检查；裁判与人类总体一致率82.99%，但分差小于10时降至68.57%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把3D创作从单物体、固定视角推进到可编辑工程与多视图一致性评测，为诊断智能体在空间结构、物理接触和迭代修正上的短板提供了统一基线。
article.limitations: 每个任务每模型只运行一次，未报告重复运行方差；评分依赖自动裁判，小分差样本与人类一致率仅68.57%，且未引入参考解或几何IoU等确定性指标，结论仍需谨慎。

page_papers.title: RL Starts before RL: On Policy Distillation for Better Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves reasoning, but its performance depends on the policy from which training begins. We study on-policy distillation (OPD) as a preparation stage for RL and ask whether its benefits extend beyond improvements in the distilled model's initial accuracy. Under shared RL settings, students initialized with OPD reach higher final performance than those trained with direct RL or supervised fine-tuning followed by RL. This advantage can emerge even when OPD produces little immediate improvement in accuracy. Pre-RL Pass@k does not fully explain the benefit: similar or even higher values do not necessarily lead to better performance after RL. Behavioral analyses point to alignment with the teacher's distribution beyond top-1 agreement as a possible explanation. Such alignment may favor higher-quality reasoning paths while retaining alternatives that RL can further refine using outcome feedback. We further examine how trajectory sources and divergence objectives affect the value of distillation for subsequent RL. Standard reverse-KL OPD performs better before RL, but forward-KL OPD overtakes it afterward. Student rollouts outperform teacher rollouts under both objectives before and after RL. These findings highlight the importance of both objective choice and the states receiving supervision for subsequent RL. Our results support OPD as preparation for RL and favor forward KL when OPD is followed by RL in our comparison.

Abstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) improves reasoning, but its performance depends on the policy from which training begins. We study on-policy distillation (OPD) as a preparation stage for RL and ask whether its benefits extend beyond improvements in the distilled model’s initial accuracy. Under shared RL settings, students initialized with OPD reach higher final performance than those trained with direct RL or supervised fine-tuning followed by RL. This advantage can emerge even when OPD produces little immediate improvement in accuracy. Pre-RL Pass@
k
k
does not fully explain the benefit: similar or even higher values do not necessarily lead to better performance after RL. Behavioral analyses point to alignment with the teacher’s distribution beyond top-1 agreement as a possible explanation. Such alignment may favor higher-quality reasoning paths while retaining alternatives that RL can further refine using outcome feedback. We further examine how trajectory sources and divergence objectives affect the value of distillation for subsequent RL. Standard reverse-KL OPD performs better before RL, but forward-KL OPD overtakes it afterward. Student rollouts outperform teacher rollouts under both objectives before and after RL. These findings highlight the importance of both objective choice and the states receiving supervision for subsequent RL. Our results support OPD as preparation for RL and favor forward KL when OPD is followed by RL in our comparison.

Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important approach to improving reasoning in language models
[
25
,
5
,
31
]
. By learning from feedback on complete responses, a model can improve its ability to solve tasks through repeated training. Its final performance, however, also depends on the policy from which training begins. The starting policy shapes what the model generates during training and how it responds to feedback. Preparing the model before RL is therefore an important part of the training process. The challenge is that a model’s current accuracy does not necessarily tell us how well it will learn afterward.
A common preparation step is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on solutions generated by a stronger teacher
[
16
,
12
]
. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers another route: the student generates its own responses, and the teacher provides a distribution over possible next tokens along those responses
[
1
,
19
]
. This allows the student to learn from teacher feedback on the prefixes it actually encounters. Although OPD is typically evaluated by the performance of the distilled student, the resulting policy can also serve as a starting point for RL. This raises the central question of our study: does OPD prepare students for better RL, beyond improving their immediate accuracy?

These findings motivate a closer look at how OPD changes the student’s distribution over reasoning continuations. Agreement with the teacher’s most likely token captures only one aspect of this distribution. In our comparisons, SFT can achieve slightly higher top-1 agreement than OPD while showing greater distributional divergence and lower token uncertainty. Strong agreement on the preferred token can therefore coexist with a more concentrated policy, leaving unclear how much flexibility remains for subsequent learning. OPD shows closer distributional alignment while retaining uncertainty over alternatives. Our hypothesis is that this combination helps align the student with the stronger teacher’s solution space while preserving potentially high-quality reasoning paths that RL can further reshape. Feedback on complete responses may then help the student adjust the probabilities of these paths and improve task success. This offers a possible explanation for OPD’s downstream benefit beyond what initial accuracy or Pass@
k
k
alone reveals.
The same distinction between current performance and later learning appears when we change the distillation recipe. We compare student- and teacher-generated trajectories under reverse KL (RKL) and forward KL (FKL), using full teacher distributions in each case. Standard reverse-KL OPD performs better before RL, but forward-KL OPD overtakes it afterward. Student rollouts also outperform teacher rollouts under both objectives before and after RL. These findings highlight both the choice of objective and the states at which teacher supervision is applied when preparing a model for subsequent RL.
These results place OPD within a broader question about preparing models for further learning. Previous work on the SFT-to-RL transition has shown that improving an intermediate model’s standalone performance need not improve its usefulness for RL
[
15
,
23
]
. Our study examines this issue for on-policy teacher transfer, connecting downstream performance with behavioral analysis and choices in the distillation recipe. The evidence supports OPD as a useful preparation stage in the evaluated settings and motivates following the student through RL when assessing the value of distillation.
Our contributions are:
•
We evaluate OPD as preparation for RL and show that it yields higher final performance than direct RL and SFT followed by RL under shared downstream training settings.
•
We offer a possible explanation for OPD’s benefit: closer alignment with the teacher’s distribution may provide a better solution space for subsequent RL, while retained uncertainty preserves alternative reasoning paths.
•
We show that forward KL is the better choice when OPD is followed by RL in our comparison, despite reverse KL’s stronger standalone distillation performance.
Together, these findings support treating OPD as preparation for better RL and choosing distillation recipes by the performance achieved after subsequent training.

Experimental Setup
3.1
Models and Preparation before RL
We compare ways of preparing the same base student for RL. Text experiments use Qwen3-8B
[
30
]
as the student and Qwen3-32B as the teacher; vision-language (VL) experiments use Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B
[
2
]
. Both teachers are RL-trained. In Base
→
\rightarrow
RL, the base student enters RL directly. In SFT
→
\rightarrow
RL, supervised next-token prediction on verified teacher-generated responses prepares the student for RL. In OPD
→
\rightarrow
RL, the student first matches full teacher distributions at its own generated prefixes using reverse KL. Base, SFT, and OPD denote the resulting checkpoints entering RL.
To examine how the preparation recipe affects subsequent learning, we also compare reverse and forward KL on student- and teacher-generated trajectories using the VL model pair. Both trajectory sources receive full teacher distributions, distinguishing teacher-trajectory distillation from SFT with hard token targets. The distillation objectives and the VL OPD RKL/FKL configuration are described in Appendix

Shared RL Settings and Evaluation
Teacher transfer and downstream RL use separate reasoning prompt datasets, with sources and sizes detailed in Appendix

We evaluate Base, SFT, and OPD before and after RL on eight text and twenty VL benchmarks, with equal task weights within each setting. VL RL mainly uses math-related training data, while evaluation spans STEM and puzzle reasoning, general VQA, instruction following, OCR, and mathematics. Training and evaluation prompts are distinct; complete task lists and checkpoint scores appear in Appendix

The text setting makes the role of preparation particularly clear. OPD changes the initial average only slightly, from 36.48 to 37.02, yet the gap over Base grows from 0.54 points before RL to 7.28 points afterward. SFT starts higher than OPD at 37.75 but finishes lower at 47.48. On AIME24, OPD even starts below Base (24.17 versus 24.90), then reaches 57.71 after RL compared with 47.40 from Base. OPD gains 22.16 points during RL overall. These comparisons show that a small immediate accuracy gain can accompany a much larger downstream advantage, and that the stronger checkpoint before RL need not yield the stronger model afterward.
In VL, OPD leads Base by 1.83 points before RL and retains a 1.34-point advantage afterward. The smaller margin than in text may partly reflect math-focused RL training alongside broader evaluation on twenty benchmarks spanning mathematics, STEM/puzzle reasoning, general VQA, instruction following, and OCR. The 1.34-point average gain is nevertheless notable, with improvements over direct RL on 16 of twenty benchmarks. RL improves the OPD checkpoint by another 2.36 points, with gains on 19 of twenty tasks. RL initialized with OPD achieves the highest final score of 63.02, compared with 61.68 for direct RL and 61.33 for RL initialized with SFT.
Takeaway.
Standard RKL OPD prepares students for higher post-RL performance than direct RL or SFT followed by RL in our comparisons. This benefit can emerge even when the immediate accuracy gain from OPD is small.

Understanding the Benefits of OPD for RL
The results in Sec.
4
show that OPD can improve performance after RL even when its immediate accuracy gain is small. We now examine what changes in the policy before RL. We first test whether initial correct-answer coverage explains the downstream advantage, then examine teacher distributional alignment and retained token uncertainty. All diagnostics describe the checkpoints entering RL, using the shared prompt sets in Sec.
3.3
.

The text comparison shows a limit of this explanation. Base and OPD have nearly overlapping curves: their Pass@1 values are 18.4% and 19.3%, and their Pass@64 values are 80.4% and 80.0%. Nevertheless, they reach final benchmark averages of 51.90 and 59.18 after RL. Their correct-count distributions and group-outcome probabilities are also similar. For diagnostic groups of eight, the estimated mixed-correctness rates are 53.54% for Base and 54.41% for OPD. These summaries reveal little of the eventual performance gap.
Coverage does improve in VL, where OPD raises Pass@1 from 40.0% to 48.1% and Pass@64 from 91.4% to 92.7% relative to Base. The KL comparison provides another case where coverage alone is insufficient: RKL and FKL have the same pre-RL Pass@64 of 92.68%, yet FKL finishes 1.85 points higher after RL (Sec.
6
). Thus, increased coverage can accompany stronger downstream performance, but the measured Pass@
k
k
values do not fully explain the benefit of preparation across these comparisons.
Similar aggregate coverage does not imply that policies solve the same prompts or follow the same reasoning paths. It also does not specify how probabilities will change during RL. The group diagnostics add information about reward variation: both all-wrong and all-correct groups lack a within-group outcome contrast. They still characterize sampled outcomes before training rather than the policy’s subsequent response to optimization. This motivates examining how OPD changes the distribution over continuations.
5.2
Teacher Alignment beyond Top-1 Agreement
We compare student and teacher predictions at prefixes visited by each policy, measuring both top-1 agreement and JS divergence between their normalized top-20 records. These metrics capture different aspects of teacher alignment: the preferred token can agree even when the probabilities assigned to alternative tokens differ substantially.

OPD reduces the recorded distributional divergence from the teacher in both settings (Fig.
4

curves are close. OPD therefore changes teacher alignment without requiring a large increase in initial correct-answer frequency.
The comparison with SFT shows why top-1 agreement alone is incomplete. Text SFT has higher top-1 agreement than OPD, 94.25% versus 93.82%, but also higher JS, 0.01720 versus 0.01468. The same pattern appears in VL: SFT has 83.88% top-1 agreement compared with OPD’s 83.67%, while its JS is higher, 0.07208 versus 0.06431. Agreement on the most likely token therefore does not establish closeness of the surrounding distribution.
5.3
Retaining Uncertainty for Subsequent Learning
Closer teacher alignment leaves open how much uncertainty remains over alternative continuations. We examine token entropy at positions matching a fixed reasoning-word lexicon, with separate summaries for correct and incorrect responses (Fig.
4
, right column). OPD retains entropy comparable to Base: 1.048 versus 0.971 in text and 0.629 versus 0.622 in VL. SFT has lower values, 0.242 and 0.214, respectively. The OPD–SFT difference also appears within both correctness groups, so it is not explained solely by the proportion of correct responses.
Taken together, the alignment and entropy measurements suggest a possible explanation for OPD’s benefit. Teacher feedback may shift probability toward higher-quality continuations while retaining alternatives that remain useful for subsequent learning. Outcome-based RL can then adjust the probabilities of complete responses using task feedback. In this account, OPD helps shape the choices available to the student, while RL refines how often those choices lead to successful answers. This connects the downstream advantage to changes in the policy distribution that initial accuracy or Pass@
k
k
alone does not describe.
Takeaway.
Our analysis of standard RKL OPD suggests that closer alignment with the teacher’s distribution may provide a better solution space for subsequent RL, with retained uncertainty preserving alternatives for further refinement.

7
Discussion
Our results support treating OPD as part of the design of RL. A preparation stage can yield little immediate accuracy improvement yet lead to substantially better performance after training. The objective comparison makes the same point at the level of the distillation recipe: the strongest distilled checkpoint need not be the best starting policy for RL. The advantage of student rollouts under both objectives supports evaluating distillation choices by subsequent RL performance.
Our behavioral analysis of standard RKL OPD offers a possible explanation for its value as preparation for RL. In our distributional probes, OPD shows closer teacher alignment beyond top-1 agreement while retaining uncertainty over alternatives, even when initial accuracy and measured Pass@
k
k
change little. We hypothesize that this combination provides a better solution space for subsequent RL, understood as the reasoning continuations available to the policy and the probabilities assigned to them. Teacher alignment may favor higher-quality continuations, while retained uncertainty may preserve alternatives for exploration and refinement. RL can then use outcome feedback on complete responses to adjust these probabilities. In this account, OPD’s benefit lies partly in shaping how the policy can learn afterward, beyond improving what it already answers correctly.
Our analysis characterizes teacher distributional alignment and retained uncertainty jointly. Future work could further disentangle their individual contributions and examine how alternative continuations are reinforced during RL. Such studies could guide the design of distillation objectives that improve subsequent learning, as well as criteria for selecting starting policies before running RL.
8
Conclusion
Our results show that OPD improves final performance over direct RL and SFT followed by RL, even when its immediate accuracy gain is small. Its benefit extends beyond what pre-RL Pass@
k
k
reveals, with closer alignment to the teacher’s distribution and retained uncertainty offering a possible explanation. This focus on subsequent learning also informs the distillation recipe: FKL is preferable for OPD followed by RL, and student rollouts outperform teacher rollouts under both objectives in our comparison. Together, these findings support OPD as preparation for better RL and highlight the importance of shaping starting policies for the learning that follows.

Token entropy is aggregated with a fixed lexical classifier. article.headline: OPD 可为后续 RL 提供更好起点
article.lede: 研究比较 OPD、SFT 与直接 RL，发现 OPD 初始化在 RL 后平均分最高，但收益不能由 Pass@k 解释。
article.problem: RL 的最终表现取决于训练从哪个策略开始，而起始模型的当前准确率未必能预测它后续能学多好。论文追问：on-policy distillation（OPD）除了提升蒸馏后即时准确率，是否还能为后续 RL 提供更好的起点。
article.method: 作者在同一学生和同一 RL 配置下比较 Base→RL、SFT→RL 与 OPD→RL：文本用 Qwen3-8B/32B，视觉语言用 Qwen3-VL-8B/32B。主 OPD 采用 reverse KL，并在学生自生成前缀上匹配完整教师分布；另在 VL 上比较 reverse/forward KL 与学生/教师轨迹。诊断包括 Pass@k、教师 top-1 一致率、top-20 JS 散度和词表位置熵。
article.results: 文本 8 个基准上，OPD→RL 最终平均 59.18，高于 Base→RL 的 51.90 和 SFT→RL 的 47.48；OPD 训练前仅 37.02，较 Base 的 36.48 高 0.54 分，RL 后差距扩至 7.28 分，OPD 在 RL 中提升 22.16 分。VL 20 个基准上 OPD→RL 为 63.02，高于 61.68 和 61.33，RL 中再涨 2.36 分。学生轨迹下 FKL 从 60.17 到 64.87，最终比 RKL 的 63.02 高 1.85 分；教师轨迹 RKL/FKL 最终为 61.90/59.20。
article.why_it_matters: 这说明蒸馏方案不该只看蒸馏后分数，而应看后续 RL 的最终表现；在本比较中，若 OPD 后接 RL，forward KL 比 reverse KL 更合适。
article.limitations: 结论基于 Qwen3/Qwen3-VL 8B 学生与 32B 教师的单一 GRPO 配置，VL 平均仅比直接 RL 高 1.34 分且任务间不均。论文把收益归因于教师分布对齐与保留不确定性，但这仍是观察性证据，未分离两者的因果贡献。
article.figure_caption_zh: RL 后的性能揭示蒸馏价值：OPD→RL 最终平均最高；学生前缀下 RKL 在 RL 前领先、FKL 在 RL 后反超。

page_papers.title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience
page_papers.abstract: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.

Introduction
Egocentric video offers a natural perspective on how humans and embodied agents perceive and interact with the world, requiring only a wearable camera without external camera setups.
By capturing the wearer’s movement and close-range interactions, it provides visual cues for recovering camera pose, scene depth, hands, and objects.
However, existing methods
[

typically recover only a subset of these tightly coupled components.
Combining outputs from different methods often requires reconciling inconsistent scales and coordinate frames, complicating their use in downstream embodied AI applications.
This motivates a unified feed-forward framework that jointly recovers the camera, scene, hands, and objects within a single model.
Training such a unified model, however, requires large-scale egocentric data with joint annotations of the camera, scene, hands, and objects.
Although egocentric video is easy to record, obtaining reliable joint annotations is considerably more difficult due to frequent hand-object occlusions, rapid head motion, and motion blur.
Existing datasets
[
7
,

,
39
,
12
,
58
]
have made progress toward this goal, often using calibrated multi-camera or motion-capture systems to support reliable annotations.
However, these systems require substantial setup and calibration, making collection difficult to scale across diverse real-world environments.
Scaling jointly annotated egocentric data therefore calls for a collection and annotation pipeline that reduces reliance on such specialized infrastructure.
To address these challenges, we present
EgoXperience
, a full-stack paradigm for egocentric 3D reconstruction, encompassing data collection, annotation, modeling, and benchmarking.
Central to its annotation pipeline is
EgoX
-Engine
, which tracks target objects across video frames and uses pre-scanned object models and observed depth to estimate and verify their 3D poses.
SLAM-estimated camera poses place these object trajectories in a shared world coordinate system alongside scene geometry and hand annotations, providing geometrically aligned supervision.
Applying this engine to 50 hours of task-driven recordings spanning workspace manipulation, cross-room interactions, and outdoor loco-manipulation yields
EgoX

, further enriched with task captions at second-level temporal resolution.
To complement this dataset, we harmonize additional public interaction datasets

under a common training formulation, aligning their geometric conventions while retaining their partial annotations.
We also establish
EgoX
-Bench
from one hour of held-out recordings, enabling joint evaluation of camera, scene depth, hand, and object reconstruction across all capture settings.
To translate this joint supervision into joint reconstruction, we introduce
EgoX
.
Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks,
EgoX
jointly reconstructs the camera, scene depth, hands, and objects at metric scale in a shared world coordinate system, all in a single forward pass.
During training, we supervise each component and additionally use the predicted camera poses to transform object and hand predictions into normalized world coordinates, where we supervise their positions and orientations.
This ties camera, hand, and object estimation together, encouraging geometrically consistent reconstruction.
Evaluated on four benchmarks,
EgoX
achieves state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand–object pose recovery. It ranks first in depth, hand, and object metrics across all four benchmarks and achieves the best camera accuracy on HOI4D. Relative to the strongest competing methods, EgoX reduces camera nATE by 68.9% on HOI4D, hand W-MPJPE
and depth AbsRel by 65.6% and 42.9% on EgoX-Bench,
