Warping-based methods are sensitive to camera scale because their explicit scene initialization and geometric conditioning depend on depth estimated from the first frame. Camera translations must therefore be expressed at a scale consistent with this depth; a mismatch produces an inconsistent initial scene and incorrect warps, which can propagate errors into subsequent predictions. This dependence on depth–camera scale calibration is a practical limitation of these explicit geometric methods. PCA projection.
For each inspected layer and denoising step, we collect the target frame’s block-output features and project the spatial tokens onto three principal components. PCA is fitted independently for each layer–step pair, with a fixed random seed and deterministic component signs. Each projected channel is scaled using its first and 99th percentiles for RGB display. Because each projection is fitted independently, we compare the spatial organization of regions within each visualization rather than matching colors across cells. As discussed in
Section
3.1
, these maps reveal where recognizable scene structure emerges across noise levels and network depth: little coherent structure is visible in the noise-dominated region, scene regions begin to take shape in the structure-formation region, and the scene layout becomes more clearly defined in the structure-established region. The onset of recognizable structure occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and in shallower layers at lower noise. Viewed alongside the attention maps, the PCA features help distinguish the emergence of scene structure from the development of cross-frame associations, showing that attention can still favor competing regions even when the scene layout is recognizable. This joint analysis motivates placing correspondence supervision near the structure-formation stage and adapting the supervised layer to the noise timestep.
Attention readout.
At the same layer and step, we extract queries and keys after normalization and rotary positional encoding. For the fixed source query, each head’s dot-product scores are softmax-normalized over all video keys. We then retain the target-frame slice and average the resulting probabilities over heads. This readout differs from both the block-output features used for PCA and the learned aggregation MLP used during training. Target-frame responses are displayed after normalization by each map’s maximum, with color mapping and interpolation used only for visualization. Thus, the color scale indicates relative spatial response within a map, not an absolute probability shared across layers or noise levels.
The denoising axis uses the actual model noise timesteps along the sampled inference trajectory. The noise-dependent shift in structure formation motivates our layer-routing schedule, whose generation performance is evaluated against fixed-layer and alternative schedules in

Appendix F
Limitations and Future Work
GAD
improves scene and dynamic consistency across all three video backbones by transferring geometric correspondences during training, while preserving the original inference procedure. Its current design suggests three directions for further improvement.
More reliable correspondence targets.
Our results demonstrate that attention distillation with geometric correspondence targets improves video consistency. The current implementation extracts these targets from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention, making their quality dependent on the teacher’s matching ability and spatial resolution. This raises a natural question: can more reliable correspondences further improve the effectiveness of attention distillation? Stronger correspondence estimators or complementary sources of matching evidence could provide more accurate and complete supervision, particularly for ambiguous appearance, occlusion, and moving objects. The correspondence-based formulation of
GAD
provides a basis for exploring such alternatives to the current geometry teacher.
Adaptive supervision placement.
Our noise-timestep routing improves geometric metrics over fixed-layer supervision, demonstrating the value of adapting supervision depth to the denoising state. The current layer assignment depends only on the noise timestep and remains fixed throughout training. As the video model learns, the layers that benefit most from correspondence supervision may also change. Conditioning routing jointly on noise timestep and training progress could better match supervision to the model’s evolving representations, extending the current mechanism while preserving the original inference procedure.
Extension to autoregressive video generation.
GAD
improves static and dynamic consistency in Wan’s bidirectional video models. Autoregressive video generation offers a natural next setting, where preserving scene identity over long rollouts and maintaining coherent object motion remain important challenges. The principle of guiding attention with correspondences also applies to associations between newly generated content and preceding frames. Adapting the distillation objectives to the available temporal context under causal attention could help autoregressive models retain scene structure and moving-object identity as generation proceeds. This offers a promising route to extending the benefits demonstrated here to autoregressive generation.

article.headline: 把几何模型的注意力蒸馏进视频扩散模型
article.lede: GAD 把冻结几何模型 VGGT-Ω 的跨帧对应关系蒸馏进视频注意力，按噪声步选择监督层，推理不增加任何开销。
article.problem: 视频扩散模型能生成观感不错的短片，却难以在视角变化和物体运动下保持场景几何与物体结构。作者进一步发现，视频注意力的跨帧响应经常分散在多个区域，即便场景结构已经可辨认，也无法可靠地关联同一场景元素。他们还观察到，可辨认的场景结构在高噪声时先出现在较深层、低噪声时先出现在较浅层，这为「在哪一层监督」提供了依据。
article.method: GAD 用冻结的几何基础模型 VGGT-Ω（1B，取零基第 13 层第 10 个注意力头）在干净视频上抽取跨帧对应关系，并把源 token 分配给目标帧的总注意力质量作为可靠性权重，对可能被遮挡或不可见的匹配降权。训练时按模型噪声时间步选择学生网络的一层（t<850 用 L5、850≤t<950 用 L15、t≥950 用 L25），在该层上同时施加帧对内的 pairwise 监督与跨多帧的 trackwise 监督，与原有 flow-matching 损失联合优化。推理阶段只使用训练后的视频模型，不加载教师、聚合 MLP 或对应关系缓存。
article.results: 在 Wan2.2 5B 上，GAD 在 RealEstate10K 与 DL3DV-10K 两个长程基准上的跨帧匹配命中率相对提升至少 30%：RealEstate10K 的 M_rate 从 0.257 升到 0.335，M_dist 从 48.90 降到 38.85 像素，旋转距离 R_dist 从 9.573 度降到 4.890 度。Wan2.1 14B 上两个数据集七项指标全部为最佳，DL3DV-10K 的 R_dist 从 5.497 降到 3.039、M_rate 从 0.365 升到 0.393。生成时长方面，5 秒的 M_rate 由 0.529 升到 0.571、15 秒由 0.257 升到 0.335。推理成本基本不变，OmniWorld-Game 上 Wan2.2 5B 耗时 69.60 秒对 70.44 秒、峰值显存同为 34.85 GB。训练使用 35K 片段、832×480 分辨率、10 个 epoch、32 张 A800。
article.why_it_matters: 跨帧对应是视频世界模型、机器人规划与自动驾驶仿真的基础能力，GAD 用纯训练期监督换来更好的几何与动态一致性，部署时不需要额外模块或采样开销。
article.limitations: 对应目标的质量受制于 VGGT-Ω 的匹配能力与空间分辨率，层路由只依赖噪声步且在训练全程固定，实验也只在 Wan 系列双向模型上验证，未涉及自回归生成，5 秒与 10 秒设置下 FID/FVD 还出现小幅回退（5 秒 FID 由 26.85 升至 27.63）。消融显示若去掉置信度加权，匹配命中率会掉到 0.230，反而低于 Wan 基线的 0.257，说明教师注意力峰值本身并不可靠。

page_papers.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
page_papers.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state–action combinations observed in expert rollouts.
Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library.
Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world-model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations.
By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

Introduction
A key goal of physical intelligence is the ability to plan and perform new tasks.
Routine tasks, such as driving to work, can be automatized and executed without much cognitive effort.
Yet novel tasks requires us to plan and simulate the consequences of our actions.

In free-space variants such as TR-Route, Avoid-T, Avoid-Peg, and Cube-Hop, MPC performance is preserved or improves relative to the corresponding base task. In contrast, contact-rich variants consistently degrade, despite using the same privileged state inputs. This suggests that the difficulty is not merely access to the relevant state factors
(
Klindt et al., 2026
;
Shi et al., 2026
)
, but whether the goal shift requires precise object interaction.
This asymmetry is consistent with prior work showing that compositional generalization requires constraints on the learned function. Additive or interaction-free settings are especially favorable, since factor-specific mechanisms can be learned from observed compositions and reused under novel recombinations
(
Dong and Ma, 2022
;
Lachapelle et al., 2023
;
Wiedemer et al., 2024a
;
Mahajan et al., 2025
)
.
This intuition aligns with the independent causal mechanisms principle, under which reusable mechanisms remain autonomous as their joint occurrence changes
(
Parascandolo et al., 2018
)
. Contact-rich variants depart from this favorable regime: action effects may no longer decompose into reusable factor-specific mechanisms. Compositional generalization may still be possible, but only with additional structure on these interactions
(
Brady et al., 2025
)
.
The same asymmetry appears in rollout prediction. Contact-rich variants show much larger error increases, often by one to three orders of magnitude, even with oracle states. Free-space variants degrade far less, and in some cases match or improve on the base-task error. Thus, removing representation learning does not make goal-shifted dynamics prediction uniformly reliable.
Metric alignment depends on task complexity.
We additionally observe that rollout error and planning performance sometimes diverge in free-space variants where planning can tolerate imperfect prediction. The closer agreement in contact-rich settings may reflect the structure of the planning problem. Rollout error measures whether the model predicts the full trajectory accurately, whereas MPC only needs to find some action sequence that reaches the goal, regardless of the exact intermediate path.
Free-space tasks often admit many such trajectories, while contact-rich tasks allow fewer viable sequences because success also depends on the correct object interaction.
5.3
Representation Effects in End-to-End World Models
End-to-end world models can degrade on both metric under the goal shift even when oracle-state predictors remain stable. Such cases show that the AnyGoal gap is not solely a failure of action-conditioned dynamics, but can also reflect encoder failure under unseen factor combinations. Due to space constraints, we discuss two main observations, and more are in Appendix
I.3
.

Factor recombination can induce observation-level shifts.
AnyGoal controls generalization at the level of physical factors, but end-to-end models observe rendered inputs

Crucially, correct factor inference on training observations need not extend to unseen compositions. Even when factors are identifiable in distribution, an encoder may fail to invert novel recombined observations without compositional-consistency constraints
(

. Thus, end-to-end world models face a representation-level generalization problem before dynamics prediction is considered.
End-to-end models must therefore infer task-relevant factors from observations generated by unseen factor combinations, in addition to learning dynamics.
Latent geometry shapes degradation under goal shifts.

(b) The 2D t-SNE projections illustrate that learned representations can organize the same underlying agent positions with substantially different geometry, which can affect prediction and planning.
TwoRoom provides a useful case where end-to-end degradation cannot be attributed to an observation-level shift.
Because agent position is the only changing factor and TR-Route positions remain marginally within the TwoRoom training support, the corresponding observations stay visually in support, enabling a controlled comparison between end-to-end models and oracle-state predictors.

This indicates that representation quality still matters: the learned latent space may fail to preserve the agent location precisely, introduce unnecessary dimensions or nuisance variation, or organize states in a geometry that is unfavorable for prediction and planning.
Thus, even visually in-support goal shifts can fail if the learned latent geometry is not aligned with the task-relevant state geometry.

Conclusion
We introduced AnyGoal, a benchmark for evaluating whether world models generalize to new behavioral goals by recombining familiar states and actions. Across a diverse set of models, goal-shift generalization remains difficult even when the relevant state and action factors are marginally covered by the training distribution.
Together, these analyses show that goal-shift failures are heterogeneous, reflecting interactions among representation, dynamics prediction, task structure, and evaluation metric.
More broadly, AnyGoal connects world-model evaluation with compositional generalization. It asks for prediction on novel joint state–action combinations within the product of marginal training supports, a reasonable but unresolved requirement for reusable dynamics. Our theoretical perspective suggests that global coverage of all state–action combinations is neither realistic nor necessary. Instead, world models need coverage of local mechanism inputs, together with objectives or architectures that identify action-conditioned mechanisms rather than behavior-policy shortcuts. By isolating goal-induced recombination as a failure mode, AnyGoal provides a controlled basis for evaluating progress toward world models that learn reusable dynamics beyond expert rollouts.

Our model selection is designed to span several substantially different
approaches to visual world modeling rather than to concentrate on a single
architectural family. In particular, we evaluate both joint-embedding

Additional Observations
Prediction Space Affects Metric Interpretation
We do not use the rollout results to directly rank JEPA-style and generative world models. These models predict in different spaces: JEPA-style models are evaluated in latent space, whereas generative models are evaluated in pixel or reconstruction space. As a result, absolute prediction errors are not directly comparable across model families, and we primarily interpret rollout degradation relative to each model’s own base-task performance.
Under this relative comparison, generative models often show smaller rollout degradation under some goal shifts, while several JEPA-style models show larger increases. However, this tendency does not translate consistently to planning: a model can show stable rollout error but poor MPC success, or larger rollout degradation while remaining competitive in control. We therefore treat prediction-space effects as an interpretation caveat rather than a model-family ranking. The results suggest that rollout robustness and downstream control utility are related but distinct properties.
Oracle state access does not guarantee better planning.
Interestingly, access to the oracle state does not always lead to stronger
planning performance. In Cube, several end-to-end models achieve higher
planning success than their oracle-state counterparts, both on the base task
and on CubeDiagonal. This should not be interpreted as evidence that learned
latents are generally superior to physical state representations, since the
end-to-end and oracle predictors differ in more than just their input space.
Rather, these results suggest that state observability and planning suitability
are distinct properties. Oracle states preserve the underlying physical factors,
but the resulting geometry may not be the most favorable one for the planner’s
cost and optimization procedure. Conversely, a learned representation may, in
some cases, emphasize task-relevant variation or compress nuisance factors in a
way that makes goal-directed optimization easier. We therefore treat planning
performance as depending not only on how much state information is available,
but also on how that information is organized in the representation space.

article.headline: AnyGoal：世界模型的组合泛化缺口
article.lede: 新基准用目标偏移任务检验世界模型能否重组熟悉的状态与动作因子，发现当前模型普遍失败。
article.problem: 世界模型要可靠用于规划和模拟，必须在专家轨迹之外的状态—动作组合上保持动力学正确。但数据覆盖、动力学泛化与下游规划性能之间的关系仍缺乏系统研究。
article.method: 作者构建 AnyGoal 基准与开源库，从常用世界模型环境派生目标偏移任务变体：单个状态因子和动作仍在训练支撑内，但其组合在专家轨迹中欠代表。他们评测多种环境与世界模型家族，并用 oracle 状态预测器、端到端模型、rollout 误差、MPC 成功率和干预动作敏感性等分析失败来源。
article.results: 在多个环境与模型家族中，目标偏移下当前模型一致出现失败；接触丰富变体的 rollout 误差常增大 1 到 3 个数量级，即使输入 oracle 状态，而自由空间变体退化小得多，部分任务持平或改善。论文还报告 5 步与 25 步预测误差，模型统一采用 frame skip 5、history length 3（Sensorimotor-WM 保持 history length 1）。图注用 KDE 做支撑检查，并将密度低于峰值参考密度 1% 的区域标灰；所给材料未列出绝对 MPC 成功率数值。
article.why_it_matters: 它把世界模型评测与组合泛化连接起来，提供可控基准来区分表示失败、动力学失败和规划指标错位。若动力学能复用局部机制，就不需要覆盖所有状态—动作组合，这为离线数据下的规划研究给出更可检验的方向。
article.limitations: 局限在于基准基于常用世界模型环境，任务与模型家族覆盖仍有限；rollout 误差在不同预测空间（潜空间 vs 像素/重建空间）不可直接比较，作者也明确不据此给模型家族排名。结论还依赖边际支撑检查与 oracle 状态设定，接触丰富任务在更真实场景中的可迁移性仍待验证。

page_papers.title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
page_papers.abstract: Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website: https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/.

RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
Yu Li
Shenghe Hu
Yuhan Wang
Yaoxiang Pu
Haotong Zhang
Yuanpei Chen
Yaodong Yang
Abstract
Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data.
Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation.
In this work, we propose
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that
RoboFFT
consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate
RoboFFT
into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website:
https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/
.
Figure 1:
We present
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policy with forward process. (a) Reverse finetuning formulates the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP, while forward finetuning aligns with the same objective as training by following the forward noising process.
(b) One framework across popular generative robot policy on simulation benchmarks.
(c) Real-world deployment with integration of real world RL.
(d) Improved performance in success rate, training stability and efficiency.

1
Introduction
Generative robot policies, typically based on diffusion and flow-based models
[
43
,
42
,
15
,
29
]
, have become a powerful paradigm for learning visuomotor skills from demonstrations by modeling complex and multi-modal action distributions
[
12
,
56
,
53
]
, which significantly improves robot action accuracy and robustness and yields substantial performance gains in complex manipulation tasks
[
12
,
53
]
. However, policies trained purely by imitation learning remain constrained by the quality and coverage of the demonstration data. Imperfect demonstrations, covariate shift, and insufficient exposure to deployment-time states can all limit the final task performance of behavior-cloned policies
[
13
,
40
]
. Online reinforcement learning (RL) naturally presents itself as a promising paradigm to further improve generative robot policies, as it empowers the policy to directly maximize task rewards by continuously interacting with and learning from the environment.
Applying policy gradient RL methods to generative robot policies is nevertheless nontrivial. Unlike autoregressive policies, whose token likelihoods are tractable, diffusion and flow-based models typically lack a tractable exact likelihood formulation. This makes popular policy gradient objectives, such as PPO, difficult to be applied directly. Existing approaches address this issue by formulating the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP embedded in the high-level environment MDP, and optimizing through this two-level decision making trajectory
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
(Fig.
1
(a), left). Despite its promising results, reverse-process finetuning introduces substantial computation and memory overhead, and may suffer from gradient instability due to long denoising chains, especially in high-dimensional and long-horizon manipulation tasks.
To address these issues, we propose
RoboFFT
, a simpler yet more effective framework for online RL finetuning of generative robot manipulation policies through the
forward
noising process, inspired by recent studies from other application domains such as image generation and simple locomotion
[
52
,
59
,
34
]
. Instead of assigning credit through the reverse denoising chain,
RoboFFT
approximates the exact log-likelihood with a more computationally stable and efficient form akin to the score / flow matching loss for pretraining, yielding a principled PPO-style objective that is aligned with the imitation-learning objective while avoiding complicated likelihood computation or backpropagation through the full reverse trajectory. For flow-based policies, we further adopt SDE sampling by injecting noise into the sampling process, enabling controllable exploration during online data collection. In practice, Monte Carlo estimation, ratio-temperature calibration and further adaptations make likelihood estimation and updates robust across different policy architectures and tasks.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
on challenging robot manipulation benchmarks such as Robomimic
[
33
]
and LIBERO
[
30
]
, which pose difficulties like high-dimensional visual observation, long horizon planning and sparse reward for finetuning. Experimental results across different tasks demonstrate substantial and consistent performance improvements over pretrained diffusion and flow policies and achieve competitive or better performance compared with representative reverse and forward process finetuning baselines, while reducing optimization overhead. We further verify the applicability of our method on more complicated VLA and real world deployment settings, and study the key designs through ablations and visualizations. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) We introduce
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework that performs policy gradient finetuning in the forward noising process for generative robot policies.
(2) We carry out practical implementation of
RoboFFT
for representative generative robot policies (flow, diffusion and VLA) on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks, showing that
RoboFFT
achieves superior performance and improved training stability and efficiency.
(3) We integrate
RoboFFT
into the real world reinforcement learning framework for practical deployment and demonstrate its effectiveness over real world tasks.
(4) We carry out a systematic ablation analysis of key design choices and conduct investigative experiments to provide empirical insights for the mechanism of
RoboFFT
.
2
Related Work
2.1
Policy Gradient for Robot Manipulation
Policy gradient and actor critic methods provide a standard framework for learning continuous-control policies from interaction data
[
50
,
45
,
28
,
41
]
. Due to the
training stability with high-dimensional action spaces, they have been widely applied to a range of robotic control problems, including dexterous manipulation, legged locomotion, and agile navigation
[
48
,
9
,
10
,
1
,
17
,
21
]
. For long-horizon manipulation, however, training from scratch remains highly exploration-intensive and is often impractical. A more practical paradigm is therefore to finetune policies initialized from demonstration data. Prior studies have shown that reinforcement learning can further improve such demonstration-initialized policies beyond behavior cloning while substantially reducing the exploration burden
[
38
,
46
,
37
]
. RoboFFT follows this finetuning paradigm, while focusing on diffusion- and flow-based robot policies whose action distributions are implicitly induced by generative sampling processes, making the likelihood ratio computation required by policy gradient methods nontrivial.
2.2
RL for Generative Models
Reinforcement learning has recently been widely applied to generative model finetuning in offline
[
3
,
35
,
16
,
49
,
14
,
36
,
7
]
, offline-to-online
[
11
,
26
]
, and online settings
[
39
,
57
,
54
,
34
,
52
,
59
]
. Online finetuning for diffusion and flow models can be broadly categorized into reverse-process and forward-process approaches. Reverse-process methods formulate the denoising or sampling trajectory as a multi-step decision process, enabling tractable per-step likelihood for policy optimization
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
. While effective, optimizing through long internal sampling chains can increase computation and memory costs and may introduce training instability. Forward-process methods instead optimize policy via constructing surrogate likelihood objectives or contrastive learning, better aligning RL finetuning with generative pretraining
[
52
,
34
,
54
,
59
]
. DiffusionNFT and AWM
[
59
,
52
]
study this idea for text-to-image generation. FPO and FPO++
[
34
,
54
]
extend it to robotic control, but mainly focus on locomotion tasks. In comparison, RoboFFT studies forward-process finetuning in more challenging robotic manipulation, and covers more extensive settings including both diffusion and flow policies, VLA finetuning, and real world deployment with practical stabilization designs.

5.4
Evaluation on Real World
To evaluate the effectiveness of
RoboFFT
on real world robotic manipulation tasks, we integrate our method into a practical real-world RL framework

[
26

RoboFFT
to an offline-to-online formulation while retaining its core components including forward noising, the matching loss surrogate ratio, and PPO-style clipping. Specifically, we first pretrain a flow-based policy using human demonstrations collected via SpaceMouse teleoperation.
We then perform multiple offline RL iterations. In each offline iteration, we perform offline PPO-style optimization on the collected rollout data, where IQL
[
25
]
is used to estimate advantages from offline trajectories. After each offline RL update, we deploy the updated policy on the real robot to collect additional trajectories, which are added to the offline dataset for the next offline RL iteration. To stabilize policy improvement and avoid drifting away from reliable human behaviors, we combine the newly collected rollout data with the original teleoperation demonstrations and conduct imitation learning to update the base policy for the next iteration.
During the online RL phase, we continue PPO-style updates initialized from the offline actor and IQL critic. We use a sparse binary

6
Limitations
Although
RoboFFT
enables stable online finetuning of generative robot policies through the forward noising process, it still has several limitations. First, the weighted score/flow matching loss is only a surrogate for the true action log-likelihood, and its scale may vary across noise schedules, action dimensions, and policy architectures. Therefore, additional calibration such as temperature scaling is still needed to ensure stable PPO-style updates. Second, our current framework relies on on-policy PPO, which has limited data efficiency and cannot fully reuse historical trajectories. This makes real-world deployment challenging, especially when data collection is restricted to a single robot. Although offline-to-online paradigms such as RL100
[
26
]
can partially alleviate this issue, they usually require iterative data collection and offline retraining, which remains time-consuming in practice. Future work may explore more sample-efficient variants that better leverage historical trajectories and human intervention data for safer and faster real world robot learning.
7
Conclusion
We present
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies. By applying forward noising to sampled actions and using the weighted score/flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio,
RoboFFT
enables PPO-style policy optimization without requiring explicit likelihood estimation. Experiments on representative simulation benchmarks show that
RoboFFT
consistently improves popular generative robot policies on long-horizon and sparse-reward manipulation tasks, while achieving better training stability and efficiency. Further integration into a real world RL framework also demonstrates its effectiveness on real robot tasks.

B.1
Robomimic Benchmark
We use Robomimic
[
33
]
as the simulated manipulation benchmark throughout our main experiments. Robomimic provides sparse-reward robot manipulation tasks collected from human demonstrations, making it a suitable testbed for evaluating whether online finetuning can improve a behavior-cloned generative policy beyond its initial demonstration-trained performance. Following the data processing and environment conventions used in DPPO and ReinFlow
[
39
,
57
]
, we evaluate four Robomimic tasks: Lift, Can, Square, and Transport. The corresponding observation and action specifications are summarized in Table
1
.
The four tasks cover different manipulation difficulties. Lift requires the robot to grasp and lift an object, while Can is a pick-and-place task where the robot must manipulate a can into the target container. Square is a more precision-sensitive assembly task in which the robot must manipulate a square nut and place it onto a positioning peg. Transport is a long-horizon bimanual manipulation task that requires coordinated control of two robot arms to move an object across the workspace. Thus, the benchmark spans both short-horizon single-arm manipulation and longer-horizon bimanual manipulation.
We consider both state-input and pixel-input variants. In the state-input setting, the policy observes low-dimensional proprioceptive and object state features. In the pixel-input setting, the policy observes RGB image(s) at

Lift, Can, and Square use a 7-dimensional action space, whereas Transport uses a 14-dimensional action space due to its bimanual control setup.
All Robomimic tasks use sparse rewards. We report success rate as the primary evaluation metric. The maximum episode length

B.4
Baseline Methods and Configurations
We compare RoboFFT with representative online RL fine-tuning baselines for diffusion- and flow-based robot policies.
DPPO.
Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization
[
39
]
is a representative reverse-process fine-tuning method for diffusion policies. It formulates the reverse denoising process together with the environment interaction process as a two-level MDP, and applies PPO to optimize the Gaussian likelihoods of denoising transitions. We use DPPO as the canonical diffusion-policy RL baseline for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
ReinFlow.
ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends the reverse-process policy-gradient paradigm to flow-based policies. It injects stochasticity into the deterministic flow trajectory, turns the sampler into a discrete-time Markov process with tractable Gaussian transition probabilities, and performs PPO-style optimization over the internal sampling trajectory. We use ReinFlow as the primary flow-policy baseline.
FPO.
Flow Policy Optimization
[
34
]
is a forward-process policy-gradient method that constructs a PPO-style surrogate ratio from conditional flow matching losses. We adapt FPO into our online fine-tuning codebase for Robomimic. To ensure fair comparison under the same tasks and pretrained policies, most environment and optimizer settings are shared with RoboFFT. The main algorithmic differences are that FPO does not use our SDE explorative sampling strategy and ratio-temperature calibration adopted in RoboFFT, while following the original FPO convention of using

DRWR.
DRWR is a lightweight diffusion reward-weighted regression baseline following the implementation convention in DPPO

. It performs forward-noise matching style updates weighted by rewards or returns, and serves as a simple forward-process reference that is architecturally close to our approach but does not use the PPO-style objective and the many critical designs introduced by our work.
For all baselines, we match the Robomimic environment wrappers, observation preprocessing, action chunking, base-policy training data, and evaluation protocol whenever applicable. The hyperparameters of DPPO, ReinFlow, and DRWR follow their original implementations unless a task-specific adaptation is necessary. Since the released ReinFlow manipulation implementation focuses on pixel-input Robomimic tasks, for state-input tasks we adapt secondary settings such as optimizer and update-batch configurations while keeping the core ReinFlow design unchanged. For fair comparison, the number of inference steps and finetuning steps are tuned on each task, so that each baseline achieves its nearly best performance. Appendix C
Additional Analyses for the Robomimic Experiments
C.1
Performance Analysis
This subsection provides additional discussion for the main Robomimic comparison in Sec.
5.1
, where the comprehensive performance of RoboFFT-F, RoboFFT-D and the baseline methods are evaluated under both state-input and pixel-input settings.
Across the easier
Lift
and
Can
tasks, RoboFFT-D and RoboFFT-F reach final success rates comparable to reverse-process baselines such as DPPO and ReinFlow. Their convergence can be slightly slower in some early-stage curves, but the final policy quality remains competitive. This suggests that the forward-process surrogate ratio preserves enough policy-gradient signal for improving already competent pretrained policies, while avoiding explicit likelihood computation through the reverse denoising chain.
The advantage of RoboFFT becomes more pronounced on the harder tasks. On
Square
and
Transport
, especially with pixel observations, RoboFFT shows a more sustained improvement trend and stronger final performance. Reverse-process methods can suffer from instability or later performance recession, likely because optimizing through a long internal sampling chain introduces a more complicated credit-assignment path and a heavier computation graph, making the gradients and parameter updates instable. In comparison, RoboFFT directly applies forward noising to the final rollout action and optimizes a matching-loss-based surrogate ratio, which keeps the optimization path closer to imitation pretraining.
The forward-process baselines, DRWR and FPO, are generally less competitive in the Robomimic manipulation setting. DRWR uses reward-weighted regression and does not include a PPO-style trust region, making it more sensitive to high-variance reward weights in sparse-reward tasks. FPO uses a forward-process PPO-style ratio, but in our implementation it lacks the manipulation-oriented stabilization designs used in RoboFFT, including controlled SDE exploration and ratio-temperature calibration. These differences help explain why simply applying a forward matching loss is not sufficient for robust online fine-tuning on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

PPO-Style Clipped Update.
RoboFFT can be viewed as augmenting advantage-weighted score / flow matching with a PPO-style trust region. To clarify the role of this constraint, we consider RoboFFT w/o PPO, which removes the clipped ratio objective and instead applies a simpler advantage-weighted matching update. This variant is conceptually closer to reward-weighted or energy-weighted flow matching baselines
[
39
]
, where the current policy is updated directly according to weighted matching losses without a clipped likelihood-ratio surrogate.
For fair comparison, we align learning rates and other optimization hyperparameters with the reward-weighted regression baseline whenever applicable. Fig.
12(c)
shows that the w/o PPO variant suffers from less stable early fine-tuning, while the full RoboFFT objective maintains smoother improvement. The performance gap can shrink in later stages, but the early instability indicates that the clipped ratio is useful for preventing overly aggressive updates induced by the surrogate matching-loss difference.

E.7
Interpretation of the t-SNE Visualization
The t-SNE visualization in Fig.
15
provides a complementary view of how RoboFFT reshapes the action distribution beyond a single rollout trajectory. Compared with the pretrained policy, whose sampled action chunks are more diffusely distributed and contain many low- or negative-advantage samples, the finetuned policy forms a more concentrated region with noticeably higher diagnostic advantages. In particular, after fine-tuning, a dense cluster of positive-advantage actions emerges in the embedding space, indicating that RoboFFT increases the probability mass around actions that are preferred by the diagnostic critic
Q
viz
Q_{\mathrm{viz}}
.
This observation is consistent with the rollout-timeline analysis in Fig.
7
. The timeline visualization shows that, at key decision stages such as grasping, transporting, and aligning the object, the finetuned policy improves the average action quality while reducing sample diversity. The t-SNE visualization further shows that this effect is not restricted to one selected trajectory: across a broader set of anchor states collected from successful and failed rollouts, the finetuned policy tends to move sampled action chunks toward higher-advantage regions. Together, these results suggest that RoboFFT improves the pretrained generative policy by concentrating its action distribution around more task-relevant and higher-quality action modes, rather than merely increasing random exploration. Note that the density of a t-SNE embedding is an intuitive signal of action mode concentration instead of a direct estimate of
policy likelihood or the number of behavioral modes. The observed concentration therefore does not by itself establish
either mode collapse or preservation of all useful modes.

Appendix H
Extended Related Work
H.1
Generative Models for Robot Manipulation
Generative models have become an increasingly important policy class for robot manipulation, as they provide expressive distributions over complex and potentially multimodal action sequences. Early approaches
[
58
,
27
]
formulate imitation learning with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). More recently, diffusion-based policies have demonstrated substantially greater expressiveness for continuous control. Diffusion Policy
[
12
,
19
]
models the conditional action distribution through an iterative denoising process, enabling stable learning of high-dimensional and multimodal action distributions and motivating a broad family of diffusion-based manipulation policies. Flow-matching models provide an alternative generative formulation by learning continuous transport from a simple noise distribution to the action distribution. Methods such as ManiFlow
[
53
]
further improve sampling efficiency and policy expressiveness through consistency-based flow training, demonstrating strong performance on diverse manipulation tasks. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models have extended robot policies toward large-scale generalist control by leveraging pretrained vision-language representations and heterogeneous robot datasets. RT-2
[
6
]
and OpenVLA
[
22
]
generate discretized robot actions within large autoregressive vision-language models, while
π
0
\pi_{0}
[
4
]
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
18
]
combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert for continuous action generation.
H.2
RL for Generative Robot Policy
Reinforcement learning has been increasingly explored to improve generative policies beyond behavior cloning. Early studies mainly focus on offline RL with fixed datasets. Diffusion Q Learning
[
49
]
parameterizes the actor as a diffusion model and combines diffusion regression with Q value maximization, while IDQL
[
14
]
uses an implicit Q-function to select actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy. This idea has also been extended to flow-based policies. Flow Q Learning (FQL)
[
36
]
learns a flow matching behavior policy together with a one-step RL policy, avoiding recursive differentiation through iterative flow generation. Although these methods exploit the expressiveness of generative policies, their improvement is constrained by the coverage of the offline dataset and the accuracy of learned value functions.
More recent work considers online or offline-to-online adaptation of pretrained generative robot policies. One direction keeps the base policy frozen and learns a lightweight steering or residual component. DSRL
[
47
]
performs RL in the latent-noise space of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy without modifying its parameters, while residual RL methods learn corrective actions on top of a frozen behavior cloning policy
[
2
,
44
,
20
]
. These approaches preserve pretrained behaviors and reduce the complexity of online optimization, but restrict policy improvement to the residual or latent space exposed by the frozen policy.
In contrast, full policy finetuning directly updates the generative model parameters. DPPO
[
39
]
formulates diffusion denoising as a multi-step MDP and applies PPO over reverse denoising transitions. ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends likelihood-based online optimization to flow policies by injecting stochasticity into deterministic flow trajectories. Forward process methods such as FPO
[
34
]
and its extensions
[
54
]
instead construct policy-gradient objectives from flow matching losses, avoiding explicit marginal likelihood computation. Reinforced finetuning has also been extended to VLA policies, with
[
11
,
51
]
combining offline value learning and online policy optimization for real-world manipulation. RoboFFT belongs to the full policy finetuning family, but performs PPO-style optimization through the forward noising process, providing a unified framework for diffusion, flow, and VLA policies.

article.headline: 生成式机器人策略的前向过程强化学习微调
article.lede: RoboFFT 用前向加噪的匹配损失构造替代策略比率，使扩散与流策略无需显式似然即可做 PPO 式在线微调。
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配策略能从示教中学到多模态动作分布，但纯模仿学习受限于示教质量、协变量偏移与部署时的状态覆盖不足。用在线强化学习继续提升是自然选择，然而这类策略的动作似然不可解析，PPO 等策略梯度目标难以直接套用。已有做法把逆向去噪链建模为多步 MDP，但计算与显存开销大，长采样链还容易带来梯度不稳。
article.method: RoboFFT 对 rollout 采样得到的动作做前向加噪，复用预训练时的加权分数/流匹配损失作为替代负对数似然，用 exp(旧策略损失−当前策略损失) 构造策略比率，接入 PPO 的裁剪目标。针对确定性流采样缺乏随机性，作者向采样过程注入噪声，改成 Euler-Maruyama SDE 采样器以提供可控探索；该采样器只用于采集动作，不参与似然计算。实现上还加入蒙特卡洛估计、比率温度标定，以及针对扩散策略的 Δlog-SNR 加权、锚点正则和负优势折扣等稳定化设计。
article.results: 在 Robomimic 的 Lift、Can、Square、Transport 四个稀疏奖励任务（state 与 pixel 两种输入）上，RoboFFT 的成功率与逆向过程基线相当或更好，在 Square、Transport 等更难任务上提升更稳。效率方面，RoboFFT-F 相对 ReinFlow 取得平均 1.53× 的单轮训练加速，RoboFFT-D 在四个 state 任务上相对 DPPO 平均加速 38.0×（其蒙特卡洛样本数取 N_mc=16）。在 LIBERO-Object 与 LIBERO-Spatial 上，该方法可微调 3.3B 参数的 π0 VLA 策略并优于预训练策略、与 πRL 相当。真机四任务各测试 20 次：pick eggplant 由预训练 12/20 提升到离线 18/20、在线 20/20；peg insertion 10/20→19/20→20/20；Pour 9/20→15/20→18/20；cabinet retrieval 5/20→14/20→17/20；在 pick eggplant 上同数据预算的 BC Agg. 仅 14/20、DRWR 为 12/20。与 ReinFlow 式闭式参考比率相比，替代比率的 Spearman 秩相关约为 0.2，但相对误差在训练末期对至少 90% 的动作块低于 5%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把 RL 微调的目标拉回到与生成式预训练一致的匹配损失上，无需对整条去噪链反传即可做 PPO 式更新，为扩散、流与 VLA 策略提供了一条更省算力、更稳的后训练路径。
article.limitations: 匹配损失只是真实对数似然的替代，其尺度随噪声调度、动作维度和策略结构变化，仍需温度标定等额外校准，且与参考比率的排序相关性仅约 0.2，说明二者并不严格对应。框架依赖 on-policy PPO，数据效率有限、无法充分复用历史轨迹，真机部署需迭代采集与离线重训，单机器人场景下仍较耗时。
article.figure_caption_zh: RoboFFT 流程：先用遥操作数据以分数/流匹配损失预训练策略，用 SDE 采样器在线生成动作并接收环境奖励，再对动作前向加噪、复用匹配损失作为替代似然完成 PPO 式更新。

The pretrained policy then generates actions using an SDE sampler and receives reward feedback from the environment. page_papers.title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
page_papers.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes. The source code is publicly available at https://mias.group/MaSS.
page_papers.content:
Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
Mengtan Zhang   Yuchuan Cui   Yu Ma   Zizhan Guo   Wei Ye   Rui FanTongji University
Abstract
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes.
The source code is publicly available at
https://mias.group/MaSS
.

Beyond (a) achieving SoTA performance across diverse datasets with a unified model, MaSS is the first SSMDE method to (b) effectively benefit from increased data diversity and (c) exhibit remarkable generalizability to entirely out-of-distribution scenes.
1
Introduction
The fundamental advantage of self-supervised learning lies in its potential to leverage ubiquitous unlabeled data for scalable model training. However, most existing self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SSMDE) research
[
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
]
is predominantly confined to training models individually on single datasets or scenarios, leaving much of this potential unexplored. Recent efforts have attempted to directly train models with existing SSMDE methods on large-scale video sequences curated from online platforms
[
6
,
7
]
, as well as to incorporate vision foundation models (VFMs) as backbones
[
8
,
7
]
. Despite these advances, overall performance improvements remain limited. As demonstrated by our preliminary experiments (see Fig.
1
(b)), when existing methods are trained simultaneously on diverse monocular video data (
e.g.
, indoor, outdoor, dynamic, and adverse weather scenarios), they fail to benefit mutually from the increased diversity and do not exhibit improved generalization to out-of-distribution scenes. Instead, we observe a performance decline compared to models trained individually on a single dataset. This observation demonstrates that existing SSMDE methods have not yet achieved effective scalability to diverse data.
This study begins by investigating the challenges that arise when SSMDE is exposed to diverse data distributions during training. It is worth noting that the novel-view synthesis-based supervision inevitably introduces noisy and artifact-laden supervisory signals in scenarios involving occlusions, textureless regions, and illumination changes
[
9
,
10
]
. Even setting aside such noise, the gradients induced by self-supervised losses often fail to reflect depth errors faithfully
[
4
]
. As a result, the optimization process is inherently prone to local minima, leading to poor convergence stability
[
4
]
. Although these challenges frequently occur during self-supervised training, existing methods can still achieve reasonable accuracy on a single, homogeneous dataset
[
3
]
. This is largely because the network can exploit the structural bias inherent to that dataset, thereby compensating for weak supervision. The key evidence we find is that under the existing SSMDE framework, the coarsest, high-level feature of the depth encoder does not capture depth-related cues, such as the foreground–background relation and perspective geometry. Instead, it primarily reflects the dataset-specific structural biases. When training on diverse datasets, different data domains often require the model to learn inconsistent structural biases for their respective convergence, leading to the observed performance drop.
These findings motivate us to explicitly guide the network to learn a robust, generalized scene-structure representation for depth decoding. Based on this core idea, we develop the
MaSS
framework that
Ma
ke
S
elf-supervised depth learning
S
calable to diverse data. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM through a bidirectional interaction architecture, drawing inspiration from
[
11
]
. In this design, the depth encoder focuses on extracting geometric cues that are difficult to recover from VFM features
[
8
]
. The interacted VFM features are then fed into two feature projectors to reconstruct complementary, collapse-free representations under explicit constraints and learning objectives. Specifically, one projector is adapted to learn a contextual representation informative for depth estimation, such as object-level spatial relationships, while retaining generalized semantics with the original VFM features as anchors. The other projector is then constrained to be decoupled from the contextual one, thereby reserving its representational capacity for scene structure.
To explicitly define this representation, we introduce a scene-structure discrimination objective via contrastive learning. This objective organizes the feature space based on scene layout similarity, which is measured by the histogram distribution of predicted depth. Driven by this objective, the second projector learns transferable structural representations that capture global scene layout and perspective geometry, rather than dataset-specific biases. Together, these two complementary representations enable more reliable depth predictions while reducing their reliance on dataset-specific biases.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that MaSS outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SoTA) self-supervised methods by a large margin (as presented in Fig.
1
(a)) and achieves accuracy comparable to certain supervised depth foundation models. Moreover, MaSS represents the first self-supervised approach to achieve clear performance gains from increasing the diversity of training data (Fig.
1
(b)), resulting in notable generalizability improvements particularly on out-of-distribution scenes (Fig.
1
(c)).
2
Related Works
To alleviate the reliance on extensive ground-truth data in monocular depth estimation (MDE), SSMDE from monocular video, first introduced in the study
[
12
]
, has attracted growing attention. Within this paradigm, improvements have focused on enhancing photometric supervision
[
1
]
, addressing scale inconsistency
[
13
]
, and incorporating additional visual cues to handle occlusions and dynamic scenes
[
14
,
3
,
15
,
16
,
4
]
.
Though significant progress has been made, these SSMDE methods are typically trained on single domains with limited-scale datasets and rely on task-specific network architectures
[
17
,
18
,
19
,
20
]
. The study
[
21
]
first demonstrates the feasibility of self-supervised depth learning from heterogeneous in-the-wild videos by jointly estimating depth, camera motion, object motion, and camera intrinsics. With the rise of VFMs
[
22
,
23
]
, increasing efforts have been devoted to developing depth foundation models (DFMs)
[
24
,
25
,
26
]
trained on large-scale annotated data, achieving strong performance and generalization.
Building upon this trend, recent studies
[
6
,
7
]
have taken initial steps toward scaling SSMDE training, while the others
[
9
,
27
,
5
]
demonstrate that developing DFMs in a self-supervised fashion requires not only harnessing the large pretrained models’ capacity, but also addressing challenges unique to self-supervised learning. Among them, cross-domain learning conflicts under mixed-domain training pose a fundamental yet underexplored obstacle to scalability, which this work primarily aims to address.
Three lines of research inform our approach. The first draws on pretrained knowledge to improve depth representations. For example, the study
[
28
]
uses a pretrained semantic network to guide the learning of geometric features. The studies
[
29
,
30
]
further emphasize preserving transferable pretrained representations during adaptation. The second focuses on organizing depth representations. The prior arts
[
31
,
32
,
33
,
27
]
have introduced contrastive objectives that structure the feature space according to weather variations, color or geometric consistency, historical predictions, and relationships guided by language. The third conditions depth prediction distributions on scene characteristics to account for domain shifts. For example, the study
[
34
]
conditions these distributions on scene categories. Drawing on these insights, MaSS explicitly decouples contextual and structural representations, preserves contextual relationships derived from VFMs, and adaptively organizes structural features according to similarities in scene layout. Depth prediction is then conditioned on the resulting structural representations to reduce learning conflicts across domains.

3
Methodology
SSMDE models are prone to learning dataset-specific inductive biases and struggle to generalize across varying depth distributions during both training and inference. For example, Fig.
1
(c) presents depth predictions on out-of-distribution indoor and outdoor scenes from two representative self-supervised depth models
[
3
,
4
]
, trained on the NYUv2
[
35
]
and KITTI
[
36
]
datasets, respectively. It can be observed that the model trained on driving scenes tends to predict depth with a vanishing point, while the model trained on small rooms fails to capture the more uniform depth distributions in large halls. To find the source of such inductive biases, we investigate the internal feature representations. As shown in Fig.
2
(a), the DepthNet encoder
[
4
]
trained on driving data produces feature activation maps with a consistent low-activation region. This pattern closely resembles the biased depth predictions in Fig.
1
(c) and fails to reflect variations aligned with the actual scene geometry. These results indicate that the dataset-specific inductive biases are already embedded in the intermediate representations. The above findings inspire us with a possible solution to make self-supervised learning scalable: explicitly guide the network to learn robust, generalized structural representations that are discriminative of scene layout before decoding depth.
Figure 3:
The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework.
MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.

Such misalignment suggests that entangling contextual and structural features within a single representation pathway may lead to representational conflict and collapse.
To address this issue, we decouple contextual and structural representations using two specialized feature projectors.

Mixed dataset training.
While our models achieve strong results when trained on individual datasets, such settings do not reflect the scalability challenges posed by large-scale and diverse training data, which constitute the primary focus of this work.
To this end, we further conduct comparative experiments in a mixed-dataset training setting. Specifically, each training batch is assembled by randomly sampling data from four datasets, thereby simulating a realistic, large-scale training scenario with substantial data diversity. To maintain a comparable number of training iterations to the individual-dataset setting, the number of training epochs is reduced to one-third. Under this setting, we reproduce several SoTA methods

In contrast, our method consistently achieves clear performance improvements.

4.4
Ablation Study
Efficacy of each innovative component.
To verify that the three key components of MaSS for learning generalizable structural representations are all indispensable, we conduct ablation studies in Table
4
(a).
Removing (a1) the contrastive learning objective eliminates explicit supervision for structural representation learning, leading to a significant performance drop, particularly on zero-shot datasets.
Removing (a2) the specialized structural pathway for representation decoupling prevents the model from preserving contextual information while learning structure, resulting in consistent degradation across all datasets.
Removing (a3) the interaction architecture forces the model to learn structural representations directly from DINOv2 features, which lack sufficient geometric cues, and thus causes a substantial performance decline.
Superiority over alternative designs.
MaSS builds upon well-established components such as DINOv2
[
22
]
and ViT-Adapter
[
11
]
, making it important to verify that the superior performance stems from our design rather than from simply adopting these components. To this end, we compare MaSS with several plausible alternative configurations in Table
4
(b):
(b1) directly fine-tuning a DPT
[
59
]
head with a frozen pretrained DINOv2 backbone,
(b2) fully fine-tuning the entire DINOv2–DPT architecture, and
(b3) incorporating ViT-Adapter while fine-tuning both the adapter and the DPT head.
Results show that MaSS outperforms all these alternative designs by a large margin. This confirms our analysis that effective scaling of self-supervised depth learning requires explicitly modeling scene structure, rather than relying solely on stronger pretrained backbones.
Effect of VFM backbone.
As demonstrated in Table
4
(c), replacing the VFM backbone with a stronger self-supervised pretrained model (DINOv3
[
30
]
) leads to only marginal performance changes. This result corroborates our earlier analysis that pretrained VFMs in our framework mainly provide generalizable semantic priors and are not directly responsible for depth decoding.
This naturally raises a follow-up question: since pretrained depth or geometry foundation models encode rich geometric priors, can MaSS benefit from them, or even further enhance such models?
We investigate this question in the
Supplementary Material
.

5
Conclusion
This study revisited self-supervised depth estimation from the perspective of large-scale, mix-domain training and prediction,
recognizing that the model’s tendency to capture dataset-specific structural bias is the key barrier.
MaSS addressed this by coupling a depth encoder with a pretrained VFM and explicitly decoupling the structural representations from the contextual ones to learn scene-generalized structural representations via contrastive learning.
MaSS achieved SoTA accuracy and remarkable out-of-distribution generalization, demonstrating improved scalability with larger and more diverse data.

A.1
Details of Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures
In the main paper, we define a structural discrepancy metric to determine positive and negative samples within a training batch, thereby formulating a scene-structure discrimination objective for learning structural representations. To illustrate how the metric functions and how the objective guides representation learning, we present several quantitative examples in Fig.
S1
.
The key observations from Fig.
S1
can be summarized as follows:
(1) Our method does not trivially treat each sample as the sole positive instance, nor does it degenerate into discriminating samples based on coarse scene categories (
e.g.
, indoor vs. outdoor).
As shown in Fig.
S1
(a), Sample ① is an outdoor scene but is not considered positive relative to other outdoor samples; this is because its structural layout—a narrow passage flanked by cars and buildings—differs from more open outdoor environments. Fig.
S1
(b) provides an inverse case, where a wide-open outdoor scene (Sample ①) is correctly distinguished from narrow outdoor passages. These observations are further supplemented by Sample ⑥ in Fig.
S1
(c).
Moreover, our method captures shared structural properties across scene categories. For instance, in Fig.
S1
(d), the outdoor scene in Sample ⑥ forms positive pairs with multiple indoor samples due to their similar structure. Similarly, in Fig.
S1
(e), the indoor library aisle (Sample ①) is identified as positive relative to outdoor samples ③, ⑤, and ⑥, which share the “narrow corridor” structure. Meanwhile, it remains negative to the room scene of Sample ②. These results demonstrate that our model prioritizes underlying structural similarity over nominal scene labels.
(2) The hyperparameters of the proposed structural discrepancy metric, together with the masking strategy, effectively identify meaningful contrastive relationships. As visualized in the Discrepancy Metric and Pos./Neg. Mask columns, the resulting similarity maps align well with the expected structural relationships described in the above analysis. Meanwhile, the threshold used in our implementation effectively determines the positive and negative sample pairs accordingly.
(3) Finally, within the MaSS framework, the specialized pathway effectively learns structural representations that are discriminative with respect to different scene structures. This is evidenced by the strong consistency between the feature similarities of the learned structural representations and the in-batch structural discrepancy relationships computed from the predicted depth maps.

We provide a quantitative analysis of the data distributions across all datasets used in this work to better illustrate how our approach improves the scalability of self-supervised depth learning and enhances model generalizability.
As shown in Fig.
S2
, the training datasets (KITTI
[
36
]
, DDAD
[
46
]
, and NYUv2
[
35
]
) exhibit distinct depth distributions. These discrepancies arise from differences between indoor and outdoor environments, as well as variations in field of view (FoV) and sensor configurations during data acquisition.
In addition, Fig.
S3
presents the RGB distributions of the datasets. Since monocular depth estimation maps RGB inputs to depth outputs, diversity in both domains is crucial for robust generalization. Notably, while nuScenes shares a relatively similar depth distribution with KITTI, its RGB distribution differs significantly.
These observations help interpret the zero-shot evaluation results. For the zero-shot outdoor datasets (Waymo Open
[
48
]
, DrivingStereo
[
49
]
, and Cityscapes
[
50
]
), their depth distributions are similar to those of the driving datasets used for training, whereas their RGB distributions differ noticeably. This suggests that the limited generalization ability of previous methods is not primarily caused by differences in depth ranges. Instead, the performance degradation is largely attributed to appearance shifts, revealing the limited robustness of conventional encoder architectures with restricted pretraining. In contrast, our method learns robust and transferable contextual and structural representations from diverse appearance distributions, substantially improving generalization in depth estimation.
For the zero-shot indoor datasets (iBims-1
[
51
]
, SUN-RGBD
[
52
]
, and 7-Scenes
[
53
]
), both the depth and RGB distributions closely align with the NYUv2 training set. This relatively homogeneous distribution favors supervised depth foundation models, as similar scene statistics are already well represented in their large-scale training data. Consequently, these models have already learned similar RGB-to-depth mappings under ground-truth supervision, leading to a larger performance gap between supervised and self-supervised approaches on these datasets.
Finally, DIML
[
54
]
and DIODE
[
55
]
represent clear out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. As shown in Figs.
S2
and
S3
, they deviate substantially from the training data in both the input (RGB) and output (depth) domains, making them challenging benchmarks for evaluating the OOD generalization capability of depth estimation methods. Notably, on these datasets, our method achieves performance comparable to that of fully supervised depth foundation models.

B.3
Generalizability Evaluation on In-the-Wild Data.
While the previously discussed OOD datasets demonstrate the strong generalization capability of our model, their diversity and domain shift relative to the training data remain limited. To further evaluate robustness, we collect a set of in-the-wild images from online repositories and mobile photography, covering a wide range of real-world challenges.
As illustrated in Fig.
S4
, the first three rows (a–c) present unstructured natural scenes. Notably, (a) and (c) contain specular reflections on water surfaces, while (b) includes dense vegetation with high-frequency textures.
Rows (d–f) exhibit complex geometries and structures that differ significantly from standard urban or indoor benchmarks, such as the detailed roof tiles in (e) and the repetitive grid structure in (f).
Row (g) includes power lines to evaluate the model’s ability to estimate thin structures.
Rows (h–j) further evaluate model robustness under extreme lighting and motion blur conditions. In particular, row (j) presents a challenging case with strong visual ambiguity at a road junction caused by shadows and lighting effects.
Qualitative comparisons are conducted among SC-DepthV3
[
3

†

(trained on KITTI), and MaSS
†
. As shown in Fig.
S4
, SC-DepthV3 performs unsatisfactorily on complex and unseen structures and tends to interpret scenes with an indoor bias. When trained under the mixed-dataset setting, SC-DepthV3
†
further deteriorates, suffering from severe structural confusion caused by the diverse training data. Jasmine represents one of the strongest self-supervised generative depth models. Although it produces detailed predictions and exhibits improved generalization due to diffusion priors, extreme RGB domain shifts can cause the diffusion process to become unstable and produce depth predictions with significant errors. In contrast, our method remains robust across these challenging in-the-wild scenes, producing depth predictions with both fine-grained details and consistent structural layouts.

Qualitative monocular depth estimation results on in-the-wild, out-of-distribution data.
Figure S5:
Qualitative monocular reconstruction estimation results on in-the-wild, out-of-distribution data.
B.4
Geometric Fidelity Evaluation on In-the-Wild Data.
Since ground-truth depth is unavailable for these in-the-wild images, quantitative evaluation is infeasible. Instead, we assess the geometric correctness of the predicted depth through monocular 3D reconstruction.
We compare our method with two representative monocular reconstruction approaches, VGGT
[
38
]
and MoGe
[
62
]
. To evaluate geometric fidelity, we synthesize novel viewpoints with slight viewpoint changes relative to the original image. As shown in Fig.
S5
, VGGT produces relatively noisy depth maps on these in-the-wild scenes, leading to noticeable artifacts in the reconstructed geometry. MoGe represents one of the most robust monocular reconstruction foundation models, benefiting from strong geometric supervision during training, and achieves high-quality reconstructions in most cases, with only minor local inconsistencies observed in (b)-(d). Our method, benefiting from the inherent geometric constraints of self-supervised learning as well as effective scaling with diverse training data, achieves reconstruction results comparable to these prior approaches, with significantly less training data. These results highlight the potential of self-supervised methods for building versatile “DepthAnything”-style models from ubiquitous unlabeled data.
Appendix C
Discussion and Future Work
In addition to increasing the training data scale, as discussed in Sect.
4.5
, the scalability of SSMDE also depends on the availability of diverse and suitable training data.
Although self supervision enables learning from imagery collected in the wild, systematically curated datasets covering diverse scenes remain scarce. Existing methods therefore still rely heavily on commonly used datasets originally collected for supervised learning. Constraints imposed by data collection platforms (
e.g.
, vehicles, handheld devices, or UAVs), together with the high cost of sensor calibration and annotation, often limit these datasets to relatively homogeneous scenes, such as typical indoor rooms and common driving environments. This limited diversity may constrain the potential benefits of self-supervision. Such limited diversity may even reduce the potential advantages of self-supervised learning. Systematically curating large and diverse datasets from imagery collected in the wild is therefore a promising direction for advancing SSMDE and extending the benefits of self-supervision to other vision tasks.

article.headline: 解耦场景结构表征，让自监督深度估计可扩展
article.lede: MaSS 将深度编码器与冻结 DINOv2 双向交互，解耦上下文与结构表征，用场景布局对比学习判别结构，使自监督深度在混
article.problem: 自监督单目深度估计理论上可随无标注数据扩展，但现有方法多在单一数据集上训练，一旦混合室内、室外、动态与恶劣天气数据联合训练，性能反而下降，也无法泛化到分布外场景。作者发现，根源在于自监督信号本身噪声大，网络转而依赖数据集特有的结构偏置：深度编码器最粗的高层特征并不编码前后景关系与透视几何，而主要反映数据集偏置，不同域要求的偏置互相冲突。
article.method: MaSS 用 ViT-Adapter 式的双向交互模块把可训练深度编码器与冻结的 DINOv2 ViT-B/14 连接起来，再用一对“锚定—解耦”投影器，把交互后的 VFM 特征分成上下文表征与结构表征两条通路：前者以原始 VFM 特征的样本间语义关系为锚以保持语义，后者被约束与前者解耦，专门承载几何信息。为了让结构通路学到可迁移的场景布局，作者设计场景结构判别目标：先将预测深度图下采样 8 倍，用 20 个软分箱的直方图与对称 KL 散度衡量样本间布局差异，再以阈值 γ=0.95 构造正样本集，用多正样本 InfoNCE（温度 0.1）做对比学习。
article.results: 在 KITTI、DDAD、NYUv2、nuScenes 四个数据集上单独训练时，MaSS 的 Abs Rel 分别为 0.094、0.128、0.109、0.139，均优于此前自监督方法；在混合域训练下进一步降至 0.092、0.125、0.104、0.134（δ1 分别为 0.913、0.862、0.890、0.852）。作为对照，DCPI-Depth 混合训练后 NYUv2 的 Abs Rel 从 0.151 恶化到 0.331。在八个零样本数据集上，混合训练模型在 Waymo、DrivingStereo、Cityscapes、DIML 的 Abs Rel 为 0.123、0.100、0.103、0.104，在 DIODE 为 0.289。模型 93.2M 参数、81.6 GFLOPs、训练数据 150K，单张 RTX 4090、batch size 6 约需 2.5 天；再增加 5 万 TartanAir 样本后，作者报告在更具挑战的分布外域上 Abs Rel 与 δ1 平均改善 4.3% 与 3.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 自监督深度的核心卖点本应是无标注数据越多越好，但混合域训练一直掉点；这项工作把“数据集结构偏置”指认为可扩展性的具体瓶颈，并给出可操作的解耦加对比学习方案，为从无标注视频训练深度基础模型提供了一条不同于堆数据与换更强主干的路径。
article.limitations: 在标准室内数据集上，MaSS 仍明显落后于监督深度基础模型：iBims-1 的 Abs Rel 为 0.107，而 Depth Anything V2 为 0.045；SUN-RGBD 为 0.127 对 0.062；7-Scenes 为 0.120 对 0.074。可扩展性证据也只到 200K 样本，远小于 Depth Anything V2 的 62M，作者自己称仅为初步证据；此外训练需先跑一个 epoch 的初始化阶段，且 Median 与 LSQ* 对齐协议的差异会影响跨方法比较。
article.figure_caption_zh: MaSS 框架总览：深度编码器与冻结的预训练 VFM 通过双向交互模块相连，交互后的 VFM 特征经一对锚定—解耦投影器生成无坍缩的上下文与结构表征。

figure.caption: The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.

page_papers.title: HandsOn: A Large-Scale Simulation Benchmark for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation
page_papers.abstract: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes. The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations. Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer. Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success. Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks. HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands.
We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation.
It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes.
The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations.
Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer.
Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success.
Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using
move_eef
for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials.
Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks.
HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.
